question: How does uncertainty in data affect standard quadratic optimization problems?
answer: Uncertainty in data affects StQPs by introducing variability in the matrix used for calculations. This uncertainty can be managed through robust optimization techniques, where an uncertainty set encapsulates all known information about uncertain parameters. The decision-maker must ensure that these parameters remain within this set to avoid violations.

evidence.text:
## 1 Introduction

The standard quadratic optimization problem (StQP) consists of minimizing a quadratic form over the standard simplex

$$
\ell(\mathrm{Q}):=\min _{\mathbf{x} \in \Delta} \mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathrm{Q} \mathbf{x}
$$

where $\mathrm{Q} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is a symmetric matrix, and $\Delta:=\left\{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}: \mathbf{e}^{\top} \mathbf{x}=1, \mathbf{x} \geq \mathbf{0}\right\}$ is the standard simplex in $\mathbb{R}^{n}$. Here $\mathbf{e} \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the vector of all ones and ${ }^{\top}$ denotes transposition; $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{n}}:=\operatorname{Diag}(\mathbf{e})$ denotes the $n \times n$ identity matrix. The objective function is already in general form since any general quadratic objective function $\mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x}+2 \mathbf{c}^{\top} \mathbf{x}$ can be written in homogeneous form by defining the symmetric matrix $\mathrm{Q}:=\mathrm{A}+\mathbf{c e}^{\top}+\mathbf{e c}^{\top}$.

Even though the StQP is simple - minimization of a quadratic function under linear constraints - it is NP-hard without assumptions on the definiteness of the matrix Q. Observe that convex, but also concave instances are polynomially solvable, the latter even in closed form: $\ell(\mathrm{Q})=\min _{i} \mathrm{Q}_{i i}$. Note that $\ell(\mathrm{Q}) \geq 0$ is possible even if Q is not positive semi-definite. In fact, the condition $\ell(\mathrm{Q}) \geq 0$ characterizes copositivity [17] of Q , and follows if no entry of Q is negative (as, e.g. in the instances $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{i}}^{(\text {nom })}$ generated in Section 4 below).

Irrespective of the sign of $\ell(Q)$, its calculation can be hard for indefinite instances: indeed, Motzkin and Straus [15] showed that the maximum clique problem, a well-known NP-hard problem, can be formulated as an StQP. Hence, the StQP is often regarded as the simplest of hard problems [7] since it contains the simplest non-convex objective function which is a quadratic form, and the simplest polytope as feasible set. Still, the StQP is a very flexible optimization class that allows for modelling of diverse problems such as portfolio optimization problems [14], pairwise clustering [16] and replicator dynamics [4]. Despite of its continuous optimization nature, it also serves to model discrete problems like the maximum-clique problem as well, as witnessed by above references.

The only data required to fully characterize an StQP is the data matrix Q. However, in many applications the matrix Q is uncertain. StQPs with uncertain data have been explored in the literature. One of the most natural ways to deal with uncertain objective functions is via robust optimization [2]. In that paradigm, the decision-maker has to decide upon an uncertainty set $\mathcal{U}$ which encapsulates all the known information about the uncertain parameter. The uncertain parameter (in this case the uncertain data matrix Q ) is supposed to reside within the uncertainty set $\mathcal{U}$, as violations are not allowed [10]. Bomze et al. [6] introduced the concept of a robust standard quadratic optimization problem, which they formulated as a minimax problem

$$
\min _{\mathbf{x} \in \Delta} \max _{\mathrm{U} \in \mathcal{U}} \mathbf{x}^{\top}\left(\mathrm{Q}^{(\mathrm{nom})}+\mathrm{U}\right) \mathbf{x}
$$

with uncertainty set $\mathcal{U}$. The uncertain matrix Q consisted of a nominal part $\mathrm{Q}^{(\text {nom })}$ and an uncertain additive perturbation $U$. In their paper, the authors investigated various uncertainty sets and proved that the copositive relaxation gap is equal to the minimax gap. Moreover, they observed that the robust StQP (1) reduces to a deterministic StQP for many frequently used types of uncertainty sets $\mathcal{U}$.

Passing from a robust to stochastic setting with known expectation, a natural alternative to get rid of the uncertainty is the here-and-now problem (random quantities are designated by a tilde sign)

$$
\min _{\mathbf{x} \in \Delta} \mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{x}^{\top} \tilde{\mathbf{Q}} \mathbf{x}\right]=\min _{\mathbf{x} \in \Delta} \mathbf{x}^{\top} \mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}] \mathbf{x}
$$

where the uncertain matrix $\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}$ is replaced by its expectation $\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}]$.
Bomze et al. [5] investigated a two-stage setting where the principal submatrix was deterministic and the rest of the entries followed a known probability distribution. In this paper, we propose an alternative to the here-and-now problem. As opposed to [5] we will assume that the full data matrix $\tilde{\mathbf{Q}}$ is random according to a known distribution $\mathbb{P}$. The purpose of this note is to introduce, apparently for the first time, chance constraints for this problem class by introduction of an epigraphic variable, and moreover, to present a deterministic equivalent StQP formulation under reasonable distributional assumptions. Furthermore, we establish a close connection of our new model to robustness with Frobenius ball uncertainty sets.

question: Is there a statistically significant difference in labor productivity spillovers between Low and High peers?
answer: No, there is no statistically significant difference between the strength of spillovers of Low and High peers for labor productivity.

# 6.2 Peers characteristics 

Next, we address the estimation of heterogeneous effects derived from customer and supplier characteristics. To this end, we rely on the following regression:

$$
y_{i h c, t}=\sum_{v \in\{L o w, H i g h\}}\left(\beta_{D}^{*} \bar{y}_{i h c, t-1}^{D, v}+\beta_{U}^{*} \bar{y}_{i h c, t-1}^{U, v}\right)+\mu_{i, t}+\eta_{h c, t}+\varepsilon_{i h c, t}
$$

where $\bar{y}_{i h c, t-1}^{D, v}$ and $\bar{y}_{i h c, t-1}^{U, v}$ for a given firm $i$ denote the number of importing suppliers and customers of firm $i$ in category $v \in\{L o w, H i g h\}$ (i.e., with the value of the considered characteristic being lower or higher than the median, respectively) divided by the total number of suppliers and customers of firm $i$, respectively. Therefore, the sum of the value of these variables computed by category at the supplier (customer) side equals the value of the downstream (upstream) spillover variable used in the main analysis. ${ }^{28}$ This

We find that the spillovers, in general, tend to be stronger when coming from smaller and less productive firms. That is, big and more productive firms are relatively worse at disseminating information about importing (or are more capable of shielding such information). The only exception is the labour productivity of customers, for which we do not find a statistically significant difference between the strength of spillovers of Low and High peers. This general pattern contrasts with the findings obtained by the literature on location spillovers in imports (Bisztray et al., 2018; Békés and Harasztosi, 2020; Corcos and Haller, 2023) that arrive at the opposite conclusion. Regarding the role of wholesalers as peers, it is important to consider that a firm sourcing intermediate inputs from an importing wholesaler might reflect a pre-existing intent to import those inputs directly, hindered by barriers such as fixed costs or uncertainty about the quality of imported goods. Consequently, estimating relatively stronger downstream import spillovers when providers are wholesalers could indicate that this spurious mechanism is contaminating the significant downstream effects estimated in Section 5. However, the results in the last column of Table 4 show that firms do not learn from suppliers that are wholesalers, while they do learn from both wholesaler and non-wholesaler customers, thus effectively ruling out the aforementioned spurious mechanism.

question: How does an auction-managed AMM differ from traditional AMMs?
answer: An auction-managed AMM introduces a mechanism where a censorship-resistant onchain auction determines who temporarily acts as the "pool manager" for a constant-product AMM. This pool manager sets swap fee rates and captures fees, allowing for dynamic adaptation to market conditions, unlike traditional fixed-fee AMMs.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

Automated market makers (AMMs) have emerged as the dominant market mechanism for trading on decentralized exchanges implemented on blockchains. This paper presents a single mechanism that targets two important unsolved problems for AMMs: reducing losses to informed orderflow, and maximizing revenue from uninformed orderflow. The "auction-managed AMM" works by running a censorship-resistant onchain auction for the right to temporarily act as "pool manager" for a constant-product AMM. The pool manager sets the swap fee rate on the pool, and also receives the accrued fees from swaps. The pool manager can exclusively capture some arbitrage by trading against the pool in response to small price movements, and also can set swap fees incorporating price sensitivity of retail orderflow and adapting to changing market conditions, with the benefits from both ultimately accruing to liquidity providers. Liquidity providers can enter and exit the pool freely in response to changing rent, though they must pay a small fee on withdrawal. We prove that under certain assumptions, this AMM should have higher liquidity in equilibrium than any standard, fixed-fee AMM.

question: How has differential item functioning (DIF) analysis evolved in recent years?
answer: DIF analysis has seen significant progress recently, with more research focusing on using it to investigate measurement equivalence. Advanced methodologies, particularly multilevel models, have been developed to improve the accuracy of DIF estimation compared to traditional single-level models.

evidence.text:
# 1 Introduction 

To examine the disproportionate impact of health interventions or other determinants on health outcomes for certain populations, including disadvantaged minorities, it is crucial to establish measurement equivalence when evaluating outcomes across groups differing in gender, ethnicity, and other demographic factors. While validating psychometric instruments has been a routine practice in research, critical evaluations of measurement equivalence, particularly through differential item functioning (DIF) analysis, have historically been limited [1]. In recent years, however, there has been significant progress in this area, with a growing body of research employing DIF analysis to investigate measurement equivalence [e.g., 2-7].

This growing research underscores the need for continued evaluation of health constructs and measures to ensure fairness and validity in assessing health outcomes for diverse populations. It is worth noting that some health studies did not clearly describe the method used for DIF analysis [e.g., 3], and conventional DIF methods based on single-level models were frequently used to analyze health survey data with a nesting structure [e.g., 2], for which recent DIF methods based on multilevel models are better alternatives in terms of accuracy of DIF estimation. By employing advanced methodologies for DIF, researchers can better evaluate health measures to ensure fairness and validity in assessing health outcomes for diverse populations.

question: What does score-based method minimize during training?
answer: Score-based methods minimize the expected squared distance between the score function of the true distribution and the score function given by the model.

evidence.text:
## A. 2 Energy-Based Model Training

Energy-Based Models are a class of parametric unnormalised probabilistic models of the form $\exp \left(-E_{\theta}\right)$ originally inspired by statistical physics. Despite their flexibility, energy-based models have not seen widespread adoption in machine learning applications due to the challenges involved in training them. In particular, because the normalising constant is intractable, these models cannot be optimised using maximum likelihood estimation. Alternative training methods have been explore such as contrastive divergence (Hinton et al., 2006), score-based methods (Hyvärinen, 2005; Vincent, 2011; Song and Ermon, 2020) and energy discrepancy (Schröder et al., 2023).

Contrastive divergence (Hinton et al., 2006) is a method that approximates the gradient of the log-likelihood via short runs of a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) process. Although using short MCMC runs greatly reduces both the computation per gradient step and the variance of the estimated gradient (Carreira-Perpiñán and Hinton, 2005), it comes at the cost of producing poor approximations of the energy function. This issue arises, in part, because contrastive divergence is not the gradient of any objective function (Sutskever and Tieleman, 2010; Bengio and Delalleau, 2009) which significantly limits the theoretical understanding of its convergence.

Score-based methods provide an alternative way for training based on minimising the expected squared distance of the score function of the true distribution $\nabla_{x} \log p_{\text {data }}$ and the score function given by the model $\nabla_{x} \log p_{\theta}$, which by definition are independent of the normalising constant (Hyvärinen, 2005; Vincent, 2011). However, these methods only use gradient information and are therefore short-sighted (Song and Ermon, 2019) as they do not resolve the global characteristics of the distribution when limited data are available.

Energy discrepancy attempts to solve the problems of the two previous methods by proposing a new loss function that compares the data distribution and the energy-based model (Schröder et al., 2023). This loss is given by

$$
\mathcal{L}_{t, M, w}(\theta):=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \left(\frac{w}{M}+\frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^{M} \exp \left(E_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{z}_{i}\right)-E_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{z}_{i}+\sqrt{t} \boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}+\sqrt{t} \boldsymbol{\xi}_{i, j}^{\prime}\right)\right)\right)
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\xi}_{i, j}^{\prime} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbf{I}_{d_{z_{0}}+d_{z_{0}}}\right)$ are i.i.d. random variables and $t, M, w$ are tunable hyper-parameters. Energy discrepancy depends only on the energy function and is independent of the scores and MCMC samples from the energy-based model.

We applied these three methods to train the energy-based model in our framework, obtaining the best results with the latter. Notably, for the 2D examples, both contrastive divergence and score matching failed to converge.

question: Does regularity imply subfitness in non-distributive lattices?
answer: No, in non-distributive lattices, regularity no longer implies subfitness.

evidence.text:
# 5. Regularity 

In this section we characterize when the four completions are regular. For distributive lattices, regularity is a natural strengthening of subfitness. As we saw above, subfitness of the canonical completion is equivalent to the lattice being Boolean. As we will see below, regularity yields the same result for the ideal completion. A more subtle result occurs for the Bruns-Lakser completion. The situation for the Dedekind-MacNeille completion is further complicated by the fact that the latter need not be distributive. Regular lattices behave very differently in the non-distributive setting; in particular, regularity no longer implies subfitness. This will be discussed in more detail in a forthcoming paper. Here we will restrict our attention to Dedekind-MacNeille completions that are distributive.

The next definition is well known for frames (see, e.g., [PP12, Sec. V.5]) and generalizes directly to bounded lattices.

Definition 5.1. Let $A$ be a bounded lattice.
(1) For $a, b \in A, a$ is rather below (well inside) $b$, written $a \prec b$, provided there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$.
(2) $A$ is regular if $a \nless b$ implies the existence of $c \in A$ such that $c \prec a$ but $c \nless b$.

Remark 5.2.
(1) If $a$ has the pseudocomplement $a^{*}$, then $a \prec b$ iff $a^{*} \vee b=1$.
(2) A is regular iff every element is the join of elements rather below it. This is the usual definition of regularity in frames, but the above definition is more appealing for arbitrary bounded lattices. Observe that while arbitrary joins may not exist in $A \in$ DLat, if $A$ is regular then the join of $\{b \in A: b \prec a\}$ is $a$, so this join does exist for every $a \in A$.
(3) Every Boolean lattice is regular and in [BMPWW17, p. 360] it is shown that every regular distributive lattice is subfit. In a forthcoming paper we will show that this is no longer true for non-distributive lattices.

Our first goal is to characterize when distributive lattices are regular using Priestley duality. We do so by generalizing some existing results for frames, proved in [BGJ16, Lem. 3.3, 3.6]. Since pseudocomplements may not exist in an arbitrary distributive lattice, the proofs below are somewhat more involved. We start by characterizing the rather below relation.

Lemma 5.3. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X ,

$$
a \prec b \text { iff } \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})
$$

Proof. First suppose $a \prec b$. Then there is $c \in A$ such that $a \wedge c=0$ and $b \vee c=1$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ is an upset, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$. Thus, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$.

Conversely, suppose $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Since $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ is a closed downset, it is the intersection of clopen downsets containing it (see Fact 2.6). But then by compactness, there is a clopen downset D such that $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{D} \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Let $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ be such that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathrm{D}$. Then $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Thus, $\mathfrak{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$, and hence $\mathfrak{a} \prec \mathfrak{b}$.

Following [BGJ16, Def. 3.4], for each $V \in L(X)$, define the regular part of $V$ to be

$$
\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{~V})=\bigcup\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{~L}(\mathrm{X}): \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{~V}\}
$$

For simplicity, we abbreviate the regular part of $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ by $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$.
Proposition 5.4. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X , the following are equivalent:
(1) A is regular.
(2) $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ for each $\mathfrak{a} \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $a \in A$. Take $x \in s(a)$ and let $U$ be a clopen neighborhood of $x$ in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. We must show that $U \cap R_{a} \neq \varnothing$. Since $U$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, there are $\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{x} \in \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \subseteq \mathrm{U}$ (see Fact 2.6(1)). Without loss of generality we may assume that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ (by intersecting $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ with $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ ). Because $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \neq \varnothing$, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$, so $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{d}$. Since A is regular, there is $\mathrm{e} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{e} \prec \mathrm{c}$ and $\mathrm{e} \nless \mathrm{d}$. By Lemma 5.3, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$, so $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{c}} \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$. Thus, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}} \cap(\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})) \neq \varnothing$, so $R_{a} \cap U \neq \varnothing$, and hence $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1): Let $a \nless b$. Then $s(a) \nsubseteq s(b)$, so $R_{a} \nsubseteq s(b)$ since $R_{a}$ is dense in $s(a)$. Therefore, there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\downarrow \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{a})$ and $\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{b})$. Thus, $\mathrm{c} \prec \mathrm{a}$ (by Lemma 5.3) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, yielding that A is regular.

We next give a general characterization, akin to Theorem 4.2, of when regularity is preserved and/or reflected when moving between $A$ and $B$, where $A$ is a bounded sublattice of B. We write $\prec_{A}$ or $\prec_{B}$ to emphasize which rather below relation is being used. Clearly $a \prec_{A} b$ implies $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $a, b \in A$, however the converse is not true in general. Because of this, the proposition below requires an extra assumption. As in Theorem 4.2, distributivity plays no rôle.

Proposition 5.5. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B. Suppose that $a \prec_{A} b$ iff $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A}$.
(1) If A is join-dense in B and B is regular then A is regular.
(2) If A is both join- and meet-dense in B and A is regular then B is regular.

Proof. (1) Let $a, b \in A$ with $a \nless b$. Since $B$ is regular, there is $x \in B$ with $x \prec_{B} a$ and $x \nless b$. Because $A$ is join-dense in $B$, there is $c \in A$ with $c \leqslant x$ and $c \nless b$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \leqslant \mathrm{x} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, and hence $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Thus, A is regular.
(2) Let $x, y \in B$ with $x \nless y$. Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $B$, there are $a, b \in A$ such that $a \leqslant x, y \leqslant b$, and $a \nless b$. Because $A$ is regular, there is $c \in A$ with $c \prec_{A} a$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{x}$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{y}$. Thus, B is regular.

Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $\mathcal{D M A}$, one could expect that regularity is both preserved and reflected by the Dedekind-MacNeille completion, but this is not the case since the additional assumption in Proposition 5.5 may not be satisfied. We again emphasize that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is not always distributive and hence regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ need not imply subfitness. Thus, we make the blanket assumption that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive. While this does not necessarily imply that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, it is indeed the case provided $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.

Proposition 5.6. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. Then regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, and hence $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

Proof. If $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive, by [BMPWW17, p. 360] regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies subfitness of $\mathcal{D M A}$, and consequently subfitness of $A$ by Corollary 4.3. But then $A$ is proHeyting by Lemma 4.6. Hence, $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame and $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7.

The above proposition yields the following characterization of when a distributive Dede-kind-MacNeille completion is regular.

Proposition 5.7. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.
(2) A is subfit and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(3) A is proHeyting and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): That $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular follows from Proposition 5.6. Regular implies subfit for distributive lattices, so $\mathcal{D} M A$ is subfit, but then so is $A$ by Corollary 4.3.
$(2) \Rightarrow(3):$ This follows from Lemma 4.6.
$(3) \Rightarrow(1):$ This follows from Proposition 3.7.
We next concentrate on characterizing when $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular. Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is a frame, the rather below relation is conveniently expressible in terms of the pseudocomplement (see Remark 5.2(1)). We use Priestley duality to describe this pseudocomplement. By Theorem 2.10(2), $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong B L(X)$ and by Remark 2.11, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is the sublocale of $\mathrm{OpUp}(\mathrm{X})$ given by the nucleus $\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}$. Since the pseudocomplement in $\mathrm{OpUp}(\mathrm{X})$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{U}^{*}=\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})
$$

the pseudocomplement in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is given by

$$
\neg \mathrm{U}=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}\left(\mathrm{U}^{*}\right)=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}))
$$

Lemma 5.8. Let $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
(1) int $\downarrow$ clint $\downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})=\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})$.
(2) $\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} V$ iff $\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{V})$.
(3) If $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$, then $\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{V}$ iff $\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{V}$.

Proof. (1) The right-to-left inclusion is obvious. For the other inclusion, observe that

$$
\text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl} \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})
$$

because $\downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})$ is a closed downset (see Fact 2.6(4)).
(2) Recalling how joins are defined in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ (see Remark 2.11) and that $\mathrm{cl}_{1}=\downarrow \mathrm{cl}$, by (1) we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{~V} & \Leftrightarrow \neg \mathrm{U} \vee \mathrm{~V}=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{cl}(\neg \mathrm{U}) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{clint}_{1} \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow(\mathrm{X} \backslash \text { int } \mathrm{cl}_{1} \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{clint} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V}) \\
& \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V}) .
\end{aligned}
$$

(3) This follows from (2) since $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$ imply $\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})=\mathrm{U}$ and $\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{V})=\mathrm{V}$.

This allows us to see that when restricted to $A$, the rather below relations on $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ and $p \mathcal{H}(A$ coincide.
Proposition 5.9. For each $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b} \in \mathrm{A}, \mathfrak{a} \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} \mathfrak{b}$ iff $\mathfrak{a} \prec_{p \mathcal{H}(A} \mathfrak{b}$.
Proof. First suppose that $\mathfrak{a} \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} \mathfrak{b}$. Let $X$ be the Priestley space of $A$. Then int $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$ by Lemma 5.8(3). Let $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. Then $\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ by Lemma 3.14, and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathrm{U}=\varnothing$. Moreover, since int $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$, we have

$$
\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\{\mathrm{X} \backslash \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})\} \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathrm{X}
$$

Therefore, $U \vee_{p H(X)} s(b)=X$, so $s(a)$ is rather below $s(b)$ in $p H(X)$, and hence $a \prec_{p \cap A} b$ by Proposition 3.15 .

For the converse, suppose that $a \prec_{p \cap A} b$. By Proposition 3.15, there is $U \in \mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $s(a) \cap U=\varnothing$ and $U \vee_{p H(X)} s(b)=X$. The former gives $\downarrow s(a) \cap U=\varnothing$, so $U \subseteq X \backslash \downarrow s(a)$. The latter yields that $c l(U) \cup s(b)=X$. Therefore, $c l(X \backslash \downarrow s(a)) \cup s(b)=X$, so $(X \backslash \operatorname{int} \downarrow s(a)) \cup s(b)=X$, and hence int $\downarrow s(a) \subseteq s(b)$. Thus, $a \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} b$ by Lemma 5.8(3).

In order to show that regularity of $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is equivalent to that of $p \mathcal{O}(A$, we require the following general fact.

Proposition 5.10. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B . If A is join-dense in B , then the following are equivalent:
(1) B is regular.
(2) $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$ for each $b \in B$.
(3) $a=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} a\right\}$ for each $a \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $b \in B$. Since $B$ is regular, $b=\bigvee\left\{d \in B: d \prec_{B} b\right\}$ (see Remark 5.2(2)). Because A is join-dense in $B, d=\bigvee\{c \in A: c \leqslant d\}$. But $c \leqslant d \prec_{B} b$ implies $c \prec_{B} b$, so $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$
(2) $\Rightarrow$ (3): This is obvious.
(3) $\Rightarrow$ (1) Let $b \in B$. Since $A$ is join-dense in $B, b=\bigvee\left\{a \in A: a \leqslant b\right\}$. By assumption, $a=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} a\right\}$ for each $a \in A$. From $c \prec_{B} a \leqslant b$ it follows that $c \prec_{B} b$. Therefore, $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$, and hence $B$ is regular.

Theorem 5.11. For $A \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular iff $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is regular.
Proof. Let $a \in A$. Since $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is join-dense in $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$, it follows from Proposition 5.9 that $a=\bigvee_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A}\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} a\right\}$ iff $a=\bigvee_{p \mathcal{O}(A}\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{p \mathcal{O}(A} a\right\}$. But $A$ is join-dense in both $p \mathcal{O}(A$ and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$, and thus, by Proposition 5.10, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular iff $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is regular.

We next give a characterization of when $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular akin to Proposition 5.4.
Definition 5.12. Let $V \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$. We call

$$
R_{B L}(V):=\bigcup\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}
$$

the regular part of $V$ in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
Theorem 5.13. Let $A \in$ DLat. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(2) $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
(3) $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$.

Proof. (1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (2): Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong B L(X)$, it is enough to show that $B L(X)$ is regular iff $R_{B L}(V)$ is dense in $V$ for each $V \in B L(X)$. Let $V \in B L(X)$. We have

$$
\bigvee\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}=\operatorname{int}_{1} c l \bigcup\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}=\operatorname{int}_{1} c l\left(R_{B L}(V)\right)
$$

Therefore, by Proposition 5.10, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is regular iff $\mathrm{V}=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}\left(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})\right)$ iff $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in $V$ for each $V \in \operatorname{BL}(X)$.
$(1) \Leftrightarrow(3)$ : By Proposition 5.10, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is regular iff $\mathrm{V}=\bigvee\left\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X}): \mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{V}\right\}$ for each $V \in L(X)$. The same proof as in $(1) \Leftrightarrow(2)$ may be used to show that this is equivalent to $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ being dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$.

We now compare regularity of $A$ to that of $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

question: What does it mean for two stable groups to be principal?
answer: Two stable groups are said to be principal if they have the same connected components, i.e., $G_{1}^{0} = G_{2}^{0}$.

evidence.text:
# 3. DEFINABLE HULLS IN STABLE GROUPS 

3.1. General results. In this subsection, we will present some results of Wagner on groups and their subgroups in stable theories. We work in a sufficiently saturated model of a stable theory (with elimination of imaginaries). The results presented below remain valid for type-definable stable groups but for the sake of the presentation, we will assume that ambient model is the universe of a group $(G, \cdot)$. Moreover, we identify a formula with the corresponding definable subset.

Recall that a definable subset $\varphi(x, \bar{a})$ is generic in the stable group $G$ if $G$ is covered by finitely many bi-translates of the form $g^{-1} \cdot \varphi(x, \bar{a}) \cdot h^{-1}$ with $g$ and $h$ elements of $G$. Since the order property does not hold in stable theories, we always have that either a definable subset or its complement is generic in $G$. This yields the existence of generic types of $G$,

i.e. types that only contain generic formulae. Note that the type $p=\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ is generic if $(\circ)$ for every $h$ in $G$ independent from $g$ the product $g \cdot h$ is independent from $h$.

The connected component of $G$, denoted by $G^{0}$, is the intersection of all definable subgroups of finite index. The (left-) stabilizer of a stationary type $p=\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ is the set

$$
\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p)=\{h \in G \mid h \cdot \mathfrak{p}=\mathfrak{p}\}
$$

where $\mathfrak{p}$ is the unique global non-forking extension of $p$ and $g \cdot \mathfrak{p}$ is given by the natural action of $G$ on the space of types induced by left translation. Using the definability of types in stable theories, the stabilizer of $p$ can be written as the intersection of the definable subgroups

$$
\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p, \varphi)=\{g \in G \mid \models \forall \bar{z}\left(d_{p} \varphi(g x, \bar{z}) \leftrightarrow d_{p} \varphi(x, \bar{z})\right)\}
$$

A type is generic in $G$ if and only if its stabilizer equals $G^{0}$. We refer the reader to Poizat's volume on stable groups [24] for proofs and details.
Remark 3.1. In Section 4 we will also consider generic types and stabilizers for groups definable in simple theories. In this case, there is no notion of generic formula but a type is called generic if it satisfies the condition in (o). Since types are not necessarily stationary, the left-stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p)$ of a type $p$ is defined as the subgroup generated by the set

$$
\operatorname{St}(p)=\{h \in G \mid \exists g \models p \text { with } g \underset{A}{\perp} h \text { such that } h \cdot g \models p\}
$$

Right-stabilizers are defined analogously. More details and proofs can be found in [7].
Wagner showed in [27] that the notions for stable groups extend to non-definable subgroups of $G$.
Definition 3.2. ([28, Definitions 1.1.2, 2.1.1, 2.1.2 and 2.1.3]) Let $H$ be a (possibly nondefinable) subgroup of the stable group $(G, \cdot)$.
(1) A definable subset $\varphi(x, \bar{a})$ of $G$ is called generic for $H$ if $H$ is covered by finitely many bitranslates of $\varphi(x, \bar{a})$ by elements from $H$; that is, there are elements $g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}$ and $h_{1}, \ldots, h_{n}$ of $H$ such that for every $h$ in $H$ holds $\bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\left(g_{i} \cdot h \cdot h_{i}, \bar{a}\right)$.
(2) A type $p$ in $S_{1}(A)$ with $A \supset H$ is generic for $H$ if all its formulae are generic for $H$.
(3) The definable hull of $H$ (in $G$ ), denoted $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$, is the intersection of all definable subgroups (with parameters) of $G$ containing $H$.

As in the case of stable groups, generic types for $H$ always exist and a definable set is generic for $H$ if and only if $H$ is covered by left translates.

Consider the subspace $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ which consists of the types in $S_{1}(A)$ that are finitely satisfiable in $H$. By coheirness, each type in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ does not fork over $H$ and its restriction to $H$ is stationary. Every generic type for $H$ lies in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$, since we considered translates by elements from $H$ in the definition of genericity for $H$ in $G$.
Fact 3.3. ([27, Lemma 25, Lemma 26, Remark 27 and Lemma 28])
(1) The groups $\mathrm{dc}_{G}(H)$ and $\mathrm{dc}_{G}(H)^{0}$ are type-definable over $H$, and hence do not depend on the ambient model.

(2) A type $p$ in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ is generic for $H$ if and only if $\operatorname{Stab}_{G}(p)=\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)^{0}$. In particular, every type that is generic for $H$ in $G$ is also generic in the typedefinable group $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$.

The first part follows from the Baldwin-Saxl condition for definable groups in stable theories. For the second part, Wagner uses that a definable subgroup $H^{\prime}$ contains $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)^{0}$ if and only if the index $\left[H: H \cap H^{\prime}\right]$ is finite. The general structure of proofs is as in the definable case.

Before exploring how Wagner's results can be used in the setting of the criterion given in the next section, we first introduce the following notion:

Definition 3.4. Consider two stable groups $\left(G_{2}, \cdot\right) \subset\left(G_{1}, \cdot\right)$. We say that $G_{2}$ is principal in $G_{1}$ if they have the same connected components, i.e. $G_{1}^{0}=G_{2}^{0}$.

In his lecture notes [7], Casanovas refers to this notion as being generic since it is equivalent to the partial type defining $G_{2}$ being generic in $G_{1}$ by part (ii) of the next remark.

Remark 3.5. Let $\left(G_{2}, \cdot\right) \subset\left(G_{1}, \cdot\right)$ be two stable groups, both defined over $A$. The following conditions are equivalent:
(i) The group $G_{2}$ is principal in $G_{1}$.
(ii) Every generic type of $G_{2}$ (over $A$ ) is also a generic type of $G_{1}$.
(iii) There is some element $g$ of $G_{2}$ such that $\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ is generic in $G_{1}$.

The equivalences follow from basic facts about connected components. We will give a short proof for the sake of completeness.

Proof. $(i) \Rightarrow(i i)$ : Take a generic type $p$ of $G_{2}$, so its stabilizer $\operatorname{Stab}_{G_{2}}(p)$ equals $G_{2}^{0}=G_{1}^{0}$ by assumption. Since $G_{1}$ is a supergroup of $G_{2}$, we have $\operatorname{Stab}_{G_{1}}(p) \supset \operatorname{Stab}_{G_{2}}(p)=G_{1}^{0}$ which implies that $p$ is generic in $G_{1}$.
(ii) $\Rightarrow$ (iii): This implication is trivial.
(iii) $\Rightarrow(i)$ : We may assume that $A=\operatorname{acl}(A)$. First note that $G_{2}^{0} \subset G_{1}^{0} \cap G_{2}$ since $G_{2}$ is a subgroup of $G_{1}$. Let $g$ be as in the assumption of (iii) and take $g_{1} \equiv_{A} g$ with $g_{1} \downarrow_{A} g$. Since $G_{2}$ is definable over $A$, the type $\operatorname{tp}(g / A)$ determines a coset of the connected component $G_{2}^{0}$. In particular, the product $g_{1}^{-1} \cdot g$ lies in $G_{2}^{0}$. By the independence $g_{1} \downarrow_{A} g$ and genericity of $g$ in $G_{1}$ we also get that $g_{1}^{-1} \cdot g$ is generic in $G_{1}$. Hence, the group $G_{2}^{0}$ contains a generic element of $G_{1}$ which implies that $G_{1}^{0} \subset G_{2}^{0}$.

We use the remark as follows:
Corollary 3.6. Let $G$ and $H$ be as in Definition 3.2. If the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$ is principal in $G$, then for every $A \supset H$ there exists a type $p$ in $S_{1}^{H}(A)$ which is generic in $G$.

Proof. Choose $p$ to be a generic type for $H$ over $A$, then $p$ is generic in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H)$ by Fact 3.3 (2) and thus in $G$ by Remark 3.5.

3.2. Back to our Setting. We return to the assumptions of Section 1 and fix a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ of the stable $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-theory $T_{0}$ which eliminates imaginaries and quantifiers. As in Section 3.1, we assume that $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ is the universe of a group $(G, \cdot)$. In addition, we now consider a simple $\mathcal{L}$-theory $T$ with $\mathcal{L}_{0} \subset \mathcal{L}$ such that $T_{0}^{\varphi} \subset T$ (see Remark 1.1).

Inside $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, we fix a sufficiently saturated model $\mathcal{M}$ of $T$ and work either in $\mathcal{M}$ or $\mathcal{M}_{0}$. Furthermore, let $\mathcal{N}$ be a small elementary substructure of $\mathcal{M}$ and $H$ an $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable subset of $M$. We now suppose that $(H, \cdot)$ is a group in $\mathcal{M}$ (i.e. closed under $\cdot$ and inverses).

In particular, both the $N$-points $(H(N), \cdot)$ and the $M$-points $(H(M), \cdot)$ form (possibly non-definable) subgroups of $(G, \cdot)$.
Remark 3.7. In the just described setting, the definable hulls of $H(M)$ and $H(N)$ in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ coincide, that is $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M))=\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(N))$.
Proof. Since $H(N) \subset H(M)$, we have $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(N)) \subset \operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M))$ as type-definable sets.
On the other hand, if $\psi(x)$ is an $\mathcal{L}_{0}(N)$-formula such that $H(N) \subset \psi\left(M_{0}\right)$, then (by quantifier elimination of $T_{0}$ ) $\mathcal{N} \models \forall x(H(x) \rightarrow \psi(x))$. Since $\mathcal{N} \prec \mathcal{M}$ we thus have that $H(M) \subset \psi\left(M_{0}\right)$, so $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M)) \subset \operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(N))$ by Fact 3.3 (1).

Warning: Since $(H, \cdot)$ is an $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable group in the simple theory $T$, we now have two different notions of genericity for elements in $H$. A type is said to be ( $\mathcal{L}$-)generic in $H$ if it is generic in the simple theory $T$ and generic for $H(M)$ as in Definition 3.2 if we view $(H(M), \cdot)$ as a subgroup of $(G, \cdot)$.

However, these notions are related if $T$ is stable:
Remark 3.8. Let $(G, \cdot)$ and $(H, \cdot)$ be as above and suppose that $T$ is stable. An element $g$ of $H(M)$ is generic for $H(M)$ (working in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ ) if it is $\mathcal{L}$-generic in $H$ over $N$ (working in $\mathcal{M})$.

In particular, such an element $g$ is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}(H(M))$ by Fact 3.3 (2).
Proof. First work in $\mathcal{M}$. Since $T$ is stable and $\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)$ is generic in $H$, we find for every formula $\varphi(x)$ in $\operatorname{tp}_{\mathcal{L}}(g / N)$ elements $g_{1}, \ldots, g_{n}$ and $h_{1}, \ldots, h_{n}$ of $H(M)$ such that $\mathcal{M} \models \bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\left(g_{i} \cdot h \cdot h_{i}\right)$ for every element $h$ of $H(M)$.

If $\varphi$ is a quantifier-free $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-formula, we then also have $\mathcal{M}_{0} \models \bigvee_{i=1}^{n} \varphi\left(g_{i} \cdot h \cdot h_{i}\right)$ since $\mathcal{M}$ is a substructure of $\mathcal{M}_{0}$. In particular, this is true for all formulas in $\operatorname{tp}_{0}(g / N)$ by quantifier elimination of $T_{0}$. Hence, working in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, the type $\operatorname{tp}_{0}(g / N)$ is generic for $H(M)$.

We will now consider the definable hulls in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$ of two different subsets of $\mathcal{M}$, one being contained in the other.

Lemma 3.9. Given two $\mathcal{L}(N)$-definable sets $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ such that $\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$ and $\left(H_{2}, \cdot\right)$ are groups and $\left(H_{2}, \cdot\right) \subset\left(H_{1}, \cdot\right)$, the following two conditions are equivalent:
(i) The definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.
(ii) There exists an element $h$ of $H_{2}(M)$ that is $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-generic over $N$ in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.

Proof. Suppose that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in the definable hull $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$. Working in $\mathcal{M}_{0}$, there exists an $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-Type $p$ that is finitely satisfiable in $H_{2}(N)$ and generic in

$\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$ by Remark 3.6 applied to $H_{2}(N)$ as a subgroup of $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$. By quantifier elimination of $T_{0}$, the $\mathcal{L}_{0}$-type $p$ yields a partial $\mathcal{L}$-type over $N$ in $\mathcal{M}$ which is still finitely satisfiable in $H_{2}(N)$. This means that the partial type $p \cup\left\{H_{2}(x)\right\}$ over $N$ is consistent in $\mathcal{M}$ and thus realized by an element $h$. Hence, we have found an element as in (ii).

On the other hand, an element $h$ as in (ii) lies in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(M)\right)$ which by Remark 3.7 equals $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$. Remark 3.5 yields that $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{2}(N)\right)$ is principal in $\operatorname{dc}_{G}\left(H_{1}(N)\right)$.

question: What type of functions does the target function space include?
answer: The target function space includes most common discontinuous functions appearing in science and engineering tasks.

evidence.text:
### 2.1 Target function space

We consider approximating functions belonging to

$$
S=\left\{Q: \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}:\|Q\|_{L^{1}\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)}<\infty,\|\hat{Q}\|_{L^{1}\left(\mathbb{R}^{d}\right)}<\infty\right\}
$$

where $\hat{Q}$ is the Fourier transform of $Q$. This function space can be succinctly described all absolutely integrable functions on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ with absolutely integrable Fourier transform. These functions need only be continuous almost everywhere, so most common discontinuous functions appearing in science and engineering tasks are included.

question: Is every principal filter an intersection of maximal filters when $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
# 6. BOOLEANNESS 

We finally concentrate on when the four completions are Boolean. Janowitz [Jan68, Thm. 3.11] gives a characterization for the Dedekind-MacNeille completion to be Boolean. We obtain his result as a corollary to our characterization of when the Bruns-Lakser completion is Boolean. This requires using the notion of $\wedge$-subfitness (see the introduction). Since $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit iff its order-dual is $\vee$-subfit, Proposition 4.1 immediately yields:
Proposition 6.1. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and X its Priestley dual, the following are equivalent:
(1) $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit.
(2) $a \nless b$ implies there is a maximal filter $F$ with $a \in F$ and $b \notin F$.
(3) Every principal filter is an intersection of maximal filters.
(4) $\max X$ is dense in $X$.

Corollary 6.2. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley space X .
(1) If max $X$ is closed, then $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit iff $A$ is Boolean.
(2) If A is a frame, then A is $\wedge$-subfit iff A is Boolean.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{9}$ For the last equivalence it is sufficient to observe that $R(U)=U$ for each $U \in L(X)$ iff each $U$ is a complemented element of $L(X)$.

Proof. (1) Suppose $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit. By Proposition 6.1, max $X$ is dense in $X$. But max $X$ is closed, so $\max X=X$, and hence $A$ is Boolean (see, e.g., [Gra11, p. 119]). The other implication is always true.
(2) If $A$ is a frame then max $X$ is closed (see, e.g., [Esa19, p. 47]) and hence (1) applies.

We utilize the above two results to characterize when the Bruns-Lakser completion of a distributive lattice is Boolean.

Theorem 6.3. For $A \in$ DLat, the following are equivalent.
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean.
(2) $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit.
(3) $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is Boolean.

Proof. $(1) \Rightarrow(2)$ : Let $a, b \in A$ with $a \nless b$. Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean, it is $\wedge$-subfit, so there is $u \in \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ such that $b \wedge u=0$ and $a \wedge u \neq 0$. Because $A$ is join-dense in $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A, u=\bigvee S$ for some $S \subseteq A$. Therefore, since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is a frame, $b \wedge s=0$ for each $s \in S$ and there is $t \in S$ with $a \wedge t \neq 0$. Thus, $b \wedge t=0$ but $a \wedge t \neq 0$, and hence $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit.
$(2) \Rightarrow(3)$ : Since $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is generated as a distributive lattice by relative annihilators, it is enough to show that each relative annihilator has a complement in $p \mathcal{O}(A$. By Lemma 3.14(1) and Proposition 3.15, it is sufficient to show that $X \backslash \downarrow(\mathrm{U} \backslash \mathrm{V})$ has a complement in $\mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ for any clopen upsets $U, V$ of $X$. Specifically, we show that $X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{\mathrm{C}} \cup V\right)$ is the complement of $X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)$ in $p H(X)$. Since $U^{c} \cup V$ is clopen, $X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right) \in p H(X)$ by Lemma 3.14(2). Moreover, it is straightforward to see that

$$
[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \cap\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]=\varnothing
$$

Furthermore, since $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit, max $X$ is dense in $X$ by Proposition 6.1. But

$$
\max X \subseteq[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \cup\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]
$$

so $[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \cup\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]$ is dense in $X$, and hence

$$
[X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)] \vee_{p H(X)}\left[X \backslash \downarrow\left(U^{c} \cup V\right)\right]=X
$$

Thus, $X \backslash \downarrow(U \backslash V)$ has a complement in $p H(X)$, finishing the proof that $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is Boolean.
$(3) \Rightarrow(1)$ : By Theorem 3.12, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong \mathcal{D} M(p \mathcal{O}(A)$. Therefore, $p \mathcal{O}(A$ Boolean implies that so is $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ because the Dedekind-MacNeille completion of a Boolean algebra is a Boolean algebra (see, e.g., [BD74, p. 239]).

As a consequence, we obtain:
Corollary 6.4. [Jan68, Thm. 3.11] For $A \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean iff $A$ is $\vee$-subfit and $\wedge$-subfit.

Proof. First suppose $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean. Then $\mathcal{D} M A$ is $\vee$-subfit, so $A$ is $\vee$-subfit by Corollary 4.3. Moreover, $\mathcal{D} M A$ is a frame (since every complete Boolean algebra is a frame; see, e.g., [BD74, p. 53]), so $\mathcal{D} M A \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7. Therefore, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean, so $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit by Theorem 6.3.

Conversely, suppose $A$ is $\vee$-subfit and $\wedge$-subfit. Since $A$ is $\vee$-subfit, $A$ is proHeyting by Lemma 4.6, so $\mathcal{D} M A \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7. Because $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is Boolean by Theorem 6.3. Thus, $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean.

We conclude this section by characterizing when the ideal and canonical completions are Boolean. As we will see, the condition for the ideal completion to be Boolean is more restrictive.

Proposition 6.5. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean iff A is finite and Boolean.
Proof. If A is finite, then $\mathcal{M} \cong \mathrm{A}$, so A Boolean implies that $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean. Conversely, suppose $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean. Then every ideal, being complemented, is principal, so again $\mathcal{M} \cong \mathrm{A}$. Since every infinite boolean algebra has an infinite pairwise disjoint set [Kop89, Prop. 3.4], it must also have a nonprincipal ideal. Thus, $A$ is finite.
Proposition 6.6. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat, $A^{\sigma}$ is Boolean iff A is Boolean.
Proof. Let $X$ be the Priestley space of $A$. Then $A$ is Boolean iff the order on $X$ is discrete (see, e.g., [Gra11, p. 119]), which happens iff $\mathrm{Up}(\mathrm{X})=\mathcal{P}(\mathrm{X})$, which is equivalent to $\mathrm{A}^{\sigma}$ being Boolean.

The situation summarizes as follows:
Summary 6.7. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat.
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ (resp. $p \mathcal{O}(A)$ is Boolean iff $A$ is $\wedge$-subfit iff max $X$ is dense in $X$.
(2) $\mathcal{D} M A$ is Boolean iff $A$ is both $\vee$ - and $\wedge$-subfit iff both $\min X$ and $\max X$ are dense in $X$.
(3) $A^{\sigma}$ is Boolean iff $A$ is Boolean iff $\max X$ is $X$.
(4) $\mathcal{M}$ is Boolean iff $A$ is finite and Boolean iff $\max X$ is $X$ and $X$ is finite.

question: How is spontaneous symmetry breaking characterized for discrete symmetries?
answer: Spontaneous symmetry breaking for discrete symmetries can be characterized by the behavior of the partition function in the presence of a symmetry defect, where it approaches zero in a broken phase and remains constant (non-zero) in an unbroken phase.

evidence.text:
# 2.2 $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ flavor symmetry defect and symmetry breaking 

In this subsection, we introduce a criterion using a symmetry defect to detect the spontaneous breaking of discrete symmetry. An ordinary symmetry operator is a topological object defined on a constant time slice. When the topological object is extended in the time direction, it is called a symmetry defect, which corresponds to imposing twisted boundary conditions.

Spontaneous symmetry breaking is characterized by a non-vanishing order parameter or by the long-distance limit of the two-point function of the order operator [42]. Alternatively, in the case of discrete symmetries, spontaneous breaking can be characterized by the behavior of the partition function in the presence of a symmetry defect (disordered parameter), where

$$
\lim _{V \rightarrow \infty} \frac{Z^{\prime}}{Z} \rightarrow \begin{cases}\sim e^{-N_{4} V_{\|} T_{w}} \rightarrow 0 & \text { broken phase } \\ \text { const } \neq 0 & \text { unbroken phase }\end{cases}
$$

Here, $Z$ and $Z^{\prime}$ are partition functions without and with a symmetry defect, respectively.
$V_{\|}$is the volume parallel to the domain wall, and $T_{w}$ is the domain wall tension. In systems where the discrete symmetry is spontaneously broken, the insertion of the symmetry defect induces the domain wall connecting the different vacua. The energy of the domain wall leads to an exponential suppression in the ratio of the partition function to that in the absence of the domain wall. In contrast, in phases without symmetry breaking, the partition function remains insensitive to the boundary conditions. As a result, the ratio of the partition functions is given by eq. (2.11). In Appendix A, we present the quantum Ising model as an example that can be solved analytically.

We insert a $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$ flavor symmetry (2.7) defect on a plane perpendicular to the $z$-axis. Specifically, we introduce the defect between $z=N_{3}-1$ and $z=N_{3}(=0)$.

The insertion of this defect modifies the matter field term in the action at $z=N_{3}-1$ and $\mu=z$ as

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \cos \left(\Delta_{z} \theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right)+\cos \left(\Delta_{z} \theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right) \\
& \quad \rightarrow \cos \left(\theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, 0\right)-\theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right) \\
& \quad+\cos \left(\theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, 0\right)-\theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

The other terms remain unchanged. As a result, the action with the symmetry defect $S^{\prime}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
S^{\prime}=-\beta_{H} \sum_{x_{\perp}} & {\left[\cos \left(\theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, 0\right)-\theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right)\right.} \\
& +\cos \left(\theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, 0\right)-\theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right) \\
& +\sum_{z \neq N_{3}-1}\left[\cos \left(\Delta_{z} \theta_{1}(x)+A_{z}(x)\right)+\cos \left(\Delta_{z} \theta_{2}(x)+A_{z}(x)\right)\right] \\
& \left.+\sum_{z, \mu \neq z}\left[\cos \left(\Delta_{\mu} \theta_{1}(x)+A_{\mu}(x)\right)+\cos \left(\Delta_{\mu} \theta_{2}(x)+A_{\mu}(x)\right)\right]\right]-\beta_{g} \sum_{x, \mu<\nu} \cos \left(F_{\mu \nu}(x)\right) \\
=S-\beta_{H} \sum_{x_{\perp}} & {\left[\cos \left(\theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, 0\right)-\theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right)\right.} \\
& +\cos \left(\theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, 0\right)-\theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right) \\
& \left.-\cos \left(\Delta_{z} \theta_{1}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right)\right. \\
& \left.-\cos \left(\Delta_{z} \theta_{2}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)+A_{z}\left(x_{\perp}, N_{3}-1\right)\right)\right]
\end{aligned}
$$

question: What does it mean for a state on a unital $C^{*}$-algebra to be faithful?
answer: A state is faithful if $\phi\left(x^{*} x\right)>0$ for any nonzero $x \in A$.

evidence.text:
# 2. Notation 

Let $\Gamma$ be a countable discrete group. If $Y$ is a generating set for $\Gamma$ then we denote by $B_{Y}(R)$ the elements of the $R$-ball around the identity in the Cayley graph of $\Gamma$ with the generating set $Y$. Let $\mathbb{C} \Gamma$ denote the complex group algebra associated to $\Gamma$. We equip $\mathbb{C} \Gamma$ with three separate norms. Let $x=\sum x_{g} g$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\|x\|_{1} & :=\sum_{g \in \Gamma}\left|x_{g}\right| \\
\|x\|_{2}^{2} & :=\sum_{g \in \Gamma}\left|x_{g}\right|^{2} \\
\|x\| & :=\sup \left\{\|x y\|_{2}: y \in \mathbb{C} \Gamma,\|y\|_{2} \leq 1\right\}
\end{aligned}
$$

We call these norms on $\mathbb{C} \Gamma$ the $\ell^{1}$-norm, the $\ell^{2}$-norm, and the operator norm respectively. As suggested by the definition of the operator norm, each element of $\mathbb{C} \Gamma$ can be viewed as a bounded operator on $\ell^{2}(\Gamma)$. We define the reduced group $C^{*}$-algebra $C_{r}^{*}(\Gamma)$ to be the operator norm closure of $\mathbb{C} \Gamma$ inside of $\mathbb{B}\left(\ell^{2}(\Gamma)\right)$.

A state on a unital $C^{*}$-algebra $A$ is a positive linear functional $\phi$ such that $\phi(1)=1$. We say a state $\phi$ is faithful if $\phi\left(x^{*} x\right)>0$ for any nonzero $x \in A$. We call $\phi$ a trace if $\phi(x y)=\phi(y x)$ for all $x, y \in A$. Let $A_{1}, A_{2} \subset(A, \phi)$ be subalgebras. We say that $A_{1}$ and $A_{2}$ are freely independent relative to $\phi$ if whenever $a_{k} \in A_{i_{k}}$ with $\phi\left(a_{k}\right)=0$ and $i_{k} \neq i_{k+1}$ for $1 \leq k \leq n$ then $\phi\left(a_{1} \cdots a_{n}\right)=0$. If $\left(B_{1}, \rho\right),\left(B_{2}, \rho\right)$ are unital $C^{*}$-algebras with faithful states, then there is a unital $C^{*}$-algebra with faithful state $(B, \rho)$ and embeddings $\pi_{i}:\left(B_{i}, \rho\right) \hookrightarrow(B, \rho)$ such that $\pi_{1}\left(B_{1}\right)$ and $\pi_{2}\left(B_{2}\right)$ are freely independent relative to $\rho$. We call $(B, \rho)$ the reduced free product of $\left(B_{1}, \rho_{1}\right)$ and $\left(B_{2}, \rho_{2}\right)$; we omit the states when they are clear from context (see $[4,63]$ ).

Let $\mathcal{U}$ be a free ultrafilter on the natural numbers. For a discrete group $\Gamma$ we denote by $\Gamma^{\mathcal{U}}$ the following quotient:

$$
\Gamma^{\mathcal{U}}:=\left(\prod_{N} \Gamma\right) / N_{\mathcal{U}}
$$

where $N_{\mathcal{U}}$ consists of all sequences which are eventually constant with respect to $\mathcal{U}$. More precisely, a sequence $\left(g_{n}\right)_{n} \in N$ if and only if there is $h \in \Gamma$ and $S \in \mathcal{U}$ such that $g_{n}=h$ for all $n \in S$. We call $\Gamma^{\mathcal{U}}$ an ultrapower of $\Gamma$. If $A$ is a $C^{*}$-algebra, we define $A^{\mathcal{U}}$ as

$$
A^{\mathcal{U}}:=\left\{\left(x_{n}\right)_{n}: x_{n} \in A, \sup _{n}\left\|x_{n}\right\|<\infty\right\} / I_{\mathcal{U}}
$$

where $I_{\mathcal{U}}$ consists of all norm-bounded sequences $\left(x_{n}\right)$ in $A$ with the following property: for all $\varepsilon>0$ there is $S \in \mathcal{U}$ such that for all $n \geq N,\left\|x_{n}\right\|<\varepsilon$. We call $A^{\mathcal{U}}$ an ultrapower of $A$.

question: Does FACT dissuade hospitals from lying about their data collection costs?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
# 6.1 Real-World Case Study: Inter-Hospital Skin Cancer Diagnosis 

We consider a realistic situation where a consortium of hospitals seek collaboration to train a model, privately in a FL manner, that can diagnose skin cancer. One of the hospitals is smaller and resourceconstrained. It is difficult, but not impossible, for this hospital to collect more data for training. Thus, in the absence of a truthful FL mechanism, the smaller hospital could over-report its collection costs to the server in order to contribute little to no data towards training while still reaping the rewards of a well-trained global model.

To test how FACT deals with this scenario, we train an image classification model on the HAM10000 [31] dataset. HAM10000 consists of a collection of dermatoscopic images of pigmented lesions. The goal is to train a model which can perform automated diagnosis of pigmented skin lesions, including melanoma (skin cancer). Our setup is similar to the experimental setup detailed in the previous section. One difference is that we fine-tune a ResNet50 model on HAM10000 that is pre-trained on ImageNet (a realistic approach for a hospital). HAM10000 is an imbalanced dataset, and evenly partitioning $80 \%$ of the data amongst 10 devices, as their local training sets, further exacerbates the non-iidness of the data. This too is realistic, as data is often non-iid amongst FL agents. We use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of $1 \mathrm{e}-3$ and batch size of 128 .

As expected, FACT provably dissuades any hospital from lying about its cost in order to reduce their data contribution level. Agents are incentivized to be truthful; reduction in loss is maximized when agents truthfully report their costs (see the middle plot in Figure 4). As a result, a smaller, resourced-constrained hospital would still contribute its locally optimal amount of data, or face harsh penalties (see the right plot in Figure 4). Finally, all participating hospitals are still better off participating in FACT than training alone. Participating agent loss is reduced by nearly $66 \%$ compared to local training (see the left plot in Figure 4). The effectiveness of FACT to dissuade free-riding in the real-world setting of training a skin cancer classifier across hospitals indicates that it will be successful in other real-world settings.

question: What are typical latent dimensions used for different components in numerical experiments involving PDEs?
answer: Typical latent dimensions vary by component; for instance, a dimension of 11 is used for boundary value problems and Lotka-Volterra model trajectories, while larger dimensions like 32 are employed for steady-state diffusion coefficients and Navier Stokes equation vorticity.

# D. 4 Choice of Hyperparameters 

Our method requires selecting the dimensions of the latent representations of the functional parameters and the solutions of the stochastic PDEs for the different numerical experiments. The latent dimension is selected based on the criterion that the mean relative $L^{2}$ error norm between the true function and the function reconstructed from the latent embedding using the INR remains below a certain threshold across all test data points. At the same time, we want the dimension to be low to ensure that the resulting distribution of the latent representations has a positive probability density that can be easily modelled by the energy-based model.

question: Is it true that for any element \( e \) in a rectangular band \( S \), \( S = (Se)(eS) \)?
answer: Yes, for any \( e \in S \), \( S = (Se)(eS) \).

evidence.text:
# 4 Rectangular Band Subsemigroups 

A rectangular band is a semigroup $S$ in which $a b a=a$ for any $a, b \in S$. There are several equivalent definitions, and the structure of a rectangular band as a product of a left zero and right zero subsemigroups is well known. We develop some equivalent definitions in the context of one-sided identity and zero sets, and we describe all rectangular band subsemigroups containing a particular idempotent, which reiterates this structure.
Theorem 4.1. Let $S$ be a semigroup. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
(1) $S$ is a rectangular band;
(2) $S$ is a band and for any $a, b \in S, a b=b$ if and only if $b a=a$.
(3) $S$ is a band and for any $a, b \in S, a b=a$ if and only if $b a=b$.

Proof. (1) $\Longrightarrow$ (2): If $S$ is a rectangular band, then $S$ is a band. For any $a, b \in S$ with $a b=b$, $a b a=(a b) a=b a$. Since $S$ is a rectangular band, $a b a=a$, and $b a=a$. Similarly, for any $a, b \in S$ with $b a=a, b a b=(b a) b=a b$. Since $S$ is a rectangular band, $b a b=b$, and $a b=b$.
(2) $\Longrightarrow$ (1): $S$ is a band, and for any $a, b \in S, a b=b$ if and only if $b a=a$. For any $a, b \in S$, $a(a b)=(a a) b=a b$, which implies $(a b) a=a$. Therefore $S$ is a rectangular band.

The proofs for (1) $\Longrightarrow$ (3) and (3) $\Longrightarrow$ (1) are similar.
Conditions (2) and (3) can then be explicitly expressed in terms of identity and zero sets.
Corollary 4.2. Let $S$ be a semigroup. Then the following conditions are equivalent:
(1) $S$ is a rectangular band;
(2) For any $a \in S$, lidentity $(a)=r z e r o(a) \neq \emptyset$.
(3) For any $a \in S$, ridentity $(a)=l z e r o(a) \neq \emptyset$.

Proof. Given (2) from Theorem 4.1, $S$ is a band and for any $a, b \in S, a b=b$ if and only if $b a=a$. Since $S$ is a band, $a a=a \in \operatorname{lidentity}(a), r z e r o(a)$, and $\operatorname{lidentity}(a), r z e r o(a) \neq \emptyset$. Since for any $b \in S, a b=b$ if and only if $b a=a, r z e r o(a)=\operatorname{lidentity}(a)$ by definition. Therefore (2) from Corollary 4.2 is implied.

Given (2) from Corollary 4.2, for any $a \in S$, lidentity $(a)=r z e r o(a) \neq \emptyset$. For any $a \in S$, since lidentity $(a)=r z e r o(a) \neq \emptyset$, lidentity $(a) \cap r z e r o(a) \neq \emptyset$, and by Theorem 2.6, $a$ is an idempotent, so that $S$ is a band. Since lidentity $(a)=r z e r o(a)$ for any $a \in S$, then for any $b \in S, b a=a$ if and only if $a b=b$ by definition. Therefore (2) from Theorem 4.1 is implied.

Lemma 4.3. Let $S$ be a semigroup, let $e$ be an idempotent, and let $T \subset S$. If $T=T_{L} T_{R}$ for some sets $T_{L}$ and $T_{R}$ such that $T_{L} \subset L Z(e), T_{R} \subset R Z(e)$, and $T_{R} T_{L}=\{e\}$, then $T_{L}$ and $T_{R}$ are unique.

Proof. Let $T=T_{L} T_{R}$ and $T=T_{L}^{\prime} T_{R}^{\prime}$ such that $T_{L}, T_{L}^{\prime} \subset L Z(e), T_{R}, T_{R}^{\prime} \subset R Z(e), T_{R} T_{L}=\{e\}$, and $T_{R}^{\prime} T_{L}^{\prime}=\{e\}$.

Since $T_{R} T_{L}=\{e\}$ and $T_{R}^{\prime} T_{L}^{\prime}=\{e\}, T_{L}, T_{R}, T_{L}^{\prime}, T_{R}^{\prime}$ must all be nonempty. For any nonempty $A, B$ subsets of a left zero semigroup, $A B=A$, and for any nonempty $A, B$ subsets of a right zero semigroup, $A B=B$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{L} T_{R} & =T_{L}^{\prime} T_{R}^{\prime} \\
T_{L} T_{R} T_{R} & =T_{L}^{\prime} T_{R}^{\prime} T_{R} \\
T_{L} T_{R} & =T_{L}^{\prime} T_{R} \\
T_{L} T_{R} T_{L} & =T_{L}^{\prime} T_{R} T_{L} \\
T_{L}\{e\} & =T_{L}^{\prime}\{e\} \\
T_{L} & =T_{L}^{\prime}
\end{aligned}
$$

multiply by $T_{R}$ on the right

$$
T_{R}, T_{R}^{\prime} \subset R Z(e)
$$

multiply by $T_{L}$ on the right

$$
T_{R} T_{L}=\{e\}
$$

$T_{L}, T_{L}^{\prime},\{e\} \subset L Z(e)$.

Similarly, $T_{R}=T_{R}^{\prime}$.

Theorem 4.4. Let $S$ be a semigroup, and let $e$ be an idempotent. $T$ is a rectangular band subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$ if and only if $T=T_{L} T_{R}$ for some sets $T_{L}$ and $T_{R}$ such that $e \in T_{L} \subset L Z(e)$, $e \in T_{R} \subset R Z(e)$, and $T_{R} T_{L}=\{e\}$. In this case, $T_{L}$ and $T_{R}$ are unique.

Proof. If $T$ is a rectangular band subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$, then for any $x \in T$,

$$
x=x e x=x(e e) x=(x e)(e x) \in(T e)(e T)
$$

For any $x, y \in T$,

$$
(x e)(e y)=x e y \in T
$$

because $T$ is a subsemigroup containing $x, e, y$. Therefore $T=(T e)(e T)$.
By Theorem 2.4, $T e \subset S e=l z e r o(e)$ and $e T \subset e S=r z e r o(e)$. For any $x \in T, e(x e)=e x e=e$, so $T e \subset$ ridentity $(e)$, and $T e \subset L Z(e)$. For any $x \in T,(e x) e=e x e=e$, so $e T \subset$ lidentity $(e)$, and $e T \subset R Z(e)$. For any $x, y \in T,(e x)(y e)=e(x y) e=e$ because $T$ is a rectangular band subsemigroup with $x y \in T$. Therefore $(e T)(T e)=\{e\}$.

If $T=T_{L} T_{R}$ for some sets $T_{L}$ and $T_{R}$ such that $e \in T_{L} \subset L Z(e), e \in T_{R} \subset R Z(e)$, and $T_{R} T_{L}=\{e\}$, then $e e=e \in T$.

For any $a, c \in T_{L}$ and $b, d \in T_{R}, a b, c d \in T$, and

$$
(a b)(c d)=a(b c) d=a e d=(a e) d=a d \in T
$$

Thus $T$ is a subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$.
For any $a, c \in T_{L}$ and $b, d \in T_{R}, a b, c d \in T$, and

$$
(a b)(c d)(a b)=a(b c)(d a) b=a(e e) b=a e b=a(e b)=a b
$$

Therefore $T$ is a rectangular band subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$.
$T_{L}=T e$ and $T_{R}=e T$ are unique by the previous lemma.
Corollary 4.5. Let $S$ be a rectangular band. For any $e \in S, S=(S e)(e S)$ such that $S e$ is a maximal left zero subsemigroup of $S$ and $e S$ is a maximal right zero subsemigroup of $S$.

Proof. If $S$ is a rectangular band and $e \in S$, then $e$ is an idempotent. By Theorem 3.1, $L Z(e)$ is the maximum left zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$ and $R Z(e)$ is the maximum right zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$.

For any $a \in S,(a e) e=a(e e)=a e$ and $e(a e)=e$. Therefore $a e \in L Z(e)$ and $S e \subset L Z(e)$. For any $b \in L Z(e), b=b e \in S e$, so $L Z(e) \subset S e$. Thus $L Z(e)=S e$.

For any $a \in S, e(e a)=(e e) a=e a$ and $(e a) e=e$. Therefore $e a \in R Z(e)$ and $e S \subset R Z(e)$. For any $b \in R Z(e), b=b e \in e S$, so $R Z(e) \subset e S$. Thus $R Z(e)=e S$.

Since $S$ is a rectangular band, $(e S)(S e)=\{e\}$ and $S=(S e)(e S)$.

question: Why is there a need to study maxitivity with respect to general orders beyond pointwise order?
answer: Studying maxitivity with respect to general orders allows for extending its beneficial properties to a wider class of functions beyond those defined by pointwise order. This broader perspective enables new applications and insights into how different types of order relations can influence decision-making processes under uncertainty.

evidence.text:
## 1. InTRODUCTION

In decision-making under risk and uncertainty, one typically considers a set of gambles $X$ and a function $\psi: X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, which assigns to each gamble $f \in X$ a value $\psi(f)$, representing its price, risk, or utility. In the context of imprecise probabilities, such functions are referred to as lower/upper previsions; see [31]. In financial mathematics, they are commonly called risk measures [12] or nonlinear expectations [23].

In many cases, the function $\psi$ takes the form of an expectation, where the value $\psi(f)$ represents the weighted average of the values associated with the gamble $f$. However, decisions are often based on assessments of best-case or worst-case scenarios, rather than relying on averages. These evaluations are captured by maxitive functions. A function $\psi$ is called maxitive if it satisfies the condition $\psi(f \vee g)=\max \{\psi(f), \psi(g)\}$ for any two gambles $f$ and $g$, where $f \vee g$ denotes the pointwise supremum of $f$ and $g$.

Maxitive functions play a crucial role in possibility theory $[10,11,34]$ and serve as aggregation functions in various fields such as economics, information fusion, and control theory [13, 29]. Under reasonable assumptions, these functions can be represented in terms of maxitive integrals, such as the Shilkret integral discussed in [3, 16, 24, 28]. Beyond decision theory, maxitive functions also arise in other areas, including idempotent or tropical analysis [17] and large deviations theory [15, 16, 25].

In probability theory, statistics, and particularly decision theory, a wide range of criteria exist to define order relations between gambles beyond the pointwise order [22, 27]. While most of the literature has focused on maxitivity with respect to pointwise order, less attention has been paid to maxitivity with respect to more general orders. The aim of this work is to fill this gap by studying maxitivity in the context of preorders, which enables the extension of the maxitive structure and its beneficial properties to a wider class of functions. By passing from the pointwise order to weaker stochastic

The main result of this paper provides a characterization and representation of countably maxitive functions on a preordered space. The proof relies on recent representation results from $[7,18]$ for convex monotone functions on spaces of bounded continuous functions, and incorporates dual representations of sublevel sets as discussed in [9]. A key assumption is that the preorder $\preccurlyeq$ admits a numerical representation given by $f \preccurlyeq g$ if and only if $\phi(f) \leq \phi(g)$ for all $\phi$ in some Polish space ${ }^{1} \Phi$, where the mapping $\phi \mapsto \phi(f)$ is lower semicontinuous ${ }^{2}$ for all $f \in X$. This assumption is fulfilled for typical stochastic orders. As an application of the main result, we obtain characterizations of maxitive functions with respect to the usual stochastic order, the increasing convex order, the convex order, the increasing concave order, and the dispersive order; see $[22,27]$.

The paper is structured as follows: In Section 2, we provide some motivation for maxitivity in decision-making and possibility theory. Section 3 introduces the basic concepts and definitions. In Section 4, we present and prove the main result. Section 5 explores variations of the main result in the context of different stochastic orders. Finally, the appendix provides representation results for maxitive risk measures on $C_{b}$, along with auxiliary results related to quantile functions.

question: What is the main challenge in training energy-based models?
answer: The main challenge in training energy-based models is that the normalising constant is intractable, preventing optimisation using maximum likelihood estimation.

evidence.text:
## A. 2 Energy-Based Model Training

Energy-Based Models are a class of parametric unnormalised probabilistic models of the form $\exp \left(-E_{\theta}\right)$ originally inspired by statistical physics. Despite their flexibility, energy-based models have not seen widespread adoption in machine learning applications due to the challenges involved in training them. In particular, because the normalising constant is intractable, these models cannot be optimised using maximum likelihood estimation. Alternative training methods have been explore such as contrastive divergence (Hinton et al., 2006), score-based methods (Hyvärinen, 2005; Vincent, 2011; Song and Ermon, 2020) and energy discrepancy (Schröder et al., 2023).

Contrastive divergence (Hinton et al., 2006) is a method that approximates the gradient of the log-likelihood via short runs of a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) process. Although using short MCMC runs greatly reduces both the computation per gradient step and the variance of the estimated gradient (Carreira-Perpiñán and Hinton, 2005), it comes at the cost of producing poor approximations of the energy function. This issue arises, in part, because contrastive divergence is not the gradient of any objective function (Sutskever and Tieleman, 2010; Bengio and Delalleau, 2009) which significantly limits the theoretical understanding of its convergence.

Score-based methods provide an alternative way for training based on minimising the expected squared distance of the score function of the true distribution $\nabla_{x} \log p_{\text {data }}$ and the score function given by the model $\nabla_{x} \log p_{\theta}$, which by definition are independent of the normalising constant (Hyvärinen, 2005; Vincent, 2011). However, these methods only use gradient information and are therefore short-sighted (Song and Ermon, 2019) as they do not resolve the global characteristics of the distribution when limited data are available.

Energy discrepancy attempts to solve the problems of the two previous methods by proposing a new loss function that compares the data distribution and the energy-based model (Schröder et al., 2023). This loss is given by

$$
\mathcal{L}_{t, M, w}(\theta):=\frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log \left(\frac{w}{M}+\frac{1}{M} \sum_{j=1}^{M} \exp \left(E_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{z}_{i}\right)-E_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{z}_{i}+\sqrt{t} \boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}+\sqrt{t} \boldsymbol{\xi}_{i, j}^{\prime}\right)\right)\right)
$$

where $\boldsymbol{\xi}_{i}, \boldsymbol{\xi}_{i, j}^{\prime} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(0, \mathbf{I}_{d_{z_{0}}+d_{z_{0}}}\right)$ are i.i.d. random variables and $t, M, w$ are tunable hyper-parameters. Energy discrepancy depends only on the energy function and is independent of the scores and MCMC samples from the energy-based model.

We applied these three methods to train the energy-based model in our framework, obtaining the best results with the latter. Notably, for the 2D examples, both contrastive divergence and score matching failed to converge.
