# 5. MAxitivity with RESPECT TO STOCHASTIC ORDERS 

Let $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ be an atomless probability space. ${ }^{20}$ We denote by $\mathcal{M}$ the set of all random variables $\xi: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where two of them are identified if they have the same law. Further, let $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ and $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ be the sets of all random variables in $\mathcal{M}$ which are essentially bounded, and have finite first moments, respectively. In the following, we analyze the main results of the previous section for several stochastic orders. For definitions and further details on stochastic orders, we refer to [21, 27].
5.1. Usual stochastic order. For $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$, the quantile function $q_{\xi}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is defined as the left-inverse of the cumulative distribution function, i.e.,

$$
q_{\xi}(u):=\inf \{v \in \mathbb{R}: u \leq \mathbb{P}(\xi \leq v)\}
$$

On the one hand, the quantile function $q_{\xi}$ is non-decreasing and left-continuous, see Lemma B.1. On the other hand, every function $q:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which is non-decreasing and left-continuous satisfies $q=q_{\xi}$ for some $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$, see Lemma B.3. Hence, there is a one-to-one relation between the set $\mathcal{M}$ and quantile functions.

The usual stochastic order on $\mathcal{M}$ is defined by

$$
\xi \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{st}} \eta \quad \text { if and only if } \quad q_{\xi}(u) \leq q_{\eta}(u) \text { for all } u \in(0,1)
$$

The ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {st }}\right)$ is a complete lattice, see [14, 22]. In particular, every sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}$ which is bounded from above has a supremum $\xi^{*}=\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n}$ in $\mathcal{M}$ which is determined by $q_{\xi^{*}}(u)=\sup _{n \in \mathbb{N}} q_{\xi_{n}}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$.

Let $\Phi_{\text {st }}:=\left\{\phi_{u}: u \in(0,1)\right\}$ denote the family of functions $\phi_{u}: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by $\phi_{u}(\xi):=q_{\xi}(u)$. We identify $\Phi_{\text {st }}$ with $(0,1)$, and endow $(0,1)$ with the Euclidean topology. ${ }^{21}$ Then, it holds $\xi \preccurlyeq_{\text {st }} \eta$ if and only if $\phi_{u}(\xi) \leq \phi_{u}(\eta)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. Moreover, for every $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$, the mapping $u \mapsto \phi_{u}(\xi)$ is lower semicontinuous. Therefore, the partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {st }}\right)$ satisfies the assumptions of Section 4.

Lemma 5.1. Every function $\gamma:(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ is countably stable.
Proof. Let $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}$ with $q^{*}(u):=\sup _{n \in \mathbb{N}} q_{\xi_{n}}(u) \leq \gamma(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. Then, the mapping $u \mapsto q^{*}(u)$ is real-valued, non-decreasing and left-continuous. Hence, there exists $\xi^{*} \in \mathcal{M}$ with $q^{*}(u)=q_{\xi^{*}}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. In particular, $\xi^{*}=\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n}$ and $\phi_{u}\left(\xi^{*}\right)=q^{*}(u) \leq \gamma(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{20}$ Recall that a probability space $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ is atomless if for all $A \in \mathcal{F}$ with $\mathbb{P}(A)>0$ there exists $B \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $B \subset A$ and $0<\mathbb{P}(B)<\mathbb{P}(A)$; see e.g. [6].
    ${ }^{21}(0,1)$ is not complete with the Euclidean distance. However, it is completely metrizable, that is, there exists an equivalent metric on $(0,1)$ such that $(0,1)$ with the relative Euclidean topology is a complete metric space space. In fact, every countable intersection of open subsets of a complete metric space is completely metrizable, see [33, Theorem 24.12].

For a function $\psi: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ with sublevel sets $A_{s}:=\{\xi \in \mathcal{M}: \psi(\xi) \leq s\}$, we define $\alpha_{\min }(s, u):=\sup _{\xi \in A_{s}} q_{\xi}(u)$ and $\alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u):=\inf _{s<t} \alpha_{\min }(t, u)$ for all $s \in$ $\mathbb{R}$ and $u \in(0,1)$. If $\psi$ is countably maxitive, then the sublevel sets are countably upwards directed, so that $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(s, u)$ is real-valued for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $A_{s} \neq$ $\emptyset$. As a direct application of Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.4, we obtain the following representation result for maxitive functions w.r.t. the usual stochastic order. A related representation result for maxitive functionals with respect to the usual stochastic order was investigated in parallel to our work in [4, Theorem 1].
Corollary 5.2. Let $\psi: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
(i) $\psi$ is bounded countably maxitive w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{st}}$.
(ii) $\psi$ is monotone and has countably upwards directed sublevel sets w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{st}}$.
(iii) There exists a function $\alpha: \mathbb{R} \times(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ which is non-decreasing in the first argument such that

$$
\psi(\xi)=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: \sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{q_{\xi}(u)-\alpha(s, u)\right\} \leq 0\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}
$$

The infimum is attained for all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$ with $\psi(\xi)<\infty$.
(iv) The mapping $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(s, u)$ is real-valued for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $A_{s} \neq \emptyset$. Moreover, it holds

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)} G\left(q_{\xi}(u), u\right) \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}
$$

where $G(t, u):=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: t \leq \alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u)\right\}$ for all $(t, u) \in \mathbb{R} \times(0,1)$.
If $\psi$ also has the translation property, then we get the following version of the previous result. We notice that $q_{\xi+c}=q_{\xi}+c$ for all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$, i.e., the mapping $\phi_{u}: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ has the translation property for all $u \in(0,1)$. Hence, we can apply Corollary 4.4 and obtain the following result.
Corollary 5.3. Let $\psi: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function with the translation property. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
(i) $\psi$ is bounded countably maxitive w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{st}}$.
(ii) There exists a function $\alpha: \mathbb{R} \times(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ such that

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{q_{\xi}(u)-\alpha(u)\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}
$$

(iii) The mapping $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(0, u)=\sup _{\xi \in A_{0}} q_{\xi}(u)$ is real-valued, and

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{q_{\xi}(u)-\alpha_{\min }(0, u)\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}
$$

Recall that the value at risk $\operatorname{VaR}_{u}: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ at level $u \in(0,1)$, which is defined by $\operatorname{VaR}_{u}(\xi):=q_{\xi}(u)$, is a monetary risk measure; see [12]. The previous Corollary 5.3 is closely related to [32, Theorem 4] which provides a representation result for lower semicontinuous completely maxitive functions $\mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ having the translation property. A related representation result was also shown in [2, Proposition 4] for the class of benchmark-loss VaR, which were introduced by Bignozzi et al. [2].
Remark 5.4. For every sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}$ such that $\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n}$ exists, it holds $\operatorname{VaR}_{u}\left(\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n}\right)=\sup _{n \in \mathbb{N}} \operatorname{VaR}_{u}\left(\xi_{n}\right)$. Nevertheless, the function $\operatorname{VaR}_{u}: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is not countably bounded maxitive because it may happen that $\sup _{n \in \mathbb{N}} \operatorname{VaR}_{u}\left(\xi_{n}\right)<\infty$ for an unbounded sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}$. However, $\operatorname{VaR}_{u}$ can also be defined on the set $\mathcal{M}^{*}$

of all extended random variables $\xi: \Omega \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$. Then, the supremum $\vee_{i \in I} \xi_{i}$ exists for every family $\left(\xi_{i}\right)_{i \in I} \subset \mathcal{M}^{*}$ and $\operatorname{VaR}_{u}: \mathcal{M}^{*} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ is completely maxitive.
5.2. Increasing convex stochastic order. For $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$, we define the integrated quantile function $Q_{\xi}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by

$$
Q_{\xi}(u):=\int_{u}^{1} q_{\xi}(v) \mathrm{d} v
$$

The function $u \mapsto Q_{\xi}(u)$ is concave, with $Q_{\xi}\left(0^{+}\right)=\mathbb{E}[\xi]$ and $Q_{\xi}\left(1^{-}\right)=0$. Conversely, every concave function $Q:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with $Q\left(0^{+}\right) \in \mathbb{R}$ and $Q\left(1^{-}\right)=0$ is of the form $Q=Q_{\xi}$ for some random variable $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$, see Lemma B.4. The increasing convex order on $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ is defined by

$$
\xi \preccurlyeq \text { icx } \eta \quad \text { if and only if } \quad Q_{\xi}(u) \leq Q_{\eta}(u) \quad \text { for all } u \in(0,1)
$$

The ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {icx }}\right)$ is a complete lattice, see [14, 22]. In particular, every sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}_{1}$ which is bounded from above has a supremum $\xi^{*}=\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n}$ which is determined by

$$
Q_{\xi^{*}}(u)=\operatorname{conc}\left(Q_{\xi_{1}}, Q_{\xi_{2}}, \cdots\right)(u) \quad \text { for all } u \in(0,1)
$$

Here, $\operatorname{conc}\left(Q_{\xi_{1}}, Q_{\xi_{2}}, \cdots\right)$ denotes the concave hull of the sequence $\left(Q_{\xi_{n}}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, i.e., the smallest concave function $Q^{*}:(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty]$ with $\sup _{n \in \mathbb{N}} Q_{\xi_{n}}(u) \leq Q^{*}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)^{22}$

Let $\Phi_{\text {icx }}:=\left\{\phi_{u}: u \in(0,1)\right\}$ be the family of functions $\phi_{u}: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by $\phi_{u}(\xi):=Q_{\xi}(u)$. We identify $\Phi_{\text {icx }}$ with $(0,1)$, and endow $(0,1)$ with the Euclidean topology. For every $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$, the function $u \mapsto \phi_{u}(\xi)$ is continuous. Hence, the partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {icx }}\right)$ satisfies the assumptions of Section 4.

Lemma 5.5. Every concave function $\gamma:(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ is countably stable.
Proof. Let $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}_{1}$ with $\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} Q_{\xi_{n}}(u) \leq \gamma(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. Since $\gamma$ is concave, it holds $Q^{*}(u):=\operatorname{conc}\left(Q_{\xi_{1}}, Q_{\xi_{2}}, \cdots\right)(u) \leq \gamma(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. Since $u \mapsto Q^{*}(u)$ is real-valued, we obtain $Q_{\xi^{*}}=Q^{*}$, where $\xi^{*}=\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n} \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$, and $Q_{\xi^{*}}(u)=Q^{*}(u) \leq \gamma(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$.

For a function $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ with sublevel sets $A_{s}:=\left\{\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}: \psi(\xi) \leq s\right\}$, we define $\alpha_{\min }(s, u):=\sup _{\xi \in A_{s}} Q_{\xi}(u)$ and $\alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u):=\inf _{s<t} \alpha_{\min }(t, u)$ for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $u \in(0,1)$. If $\psi$ is countably maxitive, then the sublevel sets are countably upwards directed, from which it is straightforward to verify that the mapping $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(s, u)$ is real-valued and concave for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $A_{s} \neq \emptyset .{ }^{23}$ As a direct application of Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.4, we obtain the following representation result for maxitive functions w.r.t. the increasing convex stochastic order.

Corollary 5.6. Let $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
(i) $\psi$ is bounded countably maxitive w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {icx }}$.
(ii) $\psi$ is monotone and has countably upwards directed sublevel sets w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {icx }}$.

[^0]:    ${ }^{22}$ Notice that $\operatorname{conc}\left(Q_{\xi_{1}}, Q_{\xi_{2}}, \cdots\right)$ is the pointwise infimum over all concave functions $Q:(0,1) \rightarrow$ $(-\infty, \infty]$ with $Q_{\xi_{n}}(u) \leq Q(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$ and $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
    ${ }^{23}$ As for the concavity, we notice that for $\xi_{1}, \xi_{2} \in A_{s}$, there exists $\xi^{*} \in A_{s}$ with $Q_{\xi^{*}}=\operatorname{conc}\left(Q_{\xi_{1}}, Q_{\xi_{2}}\right)$ such that $\lambda Q_{\xi_{1}}\left(u_{1}\right)+(1-\lambda) Q_{\xi_{2}}\left(u_{2}\right) \leq Q_{\xi^{*}}\left(\lambda u_{1}+(1-\lambda) u_{2}\right)$ for all $u_{1}, u_{2}, \lambda \in(0,1)$.

(iii) There exists a function $\alpha: \mathbb{R} \times(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ which is non-decreasing in the first argument and concave in the second argument such that

$$
\psi(\xi)=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: \sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{Q_{\xi}(u)-\alpha(s, u)\right\} \leq 0\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}
$$

The infimum is attained for all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$ with $\psi(\xi)<\infty$.
(iv) The mapping $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(s, u)$ is real-valued and concave for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $A_{s} \neq \emptyset$. Moreover, it holds

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)} G\left(Q_{\xi}(u), u\right) \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}
$$

where $G(t, u):=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: t \leq \alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u)\right\}$ for all $(t, u) \in \mathbb{R} \times(0,1)$.
If $\psi$ in addition has the translation property, then we can argue as follows. Since the function $\xi \mapsto Q_{\xi}$ does not have the translation property, we consider the modified family $\Phi_{\mathrm{icx}}^{\prime}:=\left\{\mathrm{ES}_{u}: u \in(0,1)\right\}$. Here, $\mathrm{ES}_{u}: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is the expected shortfall given by

$$
\mathrm{ES}_{u}(\xi):=\frac{1}{1-u} Q_{\xi}(u) \quad \text { for all } u \in(0,1)
$$

The expected shortfall is a convex risk measure; see [12]. In particular, the functions $\mathrm{ES}_{u}$ have the translation property and also induce the partial order $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icx}}$. However, by changing to the family $\Phi_{\mathrm{icx}}^{\prime}$, we also change the set of countably stable functions. More precisely, a function $\gamma:(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty]$ is countably stable w.r.t. $\Phi_{\text {icx }}$ if and only if the function $u \mapsto \frac{1}{1-u} \gamma(u)$ is countably stable w.r.t. $\Phi_{\mathrm{icx}}^{\prime}$. Moreover, the minimal penalty function $\alpha_{\min }^{\prime}$ w.r.t. $\Phi_{\mathrm{icx}}^{\prime}$ is given by

$$
\alpha_{\min }^{\prime}(s, u)=\frac{1}{1-u} \alpha_{\min }(s, u)
$$

As a consequence of Corollary 4.4, we obtain the following result.
Corollary 5.7. Let $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function with the translation property. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
(i) $\psi$ is bounded countably maxitive w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icx}}$.
(ii) There exists a concave function $\alpha:(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ such that

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{\mathrm{ES}_{u}(\xi)-\frac{1}{1-u} \alpha(u)\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}
$$

(iii) The mapping $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(0, u)$ is real-valued and concave. Moreover, it holds

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{\mathrm{ES}_{u}(\xi)-\frac{1}{1-u} \alpha_{\min }(0, u)\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}
$$

The previous Corollary 5.7 is closely related to [32, Theorem 5]. Moreover, it is shown in [32] that the function $\mathrm{ES}_{u}$ does not always preserve the maximum of two randoms variables w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icx}}$, i.e., the function $\mathrm{ES}_{u}$ is not maxitive w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icx}}$.
5.3. Convex stochastic order. The convex order on $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ is defined by

$$
\xi \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{cx}} \eta \quad \text { if and only if } \quad \mathbb{E}[\xi]=\mathbb{E}[\eta] \text { and } \xi \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icx}} \eta
$$

The partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}, \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{cx}}\right)$ is not a lattice on $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ because it is not possible to define the maximum of two random variables $\xi, \nu \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$ for which $\mathbb{E}[\xi] \neq \mathbb{E}[\eta]$. However, for $r \in \mathbb{R}$, the convex order agrees with the increasing convex order on the set

$$
\mathcal{M}_{1}^{r}:=\left\{\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}: \mathbb{E}[\xi]=r\right\}
$$

In particular, $\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}^{r}, \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{cx}}\right)$ is a complete lattice. For $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1}^{r} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ with sublevel sets $A_{s}:=\left\{\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}^{r}: \psi(\xi) \leq s\right\}$, we define $\alpha_{\min }: \mathbb{R} \times(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty]$ by $\alpha_{\min }(s, u):=\sup _{\xi \in A_{s}} Q_{\xi}(u)$ and $\alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u):=\inf _{s<t} \alpha_{\min }(t, u)$. As a direct application of Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.4, we conclude that a function $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1}^{r} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is countably maxitive with respect to $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{cx}}$, if it admits a representation similar to that in Corollary 5.6, with $\mathcal{M}_{1}$ replaced by $\mathcal{M}_{1}^{r}$.
5.4. Increasing concave stochastic order. For $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$, we define the function $\bar{Q}_{\xi}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ by

$$
\bar{Q}_{\xi}(u):=-Q_{-\xi}(u)=-\int_{u}^{1} q_{-\xi}(v) \mathrm{d} v
$$

The mapping $t \mapsto \bar{Q}_{\xi}(t)$ is convex and satisfies $\bar{Q}_{\xi}\left(0^{+}\right)=\mathbb{E}[\xi]$ and $\bar{Q}_{\xi}\left(1^{-}\right)=0$. Conversely, every convex function $\bar{Q}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ with $\bar{Q}\left(0^{+}\right) \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\bar{Q}\left(1^{-}\right)=0$ is of the form $\bar{Q}=\bar{Q}_{\xi}$ for some random variable $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$. The increasing concave stochastic order is defined by

$$
\xi \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icv}} \eta \quad \text { if and only if } \quad-\eta \preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icx}}-\xi
$$

That is, $\xi \preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }} \eta$ if and only if $\bar{Q}_{\xi}(u) \leq \bar{Q}_{\eta}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. The partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }}\right)$ is a complete lattice, see [14, 22]. In particular, every sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}_{1}$ which is bounded from above w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }}$ has a supremum $\xi^{*}=\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \xi_{n}$ which is determined by $\bar{Q}_{\xi^{*}}(u)=\vee_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \bar{Q}_{\xi_{n}}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$. We consider the family $\Phi_{\text {icv }}:=\left\{\phi_{u}: u \in(0,1)\right\}$ of functions $\phi_{u}: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by $\phi_{u}(\xi):=\bar{Q}_{\xi}(u)$. Hence, the partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{1}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }}\right)$ satisfies the conditions of Section 4. With arguments similar to those for the usual stochastic order, we get the following result.

Lemma 5.8. Every function $\gamma:(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ is countably stable.
For a function $\psi: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ with sublevel sets $A_{s}:=\left\{\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}: \psi(\xi) \leq s\right\}$, we define $\alpha_{\min }(s, u):=\sup _{\xi \in A_{s}} \bar{Q}_{\xi}(u)$ and $\alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u):=\inf _{s<t} \alpha_{\min }(t, u)$ for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $u \in(0,1)$. If $\psi$ is countably maxitive, then the sublevel sets are countably upwards directed, so that $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(s, u)$ is real-valued for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $A_{s} \neq \emptyset$. As a direct application of Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.4, we obtain the following representation result for maxitive functions w.r.t. the increasing concave stochastic order.

Corollary 5.9. Let $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function. Then, the following conditions are equivalent.
(i) $\psi$ is bounded countably maxitive w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }}$.
(ii) $\psi$ is monotone and has countably upwards directed sublevel sets w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }}$.
(ii) There exists a function $\alpha: \mathbb{R} \times(0,1) \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty)$ which is non-decreasing in the first argument such that

$$
\psi(\xi)=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: \sup _{u \in(0,1)}\left\{\bar{Q}_{\xi}(u)-\alpha(s, u)\right\} \leq 0\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}
$$

The infimum is attained for all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$ with $\psi(\xi)<\infty$.
(iii) The mapping $u \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(s, u)$ is real-valued for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ with $A_{s} \neq \emptyset$. Moreover, it holds

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{u \in(0,1)} G\left(\bar{Q}_{\xi}(u), u\right) \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}
$$

where $G(t, u):=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: t \leq \alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u)\right\}$ for all $(t, u) \in \mathbb{R} \times(0,1)$.

In case that $\psi$ has the translation property, we can proceed as follows. Since the function $\xi \mapsto \bar{Q}_{\xi}$ does not have the translation property, we consider the modified family $\Phi_{\mathrm{icv}}^{\prime}:=\left\{\overline{\mathrm{ES}}_{u}: u \in(0,1)\right\}$, where $\overline{\mathrm{ES}}_{u}: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is defined by $\overline{\mathrm{ES}}_{u}(\xi):=-\mathrm{ES}_{u}(-\xi)$. The functions $\overline{\mathrm{ES}}_{u}$ are translation invariant and induce the order $\preccurlyeq_{\mathrm{icv}}$. The families $\Phi_{\mathrm{icv}}^{\prime}$ and $\Phi_{\mathrm{icv}}$ result in the same countably stable functions. In addition, we obtain

$$
\alpha_{\min }^{\prime}(s, u)=\frac{1}{1-u} \alpha_{\min }(s, u)
$$

where $\alpha_{\min }^{\prime}$ is the minimal penalty function w.r.t. $\Phi_{\mathrm{icv}}^{\prime}$. As a consequence of Corollary 4.4, we conclude that a function $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{1} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ with the translation property is countably maxitive with respect to $\preccurlyeq_{\text {icv }}$, if it admits a representation similar to that in Corollary 5.7, with $\mathrm{ES}_{u}$ replaced by $\overline{\mathrm{ES}}_{u}$.
5.5. Dispersive stochastic order. The dispersive stochastic order on $\mathcal{M}$ is defined by

$$
\xi \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }} \eta \quad \text { if and only if } \quad q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}(u) \leq q_{\eta}(v)-q_{\eta}(u) \text { for all } 0<u \leq v<1
$$

The dispersive order is not antisymmetric. However, by considering the quotient space $\mathcal{M} / \sim$ w.r.t. the equivalence relation $\xi \sim \eta$ if and only if $\xi=\eta+c$ for some $c \in \mathbb{R}$, we obtain that the partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M} / \sim, \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}\right)$ is a lattice, see [22].

For a non-empty set $Q$ of quantile functions and $[u, v] \subset[0,1]$, we define its total variation on $[u, v]$ as

$$
\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q):=\sup _{\pi \in \Pi[u, v]} S_{\pi}(Q)
$$

where $\Pi[u, v]$ consists of all partitions $\pi=\left\{u=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}=v\right\}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$. Here, we set $S_{\pi}(Q):=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sup _{q \in Q}\left(q\left(t_{i}\right)-q\left(t_{i-1}\right)\right)$ with $q(0):=q\left(0^{+}\right)$and $q(1):=q\left(1^{-}\right)$. We say that the set $Q$ is of bounded variation if $\mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}(Q)<\infty$. It is straightforward to verify that $\mathrm{TV}_{[0, v]}=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}+\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}$ for all $0<u \leq v<1$.
Proposition 5.10. Suppose that $Q:=\left\{q_{\xi}: \xi \in A\right\}$ is of bounded variation for some $A \subset \mathcal{M}$. Then, there exists $\xi^{*} \in \mathcal{M}$ such that $q_{\xi^{*}}(t)=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, t]}(Q)$ for all $t \in(0,1]$. Moreover, $\xi^{*}$ is a supremum of $A$ w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$.

Proof. By Proposition C. 1 and the fact that $Q$ is of bounded variation, the function $t \mapsto \mathrm{TV}_{[0, t]}(Q)$ is real-valued, non-decreasing and left-continuous. Hence, there exists $\xi^{*} \in \mathcal{M}$ such that $q_{\xi^{*}}(t)=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, t]}(Q)$ for all $t \in(0,1]$. Given $u, v \in \mathbb{R}$ with $0<u \leq$ $v<1$, for every $\xi \in A$, we have that

$$
q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}(u) \leq \mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q)=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, v]}(Q)-\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}(Q)=q_{\xi^{*}}(v)-q_{\xi^{*}}(u)
$$

Thus, $\xi^{*}$ is an upper bound of $A$ w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$. On the other hand, if $\eta$ is another upper bound of $A$ w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$, we necessarily have that

$$
q_{\xi^{*}}(v)-q_{\xi^{*}}(u)=\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q) \leq \mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}\left(q_{\eta}\right)=q_{\eta}(v)-q_{\eta}(u)
$$

where we have used in the last equality that $q_{\eta}$ is non-decreasing. This implies that $\xi^{*} \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }} \eta$.
Corollary 5.11. The partially ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{\infty} / \sim, \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}\right)$ is a complete lattice.
Proof. Let $A \subset \mathcal{M}_{\infty} / \sim$ be a set which is bounded from above w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$, and denote by $A_{0}$ the set of respective representatives $\xi$ with $q_{\xi}\left(0^{+}\right)=0$. Suppose that $\xi^{*}$ is an upper bound of $A_{0}$. Then

$$
\mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}\left(A_{0}\right) \leq \mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}\left(q_{\xi^{*}}\right)=q_{\xi^{*}}\left(1^{-}\right)-q_{\xi^{*}}\left(0^{+}\right)<\infty
$$

Hence, $A_{0}$ is of bounded variation and has a supremum in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$ by Proposition 5.10. Then passing to the quotient, $A$ has a unique supremum in $\mathcal{M}_{\infty} / \sim$.

It follows from Proposition 5.10 that every sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ which is bounded from above w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$ has a supremum $\xi^{*} \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ which is determined by

$$
q_{\xi^{*}}(u):=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right) \quad \text { for all } u \in(0,1]
$$

Here, for $0 \leq u<v \leq 1$, we denote by $\operatorname{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q):=\sup _{\pi \in \Pi[u, v]} S_{\pi}(Q)$ the total variation along $[u, v]$ of a non-empty set $Q$ of quantile functions, where $\Pi[u, v]$ is the set of all partitions of the form $\pi=\left\{u=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}=v\right\}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$, for which we set $S_{\pi}(Q):=\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sup _{q \in Q}\left(q\left(t_{i}\right)-q\left(t_{i-1}\right)\right)$ with $q(0):=q\left(0^{+}\right)$and $q(1):=q\left(1^{-}\right)$. It follows from Proposition B. 2 that

$$
\xi \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }} \eta \quad \text { if and only if } \quad q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}^{+}(u) \leq q_{\eta}(v)-q_{\eta}^{+}(u) \text { for all } 0<u<v<1
$$

where $q_{\xi}^{+}(u):=\inf \{x \in \mathbb{R}: \mathbb{P}(\xi \leq x)>u\}$ is the right quantile function of $\xi$.
In the following, we consider the family $\Phi_{\text {disp }}:=\left\{\phi_{u, v}: 0<u<v<1\right\}$ of functions $\phi_{u, v}: \mathcal{M}_{\infty} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ defined by $\phi_{u, v}(\xi):=q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}^{+}(u)$. We identify $\Phi_{\text {disp }}$ with the set $\Delta:=\left\{(u, v) \in \mathbb{R}^{2}: 0<u<v<1\right\}$ which we endow with the Euclidean topology. ${ }^{24}$ It follows from (5.1) that the family $\Phi_{\text {disp }}$ induces the dispersive order on $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$. By Proposition B.1, the mapping $(u, v) \mapsto \phi_{u, v}(\xi)$ is lower semicontinuous on $\Delta$ for all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$. Hence, the ordered space $\left(\mathcal{M}_{\infty}, \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}\right)$ satisfies the assumptions of Section 4.

Lemma 5.12. A function $\alpha: \Delta \rightarrow[0, \infty)$ is countably stable if there exists a nondecreasing function $\beta:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $\alpha(u, v)=\beta(v)-\beta(u)$ for all $(u, v) \in \Delta$.

Proof. Suppose that $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \subset \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ satisfies $\sup _{n \in \mathbb{N}}\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}(v)-q_{\xi_{n}}^{+}(u)\right\} \leq \alpha(u, v)$ for all $(u, v) \in \Delta$. As an application of Proposition C. 2 and Proposition C.1, we obtain that

$$
\mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right)=\lim _{t \rightarrow 1^{-}} \mathrm{TV}_{[0, t]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right) \leq \beta(1)-\beta(0)<\infty
$$

By Proposition 5.10, the sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ has a supremum $\xi^{*} \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ which is determined by

$$
q_{\xi^{*}}(u)=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right) \quad \text { for all } u \in(0,1]
$$

Then for $(u, v) \in \Delta$, we obtain from $\mathrm{TV}_{[0, v]}=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}+\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}$ that

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{\xi^{*}}(v)-q_{\xi^{*}}^{+}(u) & \leq \mathrm{TV}_{[0, v]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right)-\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right) \\
& =\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}\left(\left\{q_{\xi_{n}}: n \in \mathbb{N}\right\}\right) \leq \beta(v)-\beta(u)=\alpha(u, v)
\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\alpha$ is countable stable.
A set $Q$ of quantile functions is of bounded variation if $\mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}(Q)<\infty$.
Lemma 5.13. Let $A$ be a non-empty subset of $\mathcal{M}_{\infty}$. If $A$ is countably directed w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$, then the set $Q:=\left\{q_{\xi}: \xi \in A\right\}$ is of bounded variation and satisfies

$$
\sup _{\xi \in A}\left(q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}^{+}(u)\right)=\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q) \quad \text { for all }(u, v) \in \Delta
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{24}$ Although $\Delta$ is not a complete metric space, it is completely metrizable as it is an open subset, see [33, Theorem 24.12]. In particular, $\Delta$ is a Polish space with the Euclidean topology.

Proof. By contradiction, suppose that $\mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}(Q)=\infty$. Then there exists a sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \in A$ and partitions $\pi_{1} \subset \pi_{2} \subset \cdots$ of $[0,1]$ with $\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} S_{\pi}\left(q_{\xi_{n}}\right)=\infty$. Since $A$ is countably directed, the sequence $\left(\xi_{n}\right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ has a supremum $\xi^{*} \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$. Then

$$
\infty=\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} S_{\pi_{n}}\left(q_{\xi_{n}}\right) \leq \sup _{n \rightarrow \infty} S_{\pi_{n}}\left(q_{\xi^{*}}\right) \leq \mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}\left(q_{\xi^{*}}\right)
$$

in contradiction to $\mathrm{TV}_{[0,1]}\left(q_{\xi^{*}}\right)<\infty$ since $\xi^{*}$ is essentially bounded. This shows that $Q$ is of bounded variation.

Define $\alpha(u, v):=\sup _{\xi \in A}\left(q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}^{+}(u)\right)$. For $(u, v) \in \Delta$, it follows from Proposition C. 2 that

$$
\alpha(u, v) \leq \mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q)
$$

To prove the equality, suppose by contradiction that $\alpha(u, v)<\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}(Q)$. Then by Proposition C.2, there exists a partition $\pi:=\left\{u=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{n}=v\right\}$ with

$$
\alpha(u, v)<\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sup _{\xi \in A}\left(q_{\xi}\left(t_{i}\right)-q_{\xi}^{+}\left(t_{i-1}\right)\right)<\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(q_{\xi_{i}}\left(t_{i}\right)-q_{\xi_{i}}^{+}\left(t_{i-1}\right)\right)
$$

for some $\xi_{1}, \xi_{2}, \cdots, \xi_{n} \in A$. Since $A$ is countably directed, the exists $\xi^{*} \in A$ such that $\xi_{1}, \ldots, \xi_{n} \preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }} \xi^{*}$. Then

$$
\alpha(u, v)<\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(q_{\xi^{*}}\left(t_{i}\right)-q_{\xi^{*}}^{+}\left(t_{i-1}\right)\right) \leq q_{\xi^{*}}(v)-q_{\xi^{*}}^{+}(u) \leq \alpha(u, v)
$$

which is a contradiction.
For a function $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{\infty} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ with sublevel sets $A_{s}:=\left\{\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}: \psi(\xi) \leq s\right\}$, we define $\alpha_{\min }(s, u, v):=\sup _{\xi \in A_{s}}\left(q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}^{+}(u)\right)$ and $\alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u, v):=\inf _{s<t} \alpha_{\min }(t, u, v)$ for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $(u, v) \in \Delta$.

Let $I:=\left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: A_{s} \neq \emptyset\right\}$. If $\psi$ has countably upwards directed sublevel sets, it follows from Lemma 5.13 that for every $s \in I$, the set $Q_{s}:=\left\{q_{\xi}: \xi \in A_{s}\right\}$ is of bounded variation, and $\alpha_{\min }(s, u, v)=\beta(s, v)-\beta(s, u)$ for all $(u, v) \in \Delta$ where $\beta(s, u):=\mathrm{TV}_{[0, u]}\left(Q_{s}\right)$. Moreover, the mapping $\beta: \mathbb{R} \times(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is non-decreasing in the second argument and satisfies $\beta(s, v)-\beta(s, u) \leq \beta\left(s^{\prime}, v\right)-\beta\left(s^{\prime}, u\right)$ for all $s \leq s^{\prime}$. As a direct application of Theorem 4.1, we obtain the following representation result for maxitive functions w.r.t. the dispersive stochastic order.

Corollary 5.14. Let $\psi: \mathcal{M}_{\infty} \rightarrow(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function with sublevel sets $\left(A_{s}\right)_{s \in \mathbb{R}}$. Then, the following conditions are equivalent:
(1) $\psi$ is monotone and $\left(A_{s}\right)_{s \in \mathbb{R}}$ are countably upwards directed w.r.t. $\preccurlyeq_{\text {disp }}$.
(2) There exists a function $\beta: I \times(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ which is non-decreasing in the second argument, and satisfies $\beta(s, v)-\beta(s, u) \leq \beta\left(s^{\prime}, v\right)-\beta\left(s^{\prime}, u\right)$ for all $s \leq s^{\prime}$ and $(u, v) \in \Delta$. Moreover, it holds

$$
\psi(\xi)=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: \sup _{(u, v) \in \Delta}\left\{q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}\left(u^{+}\right)-\alpha(s, u, v)\right\} \leq 0\right\} \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}
$$

where $\alpha(s, u, v):=\beta(s, v)-\beta(s, u)$ for all $s \in I$, and $\alpha(s, u, v):=\infty$ otherwise. The infimum is attained for all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}$ with $\psi(\xi)<\infty$.
(3) For every $s \in I$, the set $Q_{s}:=\left\{q_{\xi}: \xi \in A_{s}\right\}$ is of bounded variation and $\alpha_{\min }(s, u, v)=\mathrm{TV}_{[u, v]}\left(Q_{s}\right)$ for all $(u, v) \in \Delta$. Moreover, it holds

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{(u, v) \in \Delta} G\left(q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}^{+}(u), u, v\right) \quad \text { for all } \xi \in \mathcal{M}_{\infty}
$$

where $G(t, u, v):=\inf \left\{s \in \mathbb{R}: t \leq \alpha_{\min }^{+}(s, u, v)\right\}$ for all $(t, u, v) \in \mathbb{R} \times \Delta$.
We conclude with an example of a maxitive function for the dispersive order.
Example 5.15. Consider the function $\beta:[0, \infty) \times(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, defined by $\beta(s, u):=s u$. The function

$$
\psi(\xi):=\sup _{(u, v) \in \Delta} \frac{q_{\xi}(v)-q_{\xi}\left(u^{+}\right)}{v-u} \in[0, \infty]
$$

satisfies the equivalent conditions of Corollary 5.14 and is therefore bounded countably maxitive on $\mathcal{M}_{\infty} / \sim$. The value $\psi(\xi)$ corresponds to the Lipschitz constant of $q_{\xi}$. In particular, if $q_{\xi}$ is differentiable, it holds that

$$
\psi(\xi)=\sup _{s \in(0,1)} q_{\xi}^{\prime}(s)
$$

In reliability analysis, the derivative $q_{\xi}^{\prime}(s)$ is referred to as the quantile density function and measures the rate of change of the quantile function; see [30]. When $\xi$ models the uncertain time to failure of a system, $q_{\xi}(u)$ corresponds to the time at which the survival probability of the system is $1-u$. A high value of $q_{\xi}^{\prime}(u)$ implies that small reductions in survival probability correspond to larger increases in time, indicating a slower rate of reliability decline over time. Consequently, $\psi(\xi)$ acts as a measure of the speed at which the reliability of the system decreases, capturing the steepest rate of decline.

question: Is Ichigo's latency faster than that of Whisper + Llama-3 systems?
answer: Yes, Ichigo's latency is significantly faster than that of Whisper + Llama-3 systems.

### 5.2 Latency to first token

To validate the efficiency of Ichigo's Tokenized Early Fusion architecture, we conducted a comparative analysis of its latency to first token against current speech models and cascaded systems. Our benchmarking was performed on a single NVIDIA A6000-48GB GPU, performing 10 iterations of the latency test. The test set comprised 10 diverse audio files with durations ranging from 1 to 5 seconds (average length: $5.4 \pm$

2.79 seconds), reflecting real-world usage scenarios. This setup ensures a comprehensive evaluation across various audio lengths.

question: Can the Stubborn Nakamoto protocol regain liveness after an attack?
answer: Yes, the Stubborn Nakamoto protocol can regain liveness after an attack if it regains an honest majority and uses a recovery oracle.

evidence.text:
# 4.4 Recovery 

We turn to consider the recovery of Stubborn Nakamoto after an attack. An attacker with sufficient resources can cause nodes to halt and the protocol to lose liveness. But suppose that the attacker ends their efforts after some time, and the protocol regains honest majority. Can the protocol recover and regain liveness while maintaining consistency? In particular, can the protocol ensure that any block finalized by a node before or during the attack does not conflict with new blocks that are finalized after recovery?

We show that the Stubborn Nakamoto protocol can recover with external assistance that we model as a recovery oracle and that such external assistance is necessary. The recovery

oracle models a community response to the attack, allowing us to evaluate the necessary capabilities required from the community. Any protocol requires some community action to establish agreement on its rules. In particular, the Nakamoto protocol relies on an external agreement on a genesis block. ${ }^{57}$ We show that Stubborn Nakamoto can recover from an attack with a new genesis block provided by the recovery oracle.

The following defines a recovery oracle that enables the recovery of the Stubborn Nakamoto protocol. This definition formalizes the exact function the community (or another external source) must provide to the protocol. The recovery oracle is practical only if its capabilities are limited to those the community can plausibly implement. While we do not formally model the community's capabilities to achieve consensus, we bear in mind that the community must have been able to initiate the protocol and provide the genesis block (potentially through a costly process) but is unlikely to maintain real-time knowledge of every honest node's local view. Therefore, our definition of the recovery oracle relies solely on having access to the view of a single honest node.

Definition 7 (Recovery Oracle). A call to a recovery oracle at time $t$ updates the protocol's setup by creating a new genesis block $\mathrm{B}_{G}$, which extends all clear-certified blocks in the view of some arbitrarily selected honest node. The call also awakes honest nodes that halted.

In other words, a call to the recovery oracle restarts the protocol in a similar manner to the initial launch of the Nakamoto protocol: the call announces a genesis block that any future chain must extend. All honest nodes ignore blocks that do not extend the new genesis block. The recovery oracle requires some contemporary knowledge of the state of honest nodes running the protocol, as it needs to maintain consistency with all finalized blocks. However, the recovery oracle is only required to know the state of a single (arbitrarily selected) honest node. Thus, we argue that this recovery oracle can be plausibly implemented by the community. ${ }^{58}$

Theorem 5 (Consistency and liveness after recovery). Under synchrony, consider Stubborn Nakomoto with a call to the recovery oracle at time T. Suppose that the network-aware honest majority assumption holds from time $T$ onwards. Then, Stubborn Nakamoto satisfies consistency at any time and liveness after time $T$.

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{57}$ That is, the participants of the protocol must achieve agreement on the genesis block by means that are out of protocol.
    ${ }^{58}$ The Stubborn Nakamoto protocol is specifically designed to allow a recovery oracle that uses only limited capabilities (that the community can plausibly implement); see Lemma 2 and the discussion below.

An attacker with sufficient resources can cause the Stubborn Nakamoto protocol to lose liveness. Even after a call to the recovery oracle, the attacker can repeat its attack to cause the protocol to lose liveness again. Given the impossibility results mentioned above, such a loss of liveness is unavoidable for any protocol that maintains consistency. However, it is costly for the attacker to continuously violate liveness: each liveness violation requires the attacker to create an attack chain that certifies or potentially certifies a conflicting block, and all blocks in the attack chain are discarded after the call to the recovery oracle. Theorem 5 guarantees that when the attacker stops and Stubborn Nakamoto regains an honest majority, Stubborn Nakamoto recovers liveness (while maintaining consistency throughout).

Remark 3. Theorem 5 holds under the protocol modification described in Remark 1. If online nodes detect an attack chain and ignore it without halting-while invoking the recovery oracle - then late joiners will be directed to the correct ledger by the recovery oracle, ensuring consistency.

The following lemma provides the key argument for the consistency of Stubborn Nakamoto after recovery. A genesis block establishes agreement on an initial ledger. Lemma 2 implies that the recovery oracle establishes a ledger that maintains consistency with any transactions finalized by honest nodes before recovery.

Lemma 2 (Consistency guarantees for recovery). If some honest node $i$ finalizes block B, then every honest node $j$ clear-certifies block B. If some honest node $i$ finalizes block B and does not halt, then all honest nodes finalize block B.

Proof. Suppose that honest node $i$ certified block $B$ at time $t_{1}$ and finalized block $B$ at time $t_{2}=t_{1}+2 \Delta$. Let Chain $(\widehat{\mathrm{B}})$ be a logest chain in the view of node $i$ at time $t$ such that B is at least $k$-deep in Chain $(\widehat{\mathrm{B}})$.

Suppose for the sake of contradiction that some honest node $j$ does not clear-certify B. Node $j$ receives Chain $(\widehat{\mathrm{B}})$ by time $t+\Delta$. If Chain $(\widehat{\mathrm{B}})$ (or an extension of it) is a longest chain in the view of node $j$, then it must be that there is some block $\mathrm{B}^{\prime}$ such that $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \nsim \mathrm{B}$ and $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \in \mathcal{C}_{j}^{t+\Delta}$. But then we have by Lemma 1 that $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \in \mathcal{P} \mathcal{C}_{i}^{t+2 \Delta}(2 \Delta)$, which is a contradiction to $i$ finalizing $B$.

Suppose then that there is a longer chain $\operatorname{Chain}\left(\widehat{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}\right)$ in the view of node $j$ at time $t+\Delta$. Suppose that block B does not appear $k$-deep in Chain $\left(\widehat{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}\right)$ (otherwise, we reach a contradiction using the previous argument). Then there must be a block $\mathrm{B}^{\prime}$ that is at least $k$-deep in Chain $\left(\widehat{\mathrm{B}}^{\prime}\right)$ and $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \nsim \mathrm{B}$. Again, we have $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \in \mathcal{C}_{j}^{t+\Delta}$, leading to a contradiction.

For the second part of the proof, suppose that honest node $i$ certified block B at time $t_{1}$, finalized block B at time $t_{2}=t_{1}+2 \Delta$, and did not halt at time $t_{3}=t_{1}+4 \Delta$. By the previous part of the proof, every honest node $j$ clear-certified block B. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that some node $j$ did not finalize block B. Observe that node $j$ certified block B by time $t_{1}+\Delta$, and therefore it must be that node $j$ halts without finalizing $B$ at some time $t^{\prime} \leq t_{1}+3 \Delta$. But this implies that there exists some $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \in \mathcal{P C}_{j}^{t^{\prime}}(2 \Delta)$ such that $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \nsim \mathrm{B}$, and by Lemma 1 we have that $\mathrm{B}^{\prime} \in \mathcal{P C}_{i}^{t^{\prime}+\Delta}(4 \Delta) \subseteq \mathcal{P C}_{i}^{t_{3}}(4 \Delta)$ in contradiction to $i$ not halting at time $t_{3}$.

The proof of Theorem 5 follows from the lemma. A call to the recovery oracle maintains consistency and helps the protocol regain liveness when the attacker no longer controls a majority of the nodes. We remark that the theorem holds even when there are arbitrarily many calls to the recovery oracle.

Proof of Theorem 5. By Theorem 2, the protocol satisfies liveness after it recovers. By Theorem 1, if nodes $i, j$ finalize blocks $\mathrm{B}, \mathrm{B}^{\prime}$ of the same height before recovery, then $\mathrm{B}=\mathrm{B}^{\prime}$. Likewise, by Theorem 1, if nodes $i, j$ finalize blocks $\mathrm{B}, \mathrm{B}^{\prime}$ of the same height after recovery, then $\mathrm{B}=\mathrm{B}^{\prime}$. Suppose that node $i$ finalizes block B before recovery. By Lemma 2, every honest node clear-certified block B. Therefore, after recovery, the block B is part of the chain of the new genesis block $\mathrm{B}_{G}$ and is finalized by any honest node $j$.

The Stubborn Nakamoto with a recovery oracle provides strong guarantees to users. Consistency is always guaranteed, and protocol participants cannot be deceived. An attacker can disrupt liveness, but only temporarily. An attacker can force the community to take potentially costly actions to implement the recovery oracle, but attacks are costly for the attacker (who needs to create blocks that are discarded). Because the existence of a recovery oracle limits the harm an attacker can cause, the recovery oracle may completely deter attackers without ever being used.

The protocol relies on the recovery oracle, but the recovery oracle's influence over the system is highly constrained. First, this dependence is necessary only after the protocol is attacked. Second, any honest node can assume the role of the recovery oracle. Third, the ambiguity that the recovery oracle addresses is minimal, as the protocol ensures agreement on all blocks except those finalized within a brief time window.

question: How does the proposed new foundation aim to improve upon existing ones like ZFC?
answer: The proposed new foundation aims to improve upon existing ones like ZFC by introducing concepts such as the "coherent limit axiom," which better aligns with mainstream deductive practices and addresses unresolved questions within set theory, such as the continuum hypothesis.

evidence.text:
## 1. ABSTRACT

This article was motivated by the discovery of a potential new foundation for mainstream mathematics. The goals are to clarify the relationships between primitives, foundations, and deductive practice; to understand how to determine what is, or isn't, a foundation; and get clues as to how a foundation can be optimized for effective human use. For this we turn to history and professional practice of the subject. We have no asperations to Philosophy.

The first section gives a short abstract discussion, focusing on the significance of consistency. The next briefly describes foundations, explicit and implicit, at a few key periods in mathematical history. We see, for example, that at the primitive level human intuitions are essential, but can be problematic. We also see that traditional axiomatic set theories, Zermillo-Fraenkel-Choice (ZFC) in particular, are not quite consistent with mainstream practice. The final section sketches the proposed new foundation and gives the basic argument that it is uniquely qualified to be considered the foundation of mainstream deductive mathematics. The "coherent limit axiom" characterizes the new theory among ZFC-like theories. This axiom plays a role in recursion, but is implicitly assumed in mainstream work so does not provide new leverage there. In principle it should settle set-theory questions such as the continuum hypothesis.

question: What is the importance of measurement equivalence in health outcome evaluations?
answer: Measurement equivalence is crucial in health outcome evaluations to ensure that assessments are fair and valid across different demographic groups, such as those differing in gender or ethnicity. This helps identify any disproportionate impacts of health interventions on certain populations.

evidence.text:
# 1 Introduction 

To examine the disproportionate impact of health interventions or other determinants on health outcomes for certain populations, including disadvantaged minorities, it is crucial to establish measurement equivalence when evaluating outcomes across groups differing in gender, ethnicity, and other demographic factors. While validating psychometric instruments has been a routine practice in research, critical evaluations of measurement equivalence, particularly through differential item functioning (DIF) analysis, have historically been limited [1]. In recent years, however, there has been significant progress in this area, with a growing body of research employing DIF analysis to investigate measurement equivalence [e.g., 2-7].

This growing research underscores the need for continued evaluation of health constructs and measures to ensure fairness and validity in assessing health outcomes for diverse populations. It is worth noting that some health studies did not clearly describe the method used for DIF analysis [e.g., 3], and conventional DIF methods based on single-level models were frequently used to analyze health survey data with a nesting structure [e.g., 2], for which recent DIF methods based on multilevel models are better alternatives in terms of accuracy of DIF estimation. By employing advanced methodologies for DIF, researchers can better evaluate health measures to ensure fairness and validity in assessing health outcomes for diverse populations.

# 2. The Friedmann Equation and Expansion with Time 

To review, Einstein's field equations combined with the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric lead directly to the Friedmann Equation, which was also derived by Lemaître. ${ }^{18}$ This equation provides an expression for the expansion of the Universe over time ${ }^{19}$ :

$$
H^{2}=\left(\frac{\dot{a}}{a}\right)^{2}=\frac{8 \pi G}{3} \rho_{M}-k / a^{2}+\Lambda / 3
$$

Here $H$ represents the Hubble "constant", which is actually a function of time. The variable $a$ is the scale factor representing the size of the Universe. The term $\rho_{M}$ denotes the large-scale mass density of the Universe, including any contribution from radiation. The parameter $k$ represents the curvature of space, with $k$ equal to 0 indicating a flat Universe. Finally, $\Lambda$ is Einstein's cosmological constant, measured in SI units of meters ${ }^{-2}$.

Commonly, one encapsulates the key components of the Universe as,

$$
\Omega_{\mathrm{M}}+\Omega_{\Lambda}=\Omega_{\mathrm{tot}}
$$

Here, $\Omega_{\mathrm{M}}$ and $\Omega_{\Lambda}$ represent the fractions of the total mass-energy density of the Universe contributed by mass and "dark energy", respectively, normalized to a flat Universe where $\Omega_{\text {tot }}=1$. A value of $\Omega_{\text {tot }}$ less than 1 indicates an open Universe, while a value greater than 1 indicates a closed geometry. By 1993, observational constraints suggested that $\Omega_{\mathrm{M}}$ was 0.1 to 0.3 (see the following section), and $\Omega_{\Lambda}$ was generally assumed to be zero or ignored, leading to an estimate of $\Omega_{\text {tot }} \approx 0.2$. This implied an open Universe, destined to expand forever.

Yet, the plausibly flat geometry implied by theory, especially to solve the horizon problem, ${ }^{20}$ predicted that

$$
\Omega_{\mathrm{M}+} \Omega_{\Lambda}=1
$$

One may integrate eq. 1 analytically or numerically to compute the time since the Big Bang, the time since $a=0$, as a function of $\mathrm{H}_{0}, \rho_{M}$ and $\Lambda$, or equivalently as a function of $\mathrm{H}_{0}, \Omega_{\mathrm{M}}$ and $\Omega_{\Lambda} .{ }^{21}$ Carroll et al. provide useful approximations for the age of the Universe as a function of $\mathrm{H}_{0}, \Omega_{\mathrm{M}}$ and $\Omega_{\Lambda} \cdot{ }^{22}$

Extensive efforts were made to measure the deceleration of the Universe using standard candles, such as Cepheid variables, planetary nebulae, supergiants, horizontal branch stars, and both Type I and Type II supernovae. Additionally, other observables were measured to test the validity of a matter-only Universe that was decelerating. These observables included $\mathrm{H}_{0}$, the density of the Universe, the ages of the oldest known stars, the large-scale structure of the Universe, and the anisotropy of the cosmic microwave background, as summarized in the section below.

question: What is a fixed-fee AMM (ff-AMM)?
answer: A fixed-fee AMM (ff-AMM) is a standard automated market maker design with a fixed fee $f \in\left[0, f_{\max }\right]$.

# 3.1. Fixed-Fee AMM Model 

As a benchmark, we consider the standard AMM design with a fixed fee $f \in\left[0, f_{\max }\right]$, which we refer to as a fixed-fee AMM (ff-AMM). Following the discussion above, we define the instantaneous rate of aggregate expected $\mathrm{P} \& \mathrm{~L}$ of LPs in this pool in excess of the risk free rate according to

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\mathrm{LP}}(f, L) & \triangleq f H(f, L)-\operatorname{ARB} \_ \operatorname{PROFIT}(f, L)-r V(L) \\
& =\left(f H_{0}(f, L)-\mathrm{AP}_{0}(f)-r\right) V(L)
\end{aligned}
$$

where the first term in the sum is the revenue from noise traders, the second term is the loss to arbs, and the final term is a capital charge, where $r>0$ is the risk-free rate. Under free entry and exit of LPs, we define the equilibrium in the fixed-fee AMM according to a zero profit condition:
Lemma 1 (ff-AMM equilibrium). Given fee $f \in\left[0, f_{\max }\right]$, define a liquidity level $L^{*}>0$ to be a competitive equilibrium if LPs earn zero profit in excess of the risk free rate, i.e., $\Pi_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\mathrm{LP}}\left(f, L^{*}\right)=0$. Then, for any $f \in\left[0, f_{\max }\right]$, a unique equilibrium level of liquidity $L^{*}=L_{\mathrm{ff}}(f)$ exists.

question: Can a PoS protocol regain liveness once an honest majority is restored?
answer: Yes, a PoS protocol can regain liveness once an honest majority is restored.

evidence.text:
# 5.2 Necessity of Recovery Oracles 

We provide a version of the impossibility result given in Theorem 6 for PoS protocols. Consider a PoS protocol that guarantees consistency. Concurrent work of Sridhar et al. (2023) shows the feasibility of such PoS protocols under synchronous communication. But no protocol can always guarantee consistency and liveness under synchronous communication with late joiners (Pass and Shi, 2017a, Lewis-Pye and Roughgarden, 2023). ${ }^{66}$ Can a PoS

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{65}$ The protocol can avoid these costs if it can invest the staked funds. We thank Niels Gormsen for this observation.
    ${ }^{66}$ If all nodes are online and communication is synchronous, then the Dolev-Strong protocol guarantees consistency and liveness even without honest majority. But honest majority is necessary for the consistency of the Dolev-Strong protocol when late joiners are allowed.

protocol only lose liveness temporarily, halting progress while there is no honest majority, and regain liveness once honest majority is restored?

By Theorem 6, a recovery oracle is necessary if the protocol is permissionless. In practice, many PoS protocols require that active nodes approve late-joining nodes. ${ }^{67}$ This required approval can help secure the protocol by limiting the attacker's ability to simulate a conflicting protocol execution. However, such a limitation is helpful only if it introduces a different problem: the protocol can get stuck if no late-joining nodes are allowed to enter. We state this tension in the following corollary.

Corollary 1. Consider a protocol that, under synchrony, allows late joiners, always satisfies consistency, and for some $\rho>0$ and $\tau \geq 0$ satisfies liveness after time $T+\tau$ if from time $T$ onwards at least a fraction $1-\rho$ of the nodes are honest.

Then there exists some $\gamma \leq 1$ such that if a fraction $\gamma$ of the nodes crash, the protocol loses liveness forever.

The proof follows a similar argument to the proof of Theorem 6.
Proof. Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that such a protocol exists and regains liveness at some time after all nodes crash at time $t$. Then, it must be possible for late-joining nodes to join the protocol at some time $\tau>t$ despite all previous nodes crashing. Similarly to the proof of Theorem 6, the attacker can exploit this possibility to create a conflicting ledger $\log ^{\prime}$ by launching a separate collection of nodes that follow the protocol, except that they run as if all nodes crashed at time $t$.

Alternatively, suppose that the attacker controls all existing nodes at time $t$. The attacker continues running the nodes but makes it appear as if all nodes crashed. New late-joining honest nodes enter the protocol and generate the ledger Log. Because a late joiner cannot distinguish between the two scenarios, the protocol cannot guarantee consistency for late joiners.

Corollary 1 and Theorem 6 show that any protocol must require some external help under some scenarios: either to recover from attacks or to recover after all active nodes halt. In other words, some dependency on the community is unavoidable. Still, protocols can minimize this dependency by relying on external help only in rare scenarios and reducing the requirements needed for implementing such external help.

If such transactions are written to the ledger, and active nodes must process them (and can censor them), late-joining nodes will require approval from active nodes.

question: What type of random variables are used in the construction of the generalized beta density?
answer: Gamma random variables.

evidence.text:
## C. 2 Bivariate OPT
## C.2.1 Construction of the Generalized Beta Density.

The generalized beta densities used in the bivariate density estimation problems were constructed as follows. Let $G_{0} \sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha_{0}, \beta_{0}\right), G_{1} \sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha_{1}, \beta_{1}\right)$ and $G_{2} \sim \operatorname{Gamma}\left(\alpha_{2}, \beta_{2}\right)$ be three independent gamma random variables, with $\alpha_{1}, \beta_{i}>0$ for $i=0,1,2$. The joint density of $X=G_{1} /\left(G_{1}+G_{0}\right)$ and $Y=G_{2} /\left(G_{2}+G_{0}\right)$, with $x, y \in(0,1)$ has the form

$$
f(x, y)=\frac{1}{B\left(\alpha_{0}, \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}\right)} \frac{\lambda_{1}^{\alpha_{1}} x^{\alpha_{1}-1}(1-x)^{-\left(\alpha_{1}+1\right)} \lambda_{2}^{\alpha_{2}} y^{\alpha_{2}-1}(1-y)^{-\left(\alpha_{2}+1\right)}}{\left[1+\lambda_{1} x /(1-x)+\lambda_{2} y /(1-y)\right]^{\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}}
$$

and $\lambda_{i}=\beta_{i} / \beta_{0}$ for $i=1,2$ and $B\left(\alpha_{0}, \alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}\right)=\prod_{i=0,1,2} \Gamma\left(\alpha_{i}\right) / \Gamma\left(\sum \alpha_{i}\right)$ ).

question: Is there a preference cycle among choices in the Linear Exchange method?
answer: No, there are no cycles formed among choices.

evidence.text:
# Example 3. Naive Efficient Serial Dictatorship versus Linear Exchange 

Consider the following market with $C=\{a, b, c\}$ and $H=\{1,2,3\}$. The preferences, evaluations, and induced unanimity orders are as follows, where omitted homes are not unanimously acceptable and brackets indicate indifference:

![table_4](table_4)

If the Naive Serial Dictatorship uses the order $a, b, c$, then the matching is $\mu=$ $(1,3, \varnothing)$. However, the matching $\mu^{\prime}=(1,2,3)$ is unanimous and Pareto dominates $\mu$. We demonstrate how Linear Exchange produces $\mu^{\prime}$ using the same order. The rounds of Linear Exchange proceed as follows, where $i \rightarrow k$ implies that $\mu^{n+1}(i)=k$ and $i \downarrow$ implies $i \notin C^{n+1}$.

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
n=1 & n=2 & n=3 & n=4 \\
a \rightarrow 1 & b \rightarrow 3 & c \rightarrow 3 & b \rightarrow 2 \\
a \downarrow & & c \downarrow & b \downarrow
\end{array}
$$

At $n=1, a$ immediately exits with 1 because it is unanimous and her most preferred home. However, at $n=2, b$ does not immediately exit with 3 because she has a more preferred home remaining, namely, home 2 . This allows $c$ to replace $b$ at $n=3$ because 3 is $c$ 's most preferred and unanimous home. Finally, $b$ exits with 2 at $n=4$ because no SU-cycle among the children would form when $b$ is matched to 2 .

Linear Exchange could produce one other matching, $\mu^{\prime \prime}=(2,1,3)$, using an order where $b$ goes before $a$. One can check that this matching also satisfies properties (i)-(iii) in Theorem 1.

question: What is the main difference between the likelihood contribution on a data-dependent tree and a fixed tree?
answer: The main difference is the extra component $f(x \mid A)$ in $m(A)$ for a data-dependent tree.

evidence.text:
# 2.2 A partial likelihood approach to inference 

The data-dependent nature of the above full likelihood decomposition hampers fully likelihoodbased strategies such as Bayesian inference. At the same time, we recognize a striking similarity of the likelihood contribution on node $A$ in a data-dependent tree, $m(A)$, compared to the corresponding likelihood contribution $m_{\text {fix }}(A)$ with a data-independent fixed tree. Both have a binomial likelihood component corresponding to those points that fall into $A_{l}$ versus $A_{r}$. The only difference is the extra component $f(x \mid A)$ in $m(A)$. However, we make two observations: (i) the branching probabilities $F\left(A_{l} \mid A\right)$ and $F\left(A_{r} \mid A\right)$ are sufficient for determining the probability distribution $F$ almost everywhere on $\Omega$; (ii) the density at the exact partition boundaries cannot be reliably inferred anyway, even with a fixed partition tree, as those are usually the boundaries of piecewise constant densities under tree-based models.

Consequently, we proceed by treating the exact conditional density of $f(\cdot \mid A)$ at the point $x_{A}$, i.e., $f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right)$, as "nuisance" parameters. Following the seminal work on the proportional hazards model (Cox, 1972), Cox (1975) formulated the notion of partial likelihood more generally by rewriting a data set $\boldsymbol{x}$ as $\boldsymbol{x}=\left(w_{1}, \boldsymbol{x}_{1}, w_{2}, \boldsymbol{x}_{2}, \ldots, w_{N}, \boldsymbol{x}_{N}\right)$ and assumed that the full likelihood can be written as $L(f ; \boldsymbol{x})=\prod_{j=1}^{N} f\left(w_{j} \mid d_{j}\right) \prod_{j=1}^{N} f\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{j} \mid c_{j}\right)$ where $d_{j}=$ $\left(w_{1}, \boldsymbol{x}_{1}, \ldots, w_{j-1}, \boldsymbol{x}_{j-1}\right)$ and $c_{j}=\left(w_{1}, \boldsymbol{x}_{1}, \ldots, w_{j-1}, \boldsymbol{x}_{j-1}, w_{j}\right)$.

To see that under the data-dependent tree, we have a likelihood factorization exactly of this form, one can simply replace the index $j$ in Cox's notation with a coarse-to-fine indexing of the nodes in a dyadic tree. There are various ways to define such an index. All we need is to ensure that it is consistent with a partial order of the nodes, so that a parent node always has a lower index $j$ than its children. For example, we can simply let $j$ be the order of a node $A$ corresponding to the dyadic sequence of 0 and 1 corresponding to whether a descendant of $A$ 's is the left or right child of a split. Now $w_{j}$ corresponds to $x_{A}$, the value on which we divide the node $A$. In this case, $f\left(w_{j} \mid d_{j}\right)$ is $f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right)$. On the other hand, each $\boldsymbol{x}_{j}$ corresponds simply to the collection of indicators of whether each point in $A$ falls into $A_{l}$ or $A_{r}$, whose conditional likelihood given $c_{j}$ depends only on the parameters of interest, here the branching probabilities $F\left(A_{l} \mid A\right)$ and $F\left(A_{r} \mid A\right)$. The first product generally involves some nuisance parameters, which in our context correspond to the exact conditional density $f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right)$ at the partition locations that define the dyadic tree. Cox refers to the second product in the factorization, $\prod_{j=1}^{N} f\left(\boldsymbol{x}_{j} \mid c_{j}\right)$, as the "partial likelihood".

We can write the tree-based likelihood decomposition in Cox's form. Specifically,

$$
L(f ; \boldsymbol{x}, \Omega)=\prod_{j} f\left(x_{A_{j}} \mid A_{j}\right) \cdot \prod_{j} m_{\mathrm{P}}\left(A_{j}\right)=\prod_{A \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x})} f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right) \cdot \prod_{A \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x})} m_{\mathrm{P}}(A)
$$

where $m_{\mathrm{P}}(A)=F\left(A_{l} \mid A\right)^{n\left(A_{l}\right)} F\left(A_{r} \mid A\right)^{n\left(A_{r}\right)}$. The second piece in this product gives Cox's partial likelihood $L_{\mathrm{P}}(f ; \boldsymbol{x}, \Omega)=\prod_{A \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x})} m_{\mathrm{P}}(A)$, which can be written recursively as

$$
L_{\mathrm{P}}(f ; \boldsymbol{x}, A)=m_{\mathrm{P}}(A) \cdot L_{\mathrm{P}}\left(f ; \boldsymbol{x}, A_{l}\right) \cdot L_{\mathrm{P}}\left(f ; \boldsymbol{x}, A_{r}\right)=\prod_{A^{\prime} \in \mathcal{T}_{A}(\boldsymbol{x})} m_{\mathrm{P}}\left(A^{\prime}\right)
$$

It is remarkable that this partial likelihood has essentially the same form as the full likelihood under a fixed-tree decomposition. This implies that inference strategies based on

the full likelihood on a fixed tree can be applied with little change to this partial likelihood by acting as if the data-dependent tree were actually fixed, though of course the validity of the resulting inference requires further justification, which we will provide later.

One question regards how much information is discarded by ignoring the "nuisance" portion of the likelihood, namely $\prod_{A \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x})} f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right)$. It is worth noting that the information discarded is much less than a conditional likelihood approach such as the one proposed in Lavine (1995), which conditions on the full set of observed partition points. To see this, note that the total contribution from the partition points to the full likelihood is $\prod_{A \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x})} f\left(x_{A}\right)$, where $f\left(x_{A}\right)$ is the density of $f$ (not conditional on $x_{A}$ being in $A$ ) evaluated at $x_{A}$. That is, $f\left(x_{A}\right)=f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right) \cdot F(A)$. In other words, the partial likelihood retains the information about $F$ from the event that the corresponding partition point on $A$ is an observation in $A$, and only discards the information provided by its relative value within $A$. Another way to see this is that the partition point $x_{A}$ contributes to the binomial likelihood on ancestral nodes of $A$ in the partial likelihood because

$$
F(A)=\prod_{A^{\prime} \in \mathcal{A}(A)} F\left(A_{l}^{\prime} \mid A^{\prime}\right)^{\mathbf{1}\left(x_{A} \in A_{l}^{\prime}\right)} F\left(A_{r}^{\prime} \mid A^{\prime}\right)^{\mathbf{1}\left(x_{A} \in A_{r}^{\prime}\right)}
$$

where $\mathcal{A}(A)=\left\{A^{\prime} \in \mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x}): A \varsubsetneqq A^{\prime}\right\}$ are the ancestors of $A$ in $\mathcal{T}(\boldsymbol{x})$. The binomial likelihood terms on all ancestors of $A$ are indeed retained in the partial likelihood.

For this reason, the partial likelihood approach is in essence carrying out data splitting using the 0 and 1 dyadic sequence-preserving the prefix of the sequence that indicates $x \in A$, and discarding the postfix that encodes the relative value of $x$ in $A$. We will formally show that the information discarded by the partial likelihood is asymptotically negligible when the partition points are based on (non-degenerate) empirical quantiles such as the median.

It is worth noting that the partial likelihood approach, with a slight generalization, provides a unifying framework that contains the full likelihood approach based on predetermined partition locations as a special case and allows the approach to be applied to distributions that might not be continuous. To see this, in the decomposition in Eq. (2.2), we can let $m(A)=f\left(x_{A} \mid A\right)^{n\left(\left\{x_{A}\right\}\right)} \cdot F\left(A_{l} \mid A\right)^{n\left(A_{l}\right)} F\left(A_{r} \mid A\right)^{n\left(A_{r}\right)}$ where $n\left(\left\{x_{A}\right\}\right)$ is the number of observations exactly equal to $x_{A}$. In the previous situations, the fixed and observed partition locations correspond to the special case when $n\left(\left\{x_{A}\right\}\right)=0$ and $n\left(\left\{x_{A}\right\}\right)=1$, respectively. Under this unified framework, one can use a mix of partition locations that include some that sit on one or more observations and others not on any observations. Inference can then proceed using the partial likelihood as defined in Eq. (2.3) in the same way without changes.

question: What is the maximum left zero subsemigroup of a semigroup containing an idempotent element?
answer: The maximum left zero subsemigroup of a semigroup containing an idempotent element $e$ is $L Z(e) = \text{ridentity}(e) \cap \text{lzero}(e)$.

evidence.text:
# 3 Left Zero and Right Zero Subsemigroups 

Theorem 3.1. Let $S$ be a semigroup, and let $e \in S$ be an idempotent. Then
$L Z(e)=$ ridentity $(e) \cap l z e r o(e)$ is the maximum left zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$, and
$R Z(e)=$ lidentity $(e) \cap r z e r o(e)$ is the maximum right zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$.
Proof. Since $e$ is an idempotent, $e e=e \in$ lidentity $(e)$, ridentity $(e), l z e r o(e), r z e r o(e)$, so $e \in L Z(e)$ and $e \in R Z(e)$.

For any $a, b \in L Z(e)$,

$$
a b=(a e) b=a(e b)=a e=a
$$

Therefore $L Z(e)$ is a left zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$. If $L$ is a left zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$, then for any $a \in L, a e=a$ and $e a=e$, so that $a \in L Z(e)$. Thus $L \subset L Z(e)$, and $L Z(e)$ is maximal.

Similarly, $R Z(e)$ is the maximum right zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$.
Every nonempty subset of a left zero [right zero] semigroup is a subsemigroup of that semigroup. Hence for any idempotent $e$ of semigroup $S$, since $L Z(e)[R Z(e)]$ is the maximum left zero [right zero] subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$, all subsets of $L Z(e)[R Z(e)]$ containing $e$ account for all left zero [right zero] subsemigroups of $S$ containing $e$.
Corollary 3.2. Let $S$ be a semigroup, let $e \in S$ be an idempotent, and let $T \subset S$.
$T$ is a left zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$ if and only if $e \in T \subset L Z(e)$.
$T$ is a right zero subsemigroup of $S$ containing $e$ if and only if $e \in T \subset R Z(e)$.
Let $E$ be the set of idempotents in semigroup $S$. Every left [right] zero subsemigroup is an idempotent semigroup or band containing only idempotent elements, and every idempotent in $S$ is contained in a maximal left [right] zero subsemigroup. Then $\{L Z(e) \mid e \in E\}$ is the set of all maximal left zero subsemigroups in $S$, and $\{R Z(e) \mid e \in E\}$ is the set of all maximal right zero subsemigroups in $S$. For these sets and $e, f \in E$, either $L Z(e)=L Z(f)$ or $L Z(e) \cap L Z(f)=\emptyset$, and either $R Z(e)=R Z(f)$ or $R Z(e) \cap R Z(f)=\emptyset$, as seen in the following theorem.
Theorem 3.3. Let $S$ be a semigroup, and let $e, f \in S$ be idempotents. Then
$L Z(e) \cap L Z(f) \neq \emptyset$ if and only if $e f=e$ and $f e=f$ if and only if $L Z(e)=L Z(f)$, and
$R Z(e) \cap R Z(f) \neq \emptyset$ if and only if $e f=f$ and $f e=e$ if and only if $R Z(e)=R Z(f)$.
Proof. If $a \in L Z(e) \cap L Z(f)$,

$$
e f=(e a) f=e(a f)=e a=e
$$

and

$$
f e=(f a) e=f(a e)=f a=f
$$

If $e f=e$ and $f e=f$, then for any $a \in L Z(e)$,

$$
a f=(a e) f=a(e f)=a e=a
$$

and

$$
f a=(f e) a=f(e a)=f e=f
$$

so $a \in L Z(f)$. Similarly, if $a \in L Z(f), a \in L Z(e)$. Therefore $L Z(e)=L Z(f)$.
Given $L Z(e)=L Z(f)$, since $e \in L Z(e)=L Z(f), L Z(e) \cap L Z(f) \neq \emptyset$.
We could create equivalence relations to partition $S$ using $L Z(e)$ and $R Z(e)$.
Definition 3.4. Let $S$ be a semigroup. Define the following relations on $S$.
For any $x, y \in S$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x \mathcal{L} \mathcal{Z} y & \Longleftrightarrow \text { ridentity }(x) \cap l z e r o(x)=\text { ridentity }(y) \cap l z e r o(y) \\
x \mathcal{R} \mathcal{Z} y & \Longleftrightarrow \text { lidentity }(x) \cap r z e r o(x)=\text { lidentity }(y) \cap r z e r o(y)
\end{aligned}
$$

Theorem 3.5. Let $S$ be a semigroup. $\mathcal{L Z}$ and $\mathcal{R Z}$ are equivalence relations on $S$ such that, the equivalence classes of $\mathcal{L} \mathcal{Z}$ are the set of all non-idempotent elements and the maximal left zero subsemigroups of $S$, and

the equivalence classes of $\mathcal{R} \mathcal{Z}$ are the set of all non-idempotent elements and the maximal left zero subsemigroups of $S$.

Proof. By Theorem 2.6, $\operatorname{ridentity}(x) \cap l z e r o(x) \neq \emptyset$ if and only if $x$ is an idempotent, and therefore $\operatorname{ridentity}(x) \cap l z e r o(x)=\emptyset$ if and only if $x$ is not an idempotent. Let $E$ be the set of all idempotents in $S . S-E$ forms an equivalence class of non-idempotent elements, and the set of all maximal left zero subsemigroupgs of $S,\{L Z(e) \mid e \in E\}$, creates a partition of $E$ into equivalence classes in which $L Z(e)=L Z(f)$ if and only if $e f=e$ and $f e=f$.

question: How do sectoral and spatial spillovers affect inter-firm learning about imports?
answer: While sectoral and spatial spillovers exist, the study finds robust evidence of network effects even after accounting for these factors, indicating that direct connections within production networks are crucial for learning about new import opportunities.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

Using administrative data on the universe of inter-firm transactions in Spain, we show that firms learn to import from their domestic suppliers and customers. Our identification strategy exploits the panel structure of the data, the firm-time variation across import origins, and the network structure. We find evidence of both upstream and downstream network effects, even after accounting for sectoral and spatial spillovers. We estimate that an increase of 10 percentage points in the share of suppliers (customers) that are importing from a given region increases the probability of starting importing from that region by $10.7 \%$ (19.2\%). Connections with geographically distant domestic firms provide more useful information to start importing. Larger firms are more responsive to this information but less likely to disseminate it.


Key Words: Production network, Learning, Spillovers, Import.
JEL Codes: D22, D83, F14, L14.
