### 3.1 Background: Bitcoin's Nakamoto protocol

For completeness, we provide a brief description of the Nakamoto protocol. Some technical details are deferred to Appendix A.

The Blockchain data format The ledger is held in the format of a blockchain, which grows over time as new blocks are appended. A blockchain is an ordered sequence of blocks $\left(B_{0}, B_{1}, \ldots, B_{n}\right)$, where $B_{0}$ is the protocol's genesis block. Each block $B_{\ell}$ contains transaction data and a reference to the preceding block $\mathrm{B}_{\ell-1}$. A block $\mathrm{B}_{n}$ uniquely identifies a chain of preceding blocks, and we write $\operatorname{Chain}\left(\mathrm{B}_{n}\right)=\left(\mathrm{B}_{0}, \mathrm{~B}_{1}, \ldots, \mathrm{~B}_{n}\right)$. We say that block $\mathrm{B}_{n-k+1}$ is

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{25}$ For example, the attacker may have financial interests stemming from bets made outside the system.

$k$-deep in $\operatorname{Chain}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{n}}\right)$. Let $h\left(\mathrm{~B}_{\ell}\right)=\ell$ denote the height of the block, defined as the number of blocks in Chain $\left(\mathrm{B}_{\ell}\right)$ minus one.

The view of a node $i \in N$ encompasses all the information available to node $i$, including its local history and any blocks it has received. A node may receive multiple blocks of the same height, which cannot belong to the same chain.

Brief description of the Nakamoto protocol Each node (miner) organizes valid pending transactions into a suggested block. The protocol uses a hash function to select a node's block randomly. Each node calculates the hash of its block, ${ }^{26}$ and the block is valid if the hash is lower than the difficulty threshold $D .{ }^{27}$ A node that finds a block with a valid hash is said to have mined a block. A node's mining power is the number of hash computations it can attempt per unit time. Nodes can write a special transaction into their block that awards them a block reward $p_{B} .{ }^{28}$

The protocol specifies the genesis block $\mathrm{B}_{0}$ that all chains must extend. If a node mines or receives a block, it broadcasts the block to all other nodes. The protocol directs nodes to mine blocks that extend the longest chain in their view. Ties are broken arbitrarily.

The Nakamoto protocol itself does not specify when transactions are finalized. In common usage, ${ }^{29}$ finality is parameterized by a required block depth $k$, where a transaction is considered finalized by node $i$ if the transaction is within a block at least $k$-deep in the longest chain in $i$ 's view. That is, if $\operatorname{Chain}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{n}}\right)=\left(\mathrm{B}_{0}, \mathrm{~B}_{1}, \ldots, \mathrm{~B}_{\mathrm{n}}\right)$ is (one of) the longest chains in the view of node $i$, then $i$ 's local copy of the ledger is $\log _{i}=\left(\mathrm{B}_{0}, \mathrm{~B}_{1}, \ldots, \mathrm{~B}_{n-k+1}\right)$.

question: Are definitions considered arbitrary constructs in mathematics?
answer: No, major standard definitions are not arbitrary constructs; they are often the result of years of work to fix failures and consolidate partial successes and should be thought of as distilled hard-won wisdom.

evidence.text:
## 2. AbstraCTIons

"Foundation" refers to a body of deductive practice, here mainstream deductive mathematics. Historically practice comes first. Foundations are a way to analyze the body of practice, particularly its consistency.
(1) A primitive is an object, hypotheses, or method of argument that is postulated rather than deduced from something else.
(2) A primitive foundation is a collection of primitives that is complete in the sense that no other primitives are needed. Note that the methods of argument (the logic) is part of the foundation.
(3) A foundation is consistent if every chain of deductions that produces a contradiction can be shown to have a logical error.
2.1. About consistency. The operational view of consistency is "complete reliability", in the sense that the outcome of an error-free argument will never be contradicted by the outcome of any other such argument. Moreover, the outcome will not introduce errors if used as an ingredient in further arguments. Arguments by contradiction for example, assume something, deduce a contradiction, and conclude that the thing assumed must be false. Success is sensitively dependent on

everything else used in the argument being completely reliable, and that the logic itself does not introduce errors.

Consistency provides an internal criterion for correctness. In practice, however, it is far more important as a criterion for incorrectness. In reasonably ambitious research programs, 95 percent or more of attempted proofs turn out to have flaws. Sometimes, with luck and persistence, these flaws can be corrected, and the attempts converge to a valid argument. Sometimes years of effort have to be abandoned as hopeless, or outright wrong. The payoff for this painful process is closure: even outrageously counterintuitive conclusions are accepted when the arguments are carefully checked and found to be error-free.

Empirical. Gödel has shown that foundations generally cannot prove their own consistency. However, we can test consistency: make lots of deductions, and verify that any contradictions are accounted for by logical errors. Sometimes inconsistencies do not appear until work reaches a certain level of sophistication. Another wrinkle is that a foundation can be technically inconsistent but consistent in practice in the sense that methodology has evolved so as to steer people away from the inconsistencies. The main point is that empirical consistency is a property of a methodology rather than of a foundation. Explicit foundations are largely retrofits that record successful experience and narrow down potential sources of error.

Global. Evidence for consistency applies to the development as a whole, not just individual results. In other sciences, and in mathematics when trying out new methodologies, experiment can give evidence that individual conclusions are reliable, within limits and independently of most other conclusions. Foundational consistency checks are global in that they support consistency of the whole development. This is the flip side of the fact that a single genuine failure would throw doubt on the whole development.
2.2. Definitions and axioms vs primitives. We clarify usage in the mathematical community.

Definitions are located inside a developed context, and usually consist of axioms that the things being defined should satisfy. Properties of these things are to be inferred from the axioms and more-basic ingredients. In particular, while intuition and intent can guide the formation of a definition they have no logical force. Indeed, first attempts at definitions typically fail to have intended properties. Major standard definitions are often the result of years of work to fix failures and consolidate partial successes, and should be thought of as distilled hard-won wisdom. They are certainly not arbitrary constructs.

Primitive objects, hypotheses, etc. are starting points for the logical context, not defined in terms of lower-level objects. Primitive hypotheses, in particular, are not axioms in the contemporary sense. Since properties cannot be inferred from lower-level material, they depend on heuristic ideas, syntax specifications, and examples.

For example, Euclid's description of points as "things without width or length" is not a definition in the contemporary sense because "width" and "length" have not been given precise meaning. It succeeds as a primitive because this, filtered through physical experience, some pictures, and examples of usage, reliably evokes consistent understandings. Polygons are 'defined' because they are described in terms of primitives.

We emphasize that consistency at the primitive level depends heavily on different users extracting functionally equivalent understandings. This has often been a problem.
2.3. Deeper is better. In practice, definitions are often easier to learn and use with precision than are complicated primitives. For example, attempts to use the real numbers as a primitive were problematic. Now the reals are defined in terms of natural numbers, and natural numbers are defined using set theory. This approach has made full-precision understanding of the reals faster and more routine.

Curiously, another benefit of working several levels above the primitives is that it can filter out misunderstandings or ambiguities about the primitives. For instance, the traditional axiomatic approach to set theory takes 'sets' as primitives, and the primitive hypotheses proscribing their behavior are quite complicated. But these do not have to be understood in detail to get a completely solid description of the real numbers. The new approach to set theory has a similar advantage: the primitives (object generators) are several levels below sets, so sets are defined and their properties proved rather than hypothesized. This gives a more accessible, and slightly sharper, understanding of set theory.
2.4. Other views. There is a vast literature, mostly Philosophical, about the nature and role of foundations. It is far from consistent, and while there are interesting insights, cf. [Maddy], some of it is pretty silly. It does not seem to be useful to try to sort through it here.

question: How does the chance-constrained epigraphic StQP compare to robust StQPs?
answer: The chance-constrained epigraphic StQP can be less conservative than robust StQPs, particularly when the confidence level for probabilistic optimality is not excessively high. This suggests that it may offer more flexibility and efficiency under certain conditions compared to traditional robust approaches.

evidence.text:
# 5 Conclusion 

We introduced and motivated the chance-constrained epigraphic StQP, a new model for solving uncertain StQPs under distributional assumptions, and established a deterministic counterpart as an instance in the same problem class (another StQP). Our findings parallel similar observations on robust StQPs, and indeed a special variant of this model is equivalent to a particular robust formulation. However, preliminary experiments seem to suggest that the chance-constrained epigraphic StQP can be less conservative than a robust approach, if the confidence level (probabilistic optimality guarantee) is not too large.

question: How can one determine if a language's growth is boundedly supermultiplicative?
answer: A sufficient condition involves analyzing the alphabet and forbidden factors to establish constants such that for any word length, the number of permissible words falls within these bounds. If this condition holds, it implies computability for both the constants involved and the overall growth rate.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

We study some properties of the growth rate of $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{F})$, that is, the language of words over the alphabet $\mathcal{A}$ avoiding the set of forbidden factors $\mathcal{F}$. We first provide a sufficient condition on $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{A}$ for the growth of $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{F})$ to be boundedly supermultiplicative. That is, there exist constants $C>0$ and $\alpha \geqslant 0$, such that for all $n$, the number of words of length $n$ in $\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{F})$ is between $\alpha^{n}$ and $C \alpha^{n}$. In some settings, our condition provides a way to compute $C$, which implies that $\alpha$, the growth rate of the language, is also computable whenever our condition holds.

We also apply our technique to the specific setting of power-free words where the argument can be slightly refined to provide better bounds. Finally, we apply a similar idea to $\mathcal{F}$-free circular words and in particular we make progress toward a conjecture of Shur about the number of square-free circular words.

question: In what ways does the semiparametric approach improve upon traditional methods for addressing spatial confounding?
answer: The semiparametric approach improves upon traditional methods by allowing for closed-form variance estimation without needing a shift parameter or density function estimation. It uses random sample splits for better estimation of spatial trends, incorporates multiple treatment variables easily, and avoids computational difficulties associated with density function estimation.

evidence.text:
# 1. Introduction 

Public health data are often observational and exhibit spatial dependence, such as in environmental contaminations that may spread over a geographic region (Cressie, 1993). Spatial regression methods can improve efficiency, allow proper uncertainty quantification, and enhance predictive accuracy (Cressie, 1993). However, association between explanatory variables and latent functions of space in the response model can cause bias in estimated regression coefficients, and invalid statistical inference due to poor uncertainty quantification (Reich et al., 2006). This has often been termed "spatial confounding," and was first observed in Clayton et al. (1993), discussed further in Reich et al. (2006) and Hodges and Reich (2010), and studied in other papers such as Paciorek (2010). The analogous issue in spline models has been discussed in Rice (1986) and Wood (2017). Several recent papers (Gilbert et al., 2021; Dupont et al., 2023; Khan and Berrett, 2024) have discussed definitions, causes, and effects of spatial confounding in attempts to unify varying accounts.

Methods proposed to deal with spatial confounding aim to reduce bias in linear regression parameter estimates, such as in Marques et al. (2022), Guan et al. (2022), and Schnell and Papadogeorgou (2020). Methods similar to our proposal are geoadditive structural equation modeling (Thaden and Kneib, 2018), Spatial+ (Dupont et al., 2022), and a shift estimand, which does not assume a linear treatment effect, studied in Gilbert et al. (2021). Geoadditive structural equation modeling (gSEM) subtracts estimated latent functions of space from the treatment and response, and regresses those residuals onto each other. Spatial+ subtracts an estimated function of space from the treatment variable and regresses the response onto those residuals and a spatial term modeled by a thin-plate spline. The shift estimand implemented in Gilbert et al. (2021) subtracts an estimated function of space from the treatment (in order to estimate a conditional density function) and response, but without assuming a linear and additive effect of the explanatory variable. Identifiability in gSEM, Spatial+, the

shift estimand, and our method is typically due to independent, non-spatial variation in the treatment and response. In this situation, Gilbert et al. (2024) also showed that the standard generalized least squares (GLS), spline, and Gaussian process estimates are consistent even in some cases where they are misspecified due to spatial confounding, but noted that this does not imply variance estimates are accurate, and these estimators may converge at a rate slower than $n^{-1 / 2}$.
gSEM was initially proposed for areal spatial data, and its analogue for point-referenced spatial data, based on Appendix B of Thaden and Kneib (2018), has not been studied thoroughly. The subject of this paper is point-referenced spatial data, so we use "gSEM" to refer to its point-referenced implementation. Dupont et al. (2022) states that "it is not immediately clear why the method works"; Dupont et al. (2023) states that "the bias reduction will only be successful under the assumption that the initial regressions successfully remove all spatial confounders." gSEM has also lacked a closed-form variance estimate.

Literature on semiparametric regression (Robinson, 1988; Andrews, 1994; Chernozhukov et al., 2018) proves that under spatial confounding and additional regularity conditions, a class of estimators, including some nearly identical to gSEM (Robinson, 1988), can achieve $n^{-1 / 2}$-consistency and asymptotic normality, with a consistent closed-form variance estimate, even when not removing spatial confounding fully in initial regression estimates of spatial trends. Broadly speaking, these estimators first estimate the latent functions of space using nonparametric regression, subtract these estimates from the observed variables, and use those residuals to estimate the regression parameter in a second stage; the preliminary estimates of the latent functions need converge to the true values only slowly. Due to a form of orthogonality between the estimator and the preliminary estimates of the latent functions, the asymptotic variance of the estimator is unaffected by using these preliminary estimates. By either using sample-splitting as in Chernozhukov et al. (2018) or requiring

additional smoothness conditions as in Andrews (1994), asymptotic bias due to overfitting is controlled. A more detailed overview of the related semiparametric theory is presented in the Supplementary Materials section S1.

Gilbert et al. (2021) showed that a Double Machine Learning (DML) estimator can address spatial confounding using a purely nonparametric estimator of the average effect of a $\delta$-shift in a scalar treatment variable. We show that a semiparametric DML approach to spatial confounding, while restrictive in some ways, has substantial upsides. Gilbert et al. (2021) relies on theory originally meant for social network data (Ogburn et al., 2024), which with spatial data results in an unnecessarily restricted sample-splitting strategy whose validity is unproven. No closed-form variance estimate is available for the shift estimator. In our semiparametric approach, we are able to use fully random sample splits, which allows sharper, clearer regularity conditions due to better estimation of spatial trends. The parametric model for treatment effects allows closed-form variance estimation using standard empirical estimators, avoids having to specify a shift $\delta$, and easily incorporates multiple treatment variables. Our approach avoids estimating a density function, sometimes a computational difficulty. Finally, most methods for spatial confounding and spatial regression assume a linear model, so we continue to improve understanding of this common model.

We apply these semiparametric estimators to spatial confounding scenarios, using Gaussian Process (GP) regression to estimate the latent functions of space, a procedure also known as Kriging. We primarily rely on methods and theory from Chernozhukov et al. (2018), extending Chernozhukov et al.'s partially linear model to a vector treatment variable. As the two-stage estimators are termed Double Machine Learning in Chernozhukov et al. (2018), we refer to their narrower use to address spatial confounding as Double Spatial Regression (DSR). In simulations of spatial confounding, we show that DSR can provide superior performance in severe confounding scenarios. Finally, we analyze the association between

of five per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels in blood using DSR.

question: What does it mean for an element to be "rather below" another element in a bounded lattice?
answer: An element $a$ is rather below (well inside) another element $b$, written as $a \prec b$, if there exists $\mathrm{c} \in A$ such that $\mathrm{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$.

evidence.text:
# 5. Regularity 

In this section we characterize when the four completions are regular. For distributive lattices, regularity is a natural strengthening of subfitness. As we saw above, subfitness of the canonical completion is equivalent to the lattice being Boolean. As we will see below, regularity yields the same result for the ideal completion. A more subtle result occurs for the Bruns-Lakser completion. The situation for the Dedekind-MacNeille completion is further complicated by the fact that the latter need not be distributive. Regular lattices behave very differently in the non-distributive setting; in particular, regularity no longer implies subfitness. This will be discussed in more detail in a forthcoming paper. Here we will restrict our attention to Dedekind-MacNeille completions that are distributive.

The next definition is well known for frames (see, e.g., [PP12, Sec. V.5]) and generalizes directly to bounded lattices.

Definition 5.1. Let $A$ be a bounded lattice.
(1) For $a, b \in A, a$ is rather below (well inside) $b$, written $a \prec b$, provided there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$.
(2) $A$ is regular if $a \nless b$ implies the existence of $c \in A$ such that $c \prec a$ but $c \nless b$.

Remark 5.2.
(1) If $a$ has the pseudocomplement $a^{*}$, then $a \prec b$ iff $a^{*} \vee b=1$.
(2) A is regular iff every element is the join of elements rather below it. This is the usual definition of regularity in frames, but the above definition is more appealing for arbitrary bounded lattices. Observe that while arbitrary joins may not exist in $A \in$ DLat, if $A$ is regular then the join of $\{b \in A: b \prec a\}$ is $a$, so this join does exist for every $a \in A$.
(3) Every Boolean lattice is regular and in [BMPWW17, p. 360] it is shown that every regular distributive lattice is subfit. In a forthcoming paper we will show that this is no longer true for non-distributive lattices.

Our first goal is to characterize when distributive lattices are regular using Priestley duality. We do so by generalizing some existing results for frames, proved in [BGJ16, Lem. 3.3, 3.6]. Since pseudocomplements may not exist in an arbitrary distributive lattice, the proofs below are somewhat more involved. We start by characterizing the rather below relation.

Lemma 5.3. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X ,

$$
a \prec b \text { iff } \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})
$$

Proof. First suppose $a \prec b$. Then there is $c \in A$ such that $a \wedge c=0$ and $b \vee c=1$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Since $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ is an upset, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$. Thus, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$.

Conversely, suppose $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Since $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ is a closed downset, it is the intersection of clopen downsets containing it (see Fact 2.6). But then by compactness, there is a clopen downset D such that $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathrm{D} \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$. Let $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ be such that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathrm{D}$. Then $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathrm{X} \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$. Therefore, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\varnothing$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})=\mathrm{X}$. Thus, $\mathfrak{a} \wedge \mathrm{c}=0$ and $\mathrm{b} \vee \mathrm{c}=1$, and hence $\mathfrak{a} \prec \mathfrak{b}$.

Following [BGJ16, Def. 3.4], for each $V \in L(X)$, define the regular part of $V$ to be

$$
\mathrm{R}(\mathrm{~V})=\bigcup\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{~L}(\mathrm{X}): \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{~V}\}
$$

For simplicity, we abbreviate the regular part of $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ by $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$.
Proposition 5.4. For $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat with Priestley dual X , the following are equivalent:
(1) A is regular.
(2) $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ for each $\mathfrak{a} \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $a \in A$. Take $x \in s(a)$ and let $U$ be a clopen neighborhood of $x$ in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. We must show that $U \cap R_{a} \neq \varnothing$. Since $U$ is an open neighborhood of $x$, there are $\mathrm{c}, \mathrm{d} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{x} \in \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \subseteq \mathrm{U}$ (see Fact 2.6(1)). Without loss of generality we may assume that $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ (by intersecting $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$ with $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$ ). Because $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d}) \neq \varnothing$, $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$, so $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{d}$. Since A is regular, there is $\mathrm{e} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\mathrm{e} \prec \mathrm{c}$ and $\mathrm{e} \nless \mathrm{d}$. By Lemma 5.3, $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c})$, so $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{c}} \subseteq \mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{e}) \nsubseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})$. Thus, $\mathrm{R}_{\mathfrak{a}} \cap(\mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{c}) \backslash \mathfrak{s}(\mathrm{d})) \neq \varnothing$, so $R_{a} \cap U \neq \varnothing$, and hence $R_{a}$ is dense in $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$.

(2) $\Rightarrow$ (1): Let $a \nless b$. Then $s(a) \nsubseteq s(b)$, so $R_{a} \nsubseteq s(b)$ since $R_{a}$ is dense in $s(a)$. Therefore, there is $\mathrm{c} \in \mathrm{A}$ such that $\downarrow \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \subseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{a})$ and $\mathrm{s}(\mathrm{c}) \nsubseteq \mathrm{s}(\mathrm{b})$. Thus, $\mathrm{c} \prec \mathrm{a}$ (by Lemma 5.3) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, yielding that A is regular.

We next give a general characterization, akin to Theorem 4.2, of when regularity is preserved and/or reflected when moving between $A$ and $B$, where $A$ is a bounded sublattice of B. We write $\prec_{A}$ or $\prec_{B}$ to emphasize which rather below relation is being used. Clearly $a \prec_{A} b$ implies $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $a, b \in A$, however the converse is not true in general. Because of this, the proposition below requires an extra assumption. As in Theorem 4.2, distributivity plays no rôle.

Proposition 5.5. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B. Suppose that $a \prec_{A} b$ iff $a \prec_{B} b$ for all $\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b} \in \mathrm{A}$.
(1) If A is join-dense in B and B is regular then A is regular.
(2) If A is both join- and meet-dense in B and A is regular then B is regular.

Proof. (1) Let $a, b \in A$ with $a \nless b$. Since $B$ is regular, there is $x \in B$ with $x \prec_{B} a$ and $x \nless b$. Because $A$ is join-dense in $B$, there is $c \in A$ with $c \leqslant x$ and $c \nless b$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \leqslant \mathrm{x} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$, and hence $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{A}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Thus, A is regular.
(2) Let $x, y \in B$ with $x \nless y$. Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $B$, there are $a, b \in A$ such that $a \leqslant x, y \leqslant b$, and $a \nless b$. Because $A$ is regular, there is $c \in A$ with $c \prec_{A} a$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$. Therefore, $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{a}$ (by assumption) and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{~b}$, so $\mathrm{c} \prec_{\mathrm{B}} \mathrm{x}$ and $\mathrm{c} \nless \mathrm{y}$. Thus, B is regular.

Since $A$ is both join- and meet-dense in $\mathcal{D M A}$, one could expect that regularity is both preserved and reflected by the Dedekind-MacNeille completion, but this is not the case since the additional assumption in Proposition 5.5 may not be satisfied. We again emphasize that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is not always distributive and hence regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ need not imply subfitness. Thus, we make the blanket assumption that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive. While this does not necessarily imply that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, it is indeed the case provided $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.

Proposition 5.6. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. Then regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies that $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame, and hence $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

Proof. If $\mathcal{D M A}$ is distributive, by [BMPWW17, p. 360] regularity of $\mathcal{D M A}$ implies subfitness of $\mathcal{D M A}$, and consequently subfitness of $A$ by Corollary 4.3. But then $A$ is proHeyting by Lemma 4.6. Hence, $\mathcal{D M A}$ is a frame and $\mathcal{D M A} \cong \mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ by Proposition 3.7.

The above proposition yields the following characterization of when a distributive Dede-kind-MacNeille completion is regular.

Proposition 5.7. Let $\mathrm{A} \in$ DLat and $\mathcal{D M A}$ be distributive. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{D M A}$ is regular.
(2) A is subfit and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(3) A is proHeyting and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): That $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular follows from Proposition 5.6. Regular implies subfit for distributive lattices, so $\mathcal{D} M A$ is subfit, but then so is $A$ by Corollary 4.3.
$(2) \Rightarrow(3):$ This follows from Lemma 4.6.
$(3) \Rightarrow(1):$ This follows from Proposition 3.7.
We next concentrate on characterizing when $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular. Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is a frame, the rather below relation is conveniently expressible in terms of the pseudocomplement (see Remark 5.2(1)). We use Priestley duality to describe this pseudocomplement. By Theorem 2.10(2), $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong B L(X)$ and by Remark 2.11, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is the sublocale of $\mathrm{OpUp}(\mathrm{X})$ given by the nucleus $\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}$. Since the pseudocomplement in $\mathrm{OpUp}(\mathrm{X})$ is given by

$$
\mathrm{U}^{*}=\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})
$$

the pseudocomplement in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is given by

$$
\neg \mathrm{U}=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}\left(\mathrm{U}^{*}\right)=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}))
$$

Lemma 5.8. Let $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
(1) int $\downarrow$ clint $\downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})=\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})$.
(2) $\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} V$ iff $\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{V})$.
(3) If $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$, then $\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{V}$ iff $\operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{U} \subseteq \mathrm{V}$.

Proof. (1) The right-to-left inclusion is obvious. For the other inclusion, observe that

$$
\text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl} \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})
$$

because $\downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})$ is a closed downset (see Fact 2.6(4)).
(2) Recalling how joins are defined in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ (see Remark 2.11) and that $\mathrm{cl}_{1}=\downarrow \mathrm{cl}$, by (1) we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{~V} & \Leftrightarrow \neg \mathrm{U} \vee \mathrm{~V}=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{cl}(\neg \mathrm{U}) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \mathrm{clint}_{1} \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow(\mathrm{X} \backslash \text { int } \mathrm{cl}_{1} \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})) \cup \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V})=\mathrm{X} \\
& \Leftrightarrow \text { int } \downarrow \mathrm{clint} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V}) \\
& \Leftrightarrow \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{~V}) .
\end{aligned}
$$

(3) This follows from (2) since $\mathrm{U}, \mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$ imply $\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U})=\mathrm{U}$ and $\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{V})=\mathrm{V}$.

This allows us to see that when restricted to $A$, the rather below relations on $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ and $p \mathcal{H}(A$ coincide.
Proposition 5.9. For each $\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b} \in \mathrm{A}, \mathfrak{a} \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} \mathfrak{b}$ iff $\mathfrak{a} \prec_{p \mathcal{H}(A} \mathfrak{b}$.
Proof. First suppose that $\mathfrak{a} \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} \mathfrak{b}$. Let $X$ be the Priestley space of $A$. Then int $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$ by Lemma 5.8(3). Let $\mathrm{U}=\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})$. Then $\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ by Lemma 3.14, and $\mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \cap \mathrm{U}=\varnothing$. Moreover, since int $\downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a}) \subseteq \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})$, we have

$$
\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{U}) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathrm{cl}(\mathrm{X} \backslash \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})) \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\{\mathrm{X} \backslash \operatorname{int} \downarrow \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{a})\} \cup \mathfrak{s}(\mathfrak{b})=\mathrm{X}
$$

Therefore, $U \vee_{p H(X)} s(b)=X$, so $s(a)$ is rather below $s(b)$ in $p H(X)$, and hence $a \prec_{p \cap A} b$ by Proposition 3.15 .

For the converse, suppose that $a \prec_{p \cap A} b$. By Proposition 3.15, there is $U \in \mathrm{pH}(\mathrm{X})$ such that $s(a) \cap U=\varnothing$ and $U \vee_{p H(X)} s(b)=X$. The former gives $\downarrow s(a) \cap U=\varnothing$, so $U \subseteq X \backslash \downarrow s(a)$. The latter yields that $c l(U) \cup s(b)=X$. Therefore, $c l(X \backslash \downarrow s(a)) \cup s(b)=X$, so $(X \backslash \operatorname{int} \downarrow s(a)) \cup s(b)=X$, and hence int $\downarrow s(a) \subseteq s(b)$. Thus, $a \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} b$ by Lemma 5.8(3).

In order to show that regularity of $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is equivalent to that of $p \mathcal{O}(A$, we require the following general fact.

Proposition 5.10. Let A be a bounded sublattice of B . If A is join-dense in B , then the following are equivalent:
(1) B is regular.
(2) $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$ for each $b \in B$.
(3) $a=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} a\right\}$ for each $a \in A$.

Proof. (1) $\Rightarrow$ (2): Let $b \in B$. Since $B$ is regular, $b=\bigvee\left\{d \in B: d \prec_{B} b\right\}$ (see Remark 5.2(2)). Because A is join-dense in $B, d=\bigvee\{c \in A: c \leqslant d\}$. But $c \leqslant d \prec_{B} b$ implies $c \prec_{B} b$, so $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$
(2) $\Rightarrow$ (3): This is obvious.
(3) $\Rightarrow$ (1) Let $b \in B$. Since $A$ is join-dense in $B, b=\bigvee\left\{a \in A: a \leqslant b\right\}$. By assumption, $a=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} a\right\}$ for each $a \in A$. From $c \prec_{B} a \leqslant b$ it follows that $c \prec_{B} b$. Therefore, $b=\bigvee\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{B} b\right\}$, and hence $B$ is regular.

Theorem 5.11. For $A \in$ DLat, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular iff $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is regular.
Proof. Let $a \in A$. Since $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is join-dense in $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$, it follows from Proposition 5.9 that $a=\bigvee_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A}\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A} a\right\}$ iff $a=\bigvee_{p \mathcal{O}(A}\left\{c \in A: c \prec_{p \mathcal{O}(A} a\right\}$. But $A$ is join-dense in both $p \mathcal{O}(A$ and $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$, and thus, by Proposition 5.10, $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular iff $p \mathcal{O}(A$ is regular.

We next give a characterization of when $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular akin to Proposition 5.4.
Definition 5.12. Let $V \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$. We call

$$
R_{B L}(V):=\bigcup\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}
$$

the regular part of $V$ in $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
Theorem 5.13. Let $A \in$ DLat. The following are equivalent:
(1) $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$ is regular.
(2) $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$.
(3) $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$.

Proof. (1) $\Leftrightarrow$ (2): Since $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A \cong B L(X)$, it is enough to show that $B L(X)$ is regular iff $R_{B L}(V)$ is dense in $V$ for each $V \in B L(X)$. Let $V \in B L(X)$. We have

$$
\bigvee\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}=\operatorname{int}_{1} c l \bigcup\left\{U \in L(X): U \prec_{B L} V\right\}=\operatorname{int}_{1} c l\left(R_{B L}(V)\right)
$$

Therefore, by Proposition 5.10, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is regular iff $\mathrm{V}=\operatorname{int}_{1} \mathrm{cl}\left(\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})\right)$ iff $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ is dense in $V$ for each $V \in \operatorname{BL}(X)$.
$(1) \Leftrightarrow(3)$ : By Proposition 5.10, $\mathrm{BL}(\mathrm{X})$ is regular iff $\mathrm{V}=\bigvee\left\{\mathrm{U} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X}): \mathrm{U} \prec_{\mathrm{BL}} \mathrm{V}\right\}$ for each $V \in L(X)$. The same proof as in $(1) \Leftrightarrow(2)$ may be used to show that this is equivalent to $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{BL}}(\mathrm{V})$ being dense in V for each $\mathrm{V} \in \mathrm{L}(\mathrm{X})$.

We now compare regularity of $A$ to that of $\mathcal{B} \mathcal{L} A$.

question: What does the notation $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ represent?
answer: The notation $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ represents the finite field of order $q$, where $q$ is a prime power.

evidence.text:
# 2 Preliminaries
### 2.1 General Notation

We denote the set $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ by $[n]$ and let $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ be the finite field of order $q$, where $q$ is a prime power. Given a vector space $V$, the family of all linear subspaces of $V$ is denoted by $\mathcal{L}(V)$.

Given a matrix $A \in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n \times b}(b \in \mathbb{N})$ and a code $\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}$, we write $A \subseteq \mathcal{C}$ to mean that every column of $A$ belongs to $\mathcal{C}$. We then say that $\mathcal{C}$ contains $A$. We write $A_{i *}$ and $A_{*_{j}}$ to refer, respectively, to the $i$-th row and $j$-th column of $A$. We denote

$$
\operatorname{Dist}_{q}^{n, b}=\left\{A \in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{n \times b} \mid A \text { has pairwise-distinct columns }\right\}
$$

We use boldface symbols $\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1}$ to represent the all zeroes vector and the all ones vector, respectively. If $I \subseteq[b]$, we let $\mathbf{1}_{I} \in \mathbb{F}_{q}^{b}$ be the indicator vector for $I$.

question: Is universal Kriging used to estimate spatial trends in DSR?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
### 2.2 Double Spatial Regression estimator

Double Spatial Regression estimates the spatial trends $g_{0}, m_{01}, \ldots, m_{0 \ell}$ and covariate effects $\mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{00}, \mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{01}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{0 \ell}$, subtracts those from $\mathbf{Y}, \mathbf{A}_{.1}, \ldots, \mathbf{A}_{. \ell}$, and then uses these residuals to estimate $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}$. The estimates of $g_{0}, m_{01}, \ldots, m_{0 \ell}$, and $\mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{00}, \mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{01}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{0 \ell}$, are obtained

by cross-fitting: for example, to estimate the values of $g_{0}$ for the data in fold $k$, an estimate $\widehat{g}_{0}$ of the function $g_{0}$ is obtained using the data not in fold $k$, and $\widehat{g}_{0}$ is then evaluated on the data in fold $k$.

For cross-fitting, the full data set is randomly (we use a completely random sample) partitioned into $K$ folds each of size $\frac{n}{K}$, assumed to be an integer. Let $f_{i} \in\{1, \ldots, K\}$ denote the fold assignment of observation $i$. For $k=1, \ldots, K$, let $\mathbf{k}=\left\{i: f_{i}=k\right\}$ denote the set of indices assigned to fold $k$ and $\mathbf{k}^{C}=\left\{i: f_{i} \neq k\right\}$ denote the set of indices assigned to the complement of fold $k$. Then, for example, $\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{k}}$ is the vector of elements of $\mathbf{Y}$ assigned to the $k$ th fold and $\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}$ is the vector of elements of $\mathbf{Y}$ not assigned to the $k$ th fold. For a generic matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$, the $i$ th row of $\mathbf{X}$ is denoted $\mathbf{X}_{i}$, the submatrix consisting of those rows of $\mathbf{X}$ whose indices are in $\mathbf{k}$ is denoted $\mathbf{X}_{\mathbf{k}}$ (and likewise for $\mathbf{k}^{C}$ ), the $j$ th column is denoted $\mathbf{X}_{-j}$, and the $j$ th column vector of the submatrix corresponding to the $k$ th fold is denoted $\mathbf{X}_{\mathbf{k}, j}$. Denote the full data as $\mathbf{W}$, the data in fold $k$ as $\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{k}}$, and the data in the complement of fold $k$ as $\mathbf{W}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}$.

Universal Kriging using the Matèrn correlation function is used to estimate $g_{0}, m_{01}, \ldots, m_{0 \ell}$ (Stein, 1999). The Matèrn correlation function is:

$$
C_{\gamma, \tau}\left(\mathbf{S}_{i}, \mathbf{S}_{j}\right):=\frac{2^{1-\tau}}{\Gamma(\tau)}\left(\sqrt{2 \tau} \frac{\left\|\mathbf{S}_{i}-\mathbf{S}_{j}\right\|_{2}}{\gamma}\right)^{\tau} K_{\tau}\left(\sqrt{2 \tau} \frac{\left\|\mathbf{S}_{i}-\mathbf{S}_{j}\right\|_{2}}{\gamma}\right)
$$

where $K_{\tau}$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind. The Matèrn correlation function has two parameters: $\gamma$ controls the range of spatial dependence and $\tau$ controls the smoothness (mean-square differentiability) of the process. A variance parameter $\omega^{2}$ is typically defined so that $\omega^{2} C(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{B})$ is a covariance matrix.

used in (1) and (2), are denoted by a tilde and an additional subscript $k$; note that $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0}^{-}$, a preliminary estimate of $\boldsymbol{\beta}_{0}$, is included.

$$
\begin{aligned}

& \times\left(\mathbf{Y}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}-\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}^{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_{0 k}-\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}^{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{00 k}\right) \\
& \widehat{m}_{0 j}\left(\mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{k}}\right)=\widehat{\omega}_{j k} C_{\widehat{s}_{j k}, \widehat{s}_{j k}}\left(\mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{k}}, \mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}\right)\left(\widehat{\omega}_{j k} C_{\widehat{s}_{j k}, \widehat{s}_{j k}}\left(\mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}, \mathbf{S}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}\right)+\widehat{\sigma}_{j k}^{2} \mathbf{I}\right)^{-1}\left(\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}{ }_{j}-\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{k}^{C}}^{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{0 j k}\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

for $j=1, \ldots, p$. For this working prediction model we also assume homoskedasticity of all error terms, with variance parameters $\sigma_{0}^{2}, \sigma_{1}^{2}, \ldots, \sigma_{\ell}^{2}$. The estimated covariate effects for fold $k$ are $\mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{k}}^{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{00 k}, \mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{k}}^{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{01 k}, \ldots, \mathbf{Z}_{\mathbf{k}}^{T} \widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{0 \ell k}$.

To obtain universal Kriging estimates, we used the GpGp R package (Guinness, 2018), which estimates all covariance and slope parameters using restricted maximum likelihood (REML), and scales well to large samples by using the Vecchia approximation (Vecchia, 1988). Estimates are combined across folds to obtain $\widehat{g}_{0}(\mathbf{S})$ and $\widehat{m}_{01}(\mathbf{S}), \ldots, \widehat{m}_{0 \ell}(\mathbf{S})$, and $\widehat{\mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{00}}, \widehat{\mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{01}}, \ldots, \widehat{\mathbf{Z}^{T} \boldsymbol{\theta}_{0 \ell}}$. $$
\begin{aligned}

$$

\end{gathered}
$$

question: What property does $\tilde{\delta}(a x)$ satisfy that is similar to the unit impulse function?
answer: The property $\tilde{\delta}(a x)=\tilde{\delta}(x)$, which coincides with a similar property of the unit impulse function.

evidence.text:
# 2. Surreal Delta function 

Suppose we want to obtain a functional to count the number of roots of a function on an interval. For a differentiable function $f(x)$, the following expression does the thing, where applicable: $\int_{a}^{b} \delta(f(x))\left|f^{\prime}(x)\right| d x$. From now on we will call the operator $\tilde{\delta}$, defined as $\tilde{\delta}(f(x))=\delta(f(x))\left|f^{\prime}(x)\right|$, where $x$ is the integration variable, "surreal delta function". We will further generalize it.

First of all, we should notice that $\tilde{\delta}(x)$ behaves just like $\delta(x)$ in all contexts where its argument is the integration variable itself, and not some non-trivial function of it. Particularly, its Laplace and Fourier transforms are the same as of conventional Delta distribution.

Second thing to notice is that it satisfies the following property: $\tilde{\delta}(a x)=\tilde{\delta}(x)$, which coincides with the similar property of the unit impulse function, unlike the property of the conventional Delta distribution $\delta(a x)=\frac{1}{|a|} \delta(x)$.

Let us consider the Fourier transform of the constant function $f(x) \equiv 1$ :
$F(s)=\mathcal{F}[1](s)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-s t} d t$

Formally, the right-hand expression is equal to 0 at any $s \neq 0$ (by Cesaro regularization). But at $s=0$ we get the divergent integral $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} 1 d t$. This divergent integral corresponds to the surreal number $2 \omega$.

Consequently, we can formally write:
$F(x)=\mathcal{F}[1](x)= \begin{cases}2 \omega, & \text { if } x=0 \\ 0, & \text { if } x \neq 0\end{cases}$
Applying inverse Fourier transform, $\mathcal{F}^{-1}[F](t)=1=2 \pi \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\delta](t)=2 \pi \mathcal{F}^{-1}[\tilde{\delta}](t)$. This allows us to generalize the Surreal Delta function this way:
$\tilde{\delta}(x)= \begin{cases}\frac{\omega}{\pi}, & \text { if } x=0 \\ 0, & \text { if } x \neq 0\end{cases}$
We can see that the property $\tilde{\delta}(a x)=\tilde{\delta}(x)$ holds with this piece-wise definition. This function $\tilde{\delta}(x)$ is a full-fledged surreal-valued function, and can be evaluated at any point. Particularly, since $\int_{-1}^{1} \tilde{\delta}(x) d x=1$, we can consider it (in a sense) a derivative of $\operatorname{sign}(x)$ function. This shows us that an infinite value of the derivative at a point indicates a jump the function makes there.

Expanding $\omega^{p}$ as a divergent integral, Surreal Delta function can be raised to any power:
$\tilde{\delta}(x)^{p}= \begin{cases}\frac{p}{\pi^{p}} \int_{0}^{\infty} x^{p-1} d x, & \text { if } x=0 \\ 0, & \text { if } x \neq 0 .\end{cases}$

It should be noted that the Surreal Delta function is not differentiable in terms of surreal-valued functions.

question: Is the Surreal Delta function differentiable in terms of surreal-valued functions?
answer: No, it is not differentiable in terms of surreal-valued functions.

question: What is the relationship between collagen deposition and fibrosis?
answer: Increased collagen deposition through scarring is consistent with greater fibrosis.

evidence.text:
### 4.4 Multi-compartment flow as markers of kidney pathology

Multi-compartment flow showed difference based on fibrosis (Figure 3A-C) and on function (Figure 3D-F) with spectral diffusion run with $\lambda_{0.1}$. Greater fibrosis showed significant increase in tissue parenchyma flow (F-stat $=4.18, \mathrm{p}=0.015$ ), which is consistent with increased collagen deposition through scarring and decreased contribution of tubular and vascular compartments (Figure 3C). Tubular $f D$ was significantly decreased in allografts with impaired function (MannWhitney U-test stat $=-2.06, \mathrm{p}=0.039$; Figure 3E), which is consistent with reduced flow in kidney tubules due to reduced filtration.

question: Can WTT be used for quantification of flow?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
# 2. THEORY
### 2.1 Quantitative Flow and Water Transport Time from Gaussian Diffusion

For a molecule undergoing Brownian motion with diffusivity coefficient $D\left[\mathrm{~mm}^{2} / \mathrm{s}\right]$ and an assumed net drift of zero, the probability of its location at time $t$ is a 3D Gaussian: $p(\vec{x}, t)=$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2 \pi)^{k}(2 D t)^{k}}} e^{-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=0}^{k} \frac{x_{i}^{2}}{2 D t}}, \vec{x}=\left[x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots x_{i}\right]$. While mean displacement will always be 0 , the variance $\left(\sigma^{2}=2 D t\right)$ will increase over time, i.e. a larger proportion of the original ensemble will have travelled beyond a given boundary. The speed of this increase in variance can be used to calculate 'water transport time' (WTT), the time it takes for $50 \%$ of an original ensemble to have diffused out of a 1 mm diameter sphere. As validated against neutron capture microspheres for the vascular compartment in the brain ${ }^{22}$ and previously derived in detail ${ }^{23}$, in brief, the 3D gaussian probability can be converted to spherical coordinates and integrated over a sphere of a diameter of 1 .

$$
\int_{0}^{2 \pi} \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{0}^{r=0.5 m m} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left(2 \pi \sigma^{2}\right)^{3}}} e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}} r^{2}} \sin \theta d r d \theta d \phi=0.50
$$

As $\sigma$ is a function of time, solving Eq. 1 for $\sigma$ can determine the WTT as a function of diffusion coefficient $D$. Integration by parts returns

$$
\frac{4 \pi}{\left(2 \pi \sigma^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}}\left[-0.5\left(\frac{2 \sigma^{2}}{2} e^{-\frac{0.5^{2}}{2 \sigma^{2}}}\right)+\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{4}\left(2 \sigma^{2}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} \operatorname{erf}\left(\frac{0.5}{\sqrt{s}}\right)\right]=0.50
$$

and the erf approximation (Eq. 7.1.27 from Abramowitz and Stegun ${ }^{24}$ ) returns:

$$
\frac{4 \pi}{(\sqrt{0.21 \pi})^{3}} \int_{0}^{0.5} e^{-\frac{r^{2}}{0.21}} r^{2} d r=0.5021
$$

In Eq. 2, $2 \sigma^{2}=0.21 ; \sigma=0.32$. Therefore, with $\sigma=\sqrt{2 D t}$

$$
W T T=\frac{(0.32)^{2}}{2 D}
$$

WTT can be used for quantification of flow in the denominator of the central volume theory shown in Eq. 4.

$$
\text { Flow }=\frac{\text { Volume }}{\text { Time }}[\mathrm{ml} / 100 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{min}]
$$

Volume can be calculated as $\frac{f \times f_{w}}{\rho}$ with signal fraction $(f)$ of the compartment, water fraction $\left(f_{w}\right)$ of the volume, and grams per volume $(\rho)^{7}$. With Eq. 3 as time, this returns a quantitative measure of flow in $\mathrm{ml} / 100 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{min}$.

$$
\begin{gathered}
\text { Flow }=\frac{\text { Volume }}{\text { WTT }}=\frac{f \times f_{w}}{\rho\left[\frac{g}{m L}\right]} \times \frac{2 D}{(.32)^{2}}[s] \\
=f D \times \frac{2 f_{w}}{(0.32)^{2} \rho} \times 100 \times 60[\mathrm{ml} / 100 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{min}]
\end{gathered}
$$

If $f_{w}$ and $\rho$ can be approximated as constant for a given organ, $f D$ itself can be a proxy for absolute instantaneous intravoxel flow for any physiologic compartment with a known $f$ and a known $D$. Therefore, Eq. 5 is a potential method to estimate intravoxel flow of any distinct diffusing compartment including structural tissue, tubules, cerebrospinal fluid, or vascular flow, while remaining independent of bolus kinetics, spin-labelling, or contrast delay and dispersion.

question: Does a firm's position within the domestic production network influence its importing decisions?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
# 7 Concluding remarks 

In this paper, we examine a previously unexplored aspect of firms' international trade behaviour, focusing on how their position within the domestic production network influences their importing decisions. To do this, we use a rich dataset provided by the Spanish Tax Agency (AEAT), which provides information about the universe of annual firm-tofirm transactions in the period 2010-2014. Using a combination of different identification strategies, we find evidence that suppliers' and customers' importing significantly affects a firm's decision to start importing from a given geopolitical area. Larger firms are better at taking advantage of information but less effective at disseminating it (more successful in protecting it). Linkages with geographically distant firms provide relatively more useful information to start importing.

Our identification strategy relies on standard assumptions used in the literature on cross-sectional peer effects in social networks and applies insights from this literature to a panel-data production network setting. In this context, we derive new conditions under which the network instruments can be used to address the issue of correlated effects.

The approach presented in this paper offers several promising directions for further research. For instance, the information about import opportunities may propagate through

the network beyond the first-order connections, which may lead to an important amplification of the effects we study here. Furthermore, the mechanism we examine is not limited to firms' import decisions but may also play a role in shaping domestic firm-tofirm connections. We leave studying these important issues for future research.

question: What does it mean for a foundation to be consistent?
answer: A foundation is consistent if every chain of deductions that produces a contradiction can be shown to have a logical error.

evidence.text:
## 2. AbstraCTIons

"Foundation" refers to a body of deductive practice, here mainstream deductive mathematics. Historically practice comes first. Foundations are a way to analyze the body of practice, particularly its consistency.
(1) A primitive is an object, hypotheses, or method of argument that is postulated rather than deduced from something else.
(2) A primitive foundation is a collection of primitives that is complete in the sense that no other primitives are needed. Note that the methods of argument (the logic) is part of the foundation.
(3) A foundation is consistent if every chain of deductions that produces a contradiction can be shown to have a logical error.
2.1. About consistency. The operational view of consistency is "complete reliability", in the sense that the outcome of an error-free argument will never be contradicted by the outcome of any other such argument. Moreover, the outcome will not introduce errors if used as an ingredient in further arguments. Arguments by contradiction for example, assume something, deduce a contradiction, and conclude that the thing assumed must be false. Success is sensitively dependent on

everything else used in the argument being completely reliable, and that the logic itself does not introduce errors.

Consistency provides an internal criterion for correctness. In practice, however, it is far more important as a criterion for incorrectness. In reasonably ambitious research programs, 95 percent or more of attempted proofs turn out to have flaws. Sometimes, with luck and persistence, these flaws can be corrected, and the attempts converge to a valid argument. Sometimes years of effort have to be abandoned as hopeless, or outright wrong. The payoff for this painful process is closure: even outrageously counterintuitive conclusions are accepted when the arguments are carefully checked and found to be error-free.

Empirical. Gödel has shown that foundations generally cannot prove their own consistency. However, we can test consistency: make lots of deductions, and verify that any contradictions are accounted for by logical errors. Sometimes inconsistencies do not appear until work reaches a certain level of sophistication. Another wrinkle is that a foundation can be technically inconsistent but consistent in practice in the sense that methodology has evolved so as to steer people away from the inconsistencies. The main point is that empirical consistency is a property of a methodology rather than of a foundation. Explicit foundations are largely retrofits that record successful experience and narrow down potential sources of error.

Global. Evidence for consistency applies to the development as a whole, not just individual results. In other sciences, and in mathematics when trying out new methodologies, experiment can give evidence that individual conclusions are reliable, within limits and independently of most other conclusions. Foundational consistency checks are global in that they support consistency of the whole development. This is the flip side of the fact that a single genuine failure would throw doubt on the whole development.
2.2. Definitions and axioms vs primitives. We clarify usage in the mathematical community.

Definitions are located inside a developed context, and usually consist of axioms that the things being defined should satisfy. Properties of these things are to be inferred from the axioms and more-basic ingredients. In particular, while intuition and intent can guide the formation of a definition they have no logical force. Indeed, first attempts at definitions typically fail to have intended properties. Major standard definitions are often the result of years of work to fix failures and consolidate partial successes, and should be thought of as distilled hard-won wisdom. They are certainly not arbitrary constructs.

Primitive objects, hypotheses, etc. are starting points for the logical context, not defined in terms of lower-level objects. Primitive hypotheses, in particular, are not axioms in the contemporary sense. Since properties cannot be inferred from lower-level material, they depend on heuristic ideas, syntax specifications, and examples.

For example, Euclid's description of points as "things without width or length" is not a definition in the contemporary sense because "width" and "length" have not been given precise meaning. It succeeds as a primitive because this, filtered through physical experience, some pictures, and examples of usage, reliably evokes consistent understandings. Polygons are 'defined' because they are described in terms of primitives.

We emphasize that consistency at the primitive level depends heavily on different users extracting functionally equivalent understandings. This has often been a problem.
2.3. Deeper is better. In practice, definitions are often easier to learn and use with precision than are complicated primitives. For example, attempts to use the real numbers as a primitive were problematic. Now the reals are defined in terms of natural numbers, and natural numbers are defined using set theory. This approach has made full-precision understanding of the reals faster and more routine.

Curiously, another benefit of working several levels above the primitives is that it can filter out misunderstandings or ambiguities about the primitives. For instance, the traditional axiomatic approach to set theory takes 'sets' as primitives, and the primitive hypotheses proscribing their behavior are quite complicated. But these do not have to be understood in detail to get a completely solid description of the real numbers. The new approach to set theory has a similar advantage: the primitives (object generators) are several levels below sets, so sets are defined and their properties proved rather than hypothesized. This gives a more accessible, and slightly sharper, understanding of set theory.
2.4. Other views. There is a vast literature, mostly Philosophical, about the nature and role of foundations. It is far from consistent, and while there are interesting insights, cf. [Maddy], some of it is pretty silly. It does not seem to be useful to try to sort through it here.

question: What are Rees valuations and how do they relate to rational powers of ideals?
answer: Rees valuations are a set of invariants in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra that uniquely determine the rational powers of ideals. They involve determining order valuations for prime divisors in the exceptional divisor of the normalized blowup of an ideal. Rational powers, defined as intersections over discrete valuations, provide insights into filtrations like integral closures and symbolic powers.

evidence.text:
## 1. INTRODUCTION

Rees valuations and rational powers of ideals play a central role in many results in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra $[3,12,13,20,26,27,36,39,43,46,52]$. These two sets of invariants are so closely related that each uniquely determines the other (see Remark 2.11). However, explicitly computing them is a difficult task because it requires determining the order valuations for every prime divisor arising in the exceptional divisor of the normalized blowup of the ideal [50]. In fact, complete descriptions of Rees valuations in the literature are limited to monomial ideals, where they correspond to supporting hyperplanes of Newton polyhedra [38, Theorem 10.3.5]. One of the primary goals of this paper is to provide explicit descriptions of both Rees valuations and rational powers for several classes of ideals in polynomial rings that are invariant under natural actions of tori and products of general linear groups.

Originally considered by Samuel and Rees in the 1950s [50,54], the notion of rational powers of an ideal $I$ in a Noetherian domain $R$ was introduced by Lejeune-Jalabert and Teissier [45, §4.2]. The power $\overline{I^{w}}$ for $w \in \mathbb{Q}_{\geqslant 0}$ is defined as $\overline{I^{w}}:=\cap_{v}\{x \mid v(x) \geqslant w v(I)\}$, where the intersection is taken over all the discrete valuations of $\operatorname{Quot}(R)$ that are nonnegative in $R$, or alternatively, over the Rees valuations of $I$. This construction provides a powerful tool for understanding the structure of filtrations of ideals such as integral closures [36,39], symbolic powers [26], Frobenius powers [52], and multiplier ideals [44, §9.6]. Despite its historical roots, rational powers have seen limited development, as noted by Knutson in 2010, who observed that this "beautiful construction has sat essentially unused in the literature for over 50 years now" [42].

[^0]
[^0]:    2020 Mathematics Subject Classification. Primary: 13B22, 13A50, 13A18. Secondary: 14E05, 05E40.
    Key words and phrases. Rational powers, integral closures, Rees valuations, multiplier ideals, invariant ideals.
    ${ }^{1}$ The third author was partially supported by the Simons Foundation.
    ${ }^{2}$ The fourth author was partially funded by NSF Grant DMS \#2001645/2303605 and DMS \#2401522.

Let $X=X_{m \times n}$ be a generic $m \times n$ matrix, meaning its entries are distinct variables. The polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[X]$ carries a natural action of $\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) \times \mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$ defined by $(A, B) \cdot X=A^{-1} X B$, where $A \in \mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C})$ and $B \in \mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$. The ideals in the polynomial ring $\mathbb{C}[X]$ that are invariant under this action have been extensively studied in the literature, see e.g. $[6,7,10,17,18,21,35,40]$. The combination of representation theory and the theory of algebras with straightening laws has led to a wide range of explicit results about the structure and properties of these ideals. If one considers a symmetric generic matrix $Y=Y_{n \times n}$ and $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$-action on $\mathbb{C}[Y]$ given by $A \cdot Y=A Y A^{t}$, or a skew-symmetric generic matrix $Z=Z_{n \times n}$ with $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$-action on $\mathbb{C}[Z]$ given by $A \cdot Z=A Z A^{t}$, one obtains analogous well-studied invariant ideals, see e.g. the references above and $[1,2,14,19]$.

We introduce the concept of Rees package, which is a combinatorial characteristic-free construction that encapsulates the description of both Rees valuations and rational powers in terms of polyhedral data (see Definition 3.5). In our first theorem, we show that the classes of invariant ideals described above admit such a Rees package. Furthermore, in arbitrary characteristic, we show that monomial ideals in affine semigroup rings, sums of products of determinantal ideals of generic, symmetric, and skew-symmetric matrices, and products of determinantal ideals of Hankel matrices, also admit a Rees package.

Theorem A. Let $\mathbb{k}$ be an arbitrary field. The following classes of ideals admit a Rees package. In particular, their rational powers and Rees valuations can be explicitly described in terms of lattice points and supporting hyperplanes of polyhedra.
(a) (Theorem 3.9) Monomial ideals in affine semigroup rings.
(b) (Theorem 3.13, Corollary 3.16) Sums of products of determinantal ideals in $\mathbb{k}\left[X_{m \times n}\right]$ of a generic matrix $X_{m \times n}$. If $\mathbb{k}=\mathbb{C}$, more generally any $\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{C}) \times \mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$-invariant ideal of $\mathbb{C}\left[X_{m \times n}\right]$.
(c) (Theorem 3.19, Corollary 3.20) Sums of products of determinantal ideals in $\mathbb{k}\left[Y_{n \times n}\right]$ of a generic symmetric matrix $Y_{n \times n}$. If $\mathbb{k}=\mathbb{C}$, more generally any $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$-invariant ideal of $\mathbb{k}\left[Y_{n \times n}\right]$
(d) (Theorem 3.22, Corollary 3.23) Sums of products of ideals of Pfaffians in $\mathbb{k}\left[Z_{n \times n}\right]$ of a skewsymmetric generic matrix $Z_{n \times n}$. If $\mathbb{k}=\mathbb{C}$, more generally any $\mathrm{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$-invariant ideal of $\mathbb{C}\left[Z_{n \times n}\right]$.
(e) (Theorem 3.25) Products of determinantal ideals in $\mathbb{k}[W]$ of a Hankel matrix of variables $W$.

In [49], Mustaţă showed a summation formula for multiplier ideals of pairs ideal sheaves, and this formula was later generalized by Takagi [56] and by Jow-Miller [41]. Mustaţă-Takagi summation formula raises the natural question of whether similar identities hold for symbolic powers and rational powers of ideals. The former was established in [31,32] and the latter in [4] for monomial ideals. Thus we propose the following conjecture (cf. [4, Question 2.4]).

Conjecture 1.1. Let $\mathbb{k}$ be an algebraically closed field and $R$ and $S$ normal domains finitely generated over $\mathbb{k}$. Set $T:=R \otimes_{\mathbb{k}} S$. The following formula holds for every $w \in \mathbb{Q}_{\geqslant 0}$ and nonzero ideals $I \subset R$ and $J \subset S$

$$
\overline{(I T+J T)^{w}}=\sum_{\substack{0 \leqslant i \in w, \atop \alpha \in \mathbb{Q}}} \overline{I^{\alpha} J^{w-\alpha}} T
$$

We devote the last two sections of the paper to tackle this conjecture. First, we note that the restriction on the field is partially justified by a related question (see Question 4.14 and Example 4.15). We also note that the use of two different $\mathbb{k}$-algebras is essential in this conjecture, as the summation formula for rational powers does not hold in general if instead one considers two ideals in the same ring, see Example 4.11.

In Proposition 4.7 we show that if two ideals $I \subset R$ and $J \subset S$ admit a Rees package, e.g. the invariant ideals in Theorem A, then $I T+J T$ does as well. Moreover, a Rees package for $I T+J T$ can be obtained by 'gluing' those of $I$ and $J$. In particular, this shows that the Rees valuations of $I T+J T$ are obtained by pairing the ones of $I$ and $J$ (see Corollary 4.12). This result allows us to compute rational powers of more classes of ideals, see for instance Example 4.10.

In our next theorem, we use Proposition 4.7 to settle Conjecture 1.1 for ideals with a Rees package without restrictions on the field.

Theorem B (Theorem 4.8, Corollary 4.9). Adopt the notation in Conjecture 1.1 with $\mathbb{k}$ an arbitrary field. The conclusion of Conjecture 1.1 holds if I and J admit a Rees package. In particular, this holds if I and J belong to any of the classes of ideals in Theorem A, and not necessarily both from the same class.

In the following theorem, we provide further evidence for Conjecture 1.1. Here we prove an inclusion for arbitrary ideals and $w \gg 0$. This result can be seen as a weaker version of Conjecture 1.1 since we always have

$$
\sum_{\substack{0 \leqslant \tau \in w, \tau \in \mathbb{Q}} \overline{I^{\tau} J^{w-\tau}}} T=\bigcap_{\substack{0 \leqslant \tau \in w, \tau \in \mathbb{Q}} \overline{I^{\tau} T+\overline{J^{w-\tau}}} T}
$$

see Remark 5.3.
Theorem C (Theorem 5.2). Following the notation in Conjecture 1.1, there exists $w_{0} \in \mathbb{Q}_{>0}$ such that if $w_{0} \leqslant \tau \leqslant w-w_{0}, \tau \in \mathbb{Q}_{\geqslant 0}$ then

$$
\sum_{\substack{0 \leqslant i \in w, \alpha \in \mathbb{Q}} \overline{I^{\alpha} J^{w-\alpha}}} T \subseteq \overline{(I T+J T)^{w}} \subseteq \overline{I^{\tau}} T+\overline{J^{w-\tau}} T
$$

The proof of Theorem C is influenced by that of [49, Theorem 0.3]. The first step is to define rational powers of ideal sheaves in normal varieties inspired by [45, Définition 4.2.2] and [44, Definition 9.6.2], see Definition 2.16. Next, we prove the statement for ideals in discrete

valuation rings, see Corollary 5.6. Next, a careful use of Serre's vanishing theorem gives us a desired vanishing result, see Lemma 5.7. Finally, we put it all together in page 25.

We now outline the content of the paper. Section 2 includes general details about rational powers and Rees valuations, as well as the definition of rational powers of ideals sheaves. Section 3 contains the definition of Rees package and the proof of Theorem A. Section 4 includes the proof of Theorem B. This section also includes examples where our results are applied. Section 5 is devoted to the proof of Theorem C.

question: In what way do $L^{2}$-spaces differ from classical function spaces like $L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{R})$?
answer: Unlike classical function spaces such as $L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{R})$, which are more flexible in terms of transformations, these specialized $L^{2}$-spaces exhibit rigidity due to their dependence on both an automorphism group and manifold-specific transformations. This distinction arises because they lack irreducible factors.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

We describe the isometry group of $L^{2}(\Omega, M)$ for Riemannian manifolds $M$ of dimension at least two with irreducible universal cover. We establish a rigidity result for the isometries of these spaces: any isometry arises from an automorphism of $\Omega$ and a family of isometries of $M$, distinguishing these spaces from the classical $L^{2}(\Omega)=L^{2}(\Omega, \mathbb{R})$. Additionally, we prove that these spaces lack irreducible factors and that two such spaces are isometric if and only if the underlying manifolds are.

question: Does there exist a random variable such that its quantile function matches a given non-decreasing and left-continuous function?
answer: Yes, if a function is non-decreasing and left-continuous, then there exists a random variable such that its quantile function matches this given function.

evidence.text:
# Appendix B. Auxiliary results for quantile functions 

Suppose that $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ is an atomless probability space. Recall that $\mathcal{M}$ denotes the set of all random variables $\xi: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, where two of them are identified if they have the same law. Given $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$, we define the cumulative distribution function by $F_{\xi}(x):=\mathbb{P}(\xi \leq x)$ and set $F_{\xi}\left(x^{-}\right)=\sup _{y<x} F_{\xi}(y)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Moreover, the quantile function $q_{\xi}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and upper quantile function $q_{\xi}^{+}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ are defined by

$$
q_{\xi}(t):=\inf \left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: t \leq F_{\xi}(x)\right\} \quad \text { and } \quad q_{\xi}^{+}(t):=\inf \left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: t<F_{\xi}(x)\right\}
$$

Lemma B.1. For all $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$ and $t \in(0,1)$, the following statements hold:
(i) $\left[q_{\xi}(t), \infty\right)=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: t \leq F_{\xi}(x)\right\}$.
(ii) $\left(-\infty, q_{\xi}^{+}(t)\right]=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: t \geq F_{\xi}\left(x^{-}\right)\right\}$.
(iii) $\sup _{s<t} q_{\xi}(s)=\sup _{s<t} q_{\xi}^{+}(s)=q_{\xi}(t)$.
(iv) $\inf _{s>t} q_{\xi}(s)=\inf _{s>t} q_{\xi}^{+}(s)=q_{\xi}^{+}(t)$.
(v) The function $q_{\xi}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is left-continuous.
(vi) The function $q_{\xi}^{+}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is right-continuous.
(vii) The function $(s, r) \mapsto q_{\xi}(r)-q_{\xi}^{+}(s)$ is lower semicontinuous on $(0,1)^{2}$.

Proof. (i) and (ii) follow from the definitions of $q$ and $q^{+}$, using that $F_{\xi}$ is non-decreasing and right-continuous.

For $a:=\sup _{s<t} q_{\xi}(s)$, it follows from (i) that

$$
[a, \infty)=\bigcap_{s<t}\left[q_{\xi}(s), \infty\right)=\bigcap_{s<t} F_{\xi}^{-1}([s, \infty)])=F_{\xi}^{-1}([t, \infty)])=\left[q_{\xi}(t), \infty\right)
$$

where $F_{\xi}^{-1}([s, \infty))=\left\{x \in \mathbb{R}: s \leq F_{\xi}(x)\right\}$. This shows $\sup _{s<t} q_{\xi}(s)=q_{\xi}(t)$. For $s<t$, it holds $q_{\xi}(s) \leq q_{\xi}^{+}(s) \leq q_{\xi}(t)$, so that $q_{\xi}(t)=\sup _{s<t} q_{\xi}(s) \leq \sup _{s<t} q_{\xi}^{+}(s) \leq q_{\xi}(t)$, which shows (iii).

Define $G(s):=F_{\xi}\left(s^{-}\right)$for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$. For $b:=\inf _{s>t} q_{\xi}^{+}(s)$, it follows from (ii) that

$$
(-\infty, b]=\bigcap_{s>t}\left(-\infty, q_{\xi}^{+}(s)\right]=\bigcap_{s>t} G^{-1}\left((-\infty, s]\right)=G^{-1}\left((-\infty, t]\right)=\left(-\infty, q_{\xi}^{+}(t)\right]
$$

where $G^{-1}([s, \infty))=\{x \in \mathbb{R}: s \leq G(x)\}$. This shows $\inf _{s>t} q_{\xi}^{+}(s)=q_{\xi}^{+}(t)$. For $s>t$, it holds $q_{\xi}^{+}(s) \geq q_{\xi}(s) \geq q_{\xi}^{+}(t)$, so that $q_{\xi}^{+}(t)=\inf _{s>t} q_{\xi}^{+}(s) \geq \inf _{s>t} q_{\xi}(s) \geq q_{\xi}^{+}(t)$, which shows (iv).

Finally, (v), (vi) and (vii) are consequences of (iii) and (iv).
Lemma B.2. For $\xi, \eta \in \mathcal{M}$, the following statements are equivalent:
(i) $q_{\xi}(u)-q_{\xi}(t) \leq q_{\eta}(u)-q_{\eta}(t)$ for all $0<t \leq u<1$.
(ii) $q_{\xi}(u)-q_{\xi}^{+}(t) \leq q_{\eta}(u)-q_{\eta}^{+}(t)$ for all $0<t<u<1$.

Proof. (ii) $\Rightarrow(i)$ : Let $0<t \leq u<1$. For $s \in(0, t)$, it holds $q_{\xi}(u)-q_{\xi}^{+}(s) \leq$ $q_{\eta}(u)-q_{\eta}^{+}(s)$. Letting $s \rightarrow t^{-}$, it follows from (iii) in Lemma B. 1 that

$$
q_{\xi}(u)-q_{\xi}(t) \leq q_{\eta}(u)-q_{\eta}(t)
$$

$(i) \Rightarrow(i i)$ : Let $0<t<u<1$. For $s \in(t, u)$, it holds $q_{\xi}(u)-q_{\xi}(s) \leq q_{\eta}(u)-q_{\eta}(s)$. Letting $s \rightarrow t^{+}$, it follows from (iv) in Lemma B. 1 that $q_{\xi}(u)-q_{\xi}^{+}(t) \leq q_{\eta}(u)-q_{\eta}^{+}(t)$.

Lemma B.3. If $q:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is non-decreasing and left-continuous, then there exists $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$ such that $q(u)=q_{\xi}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$.

Proof. If $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$ is atomless, then there exists a uniformly distributed random variable $U$ with values in $(0,1)$ defined on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, \mathbb{P})$, see e.g. [6, Theorem 1] and [12, Proposition A.27]. Then $\xi=q(U)$ is as desired. To that end, define $F: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow[0,1]$ by

$$
F(x):=0 \vee \sup \{s \in(0,1): x \geq q(s)\}
$$

which satisfies
(1) $q(F(x)) \leq x$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ (where we set $q(0):=q\left(0^{+}\right)$and $q(1):=q\left(1^{-}\right)$),
(2) $F(q(s)) \geq s$ for all $s \in(0,1)$.

For $x \in \mathbb{R}$, it follows from (2) that $\{q(U) \leq x\} \subset\{F(q(U)) \leq F(x)\} \subset\{U \leq F(x)\}$. Hence, for every $u \in(0,1)$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
q_{\xi}(u) & =\inf \{x \in \mathbb{R}: \mathbb{P}(q(U) \leq x) \geq u\} \\
& \geq \inf \{x \in \mathbb{R}: \mathbb{P}(U \leq F(x)) \geq u\} \\
& =\inf \{x \in \mathbb{R}: F(x) \geq u\}
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $a:=\inf \{x \in \mathbb{R}: F(x) \geq u\}$, and $x_{n} \downarrow a$ with $F\left(x_{n}\right) \geq u$. It follows from (1) that $x_{n} \geq q(u)$, and therefore $q_{\xi}(u) \geq a \geq q(u)$ by letting $n \rightarrow \infty$.

As for the other inequality, we have that $\mathbb{P}(q(U) \leq q(u)) \geq \mathbb{P}(U \leq u)=u$. Hence, it follows from the definition of $q_{\xi}(u)$ that $q_{\xi}(u) \leq q(u)$.

Recall that for $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$, the integrated quantile function $Q_{\xi}:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is defined by

$$
Q_{\xi}(u):=\int_{u}^{1} q_{\xi}(v) \mathrm{d} v
$$

Lemma B.4. If $Q:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is concave and satisfies $Q\left(0^{+}\right) \in \mathbb{R}$ and $Q\left(1^{-}\right)=0$, then there exists $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$ such that $Q(u)=Q_{\xi}(u)$ for all $u \in(0,1)$.

Proof. Since $Q$ is concave, there exist a non-decreasing function $q:(0,1) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and $c \in(0,1)$ such that

$$
Q(u)=Q(c)-\int_{c}^{u} q(v) \mathrm{d} v
$$

see e.g. [26, Theorem 12A]. By replacing $q$ by its left-continuous modification, we can assume that $q$ is left-continuous. Using that $Q\left(1^{-}\right)=0$, we get that

$$
Q(u)=\int_{u}^{1} q(v) \mathrm{d} v
$$

Since $q$ is left-continuous, it follows from Lemma B. 3 that $q=q_{\xi}$ for some $\xi \in \mathcal{M}$. It remains to show that $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}}[|\xi|] & =\int_{0}^{1}\left|q_{\xi}(v)\right| \mathrm{d} v \\
& =-\int_{0}^{F_{\xi}(0)} q_{\xi}(v) \mathrm{d} v+\int_{F_{\xi}(0)}^{1} q_{\xi}(v) \mathrm{d} v \\
& =-Q\left(0^{+}\right)+2 Q\left(F_{\xi}(0)\right)<\infty
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $\xi$ has finite first moment, and consequently $\xi \in \mathcal{M}_{1}$.

question: How does strategic uncertainty affect a regime's reputation in deterring uprisings?
answer: Strategic uncertainty significantly enhances the value of a regime's reputation in deterring uprisings. When players face globalized uncertainty over their payoffs, the regime can effectively develop a strong reputation and secure favorable outcomes, even when such outcomes are not possible under complete information.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

How valuable is reputation to a regime seeking to deter uprisings? I show the answer depends almost entirely on players' strategic uncertainty over other players actions. Without higher-order uncertainty, reputational effects are overshadowed by stage-game strategic complementarities: any payoff attainable in the complete-information repeated game remains attainable in the corresponding reputation game. However, when agents face globalized uncertainty over their payoffs, the regime's value for reputation rises sharply. In particular, the regime can leverage globalized strategic uncertainty to successful develop a reputation and secure their Stackelberg payoff in all pure equilibria of the reputation game, even as that same globalized strategic uncertainty forces them to their minimax payoff in the associated complete-information repeated game. Moreover, the globalized reputation game selects a unique pooling Markov equilibria among the continuum of Markov equilibria present in the complete-information game, refining predictions about equilibrium play. To establish these results, I develop new tools for analyzing non-normalized discounted repeated games with endogenous exit, where commitment actions vary with the regime's patience.


Keywords: Repeated Global Games, Reputation, Regime Change, Endogenous Exit. JEL Codes: C73, D74, I14.
