question: Is every affine map from a complete Riemannian manifold to a geodesic metric space an isometry after rescaling?
answer: Yes, every affine map from a complete Riemannian manifold to a geodesic metric space is, up to rescaling by some constant, an isometry.

evidence.text:
# 3. Affine maps on certain products 

We characterize affine maps on products of Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least two with irreducible universal coverings.

Theorem 3.1. Let $\left(M_{1}, g_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(M_{n}, g_{n}\right)$ be complete Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least two with irreducible universal covers. For a geodesic metric space $Y$ with angles, every affine map

$$
f: M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n} \rightarrow Y
$$

is, up to factor-wise rescaling with some $c_{i} \geq 0$, an isometry $\left(M_{1}, c_{1} g_{1}\right) \times$ $\ldots \times\left(M_{n}, c_{n} g_{n}\right) \rightarrow f\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}\right)$.

We stress that, by allowing $c_{i}=0$, we allow for the case in which $\left(M_{i}, c_{i} g_{i}\right)$ collapses to a point.

Proof. Let $p=\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}\right) \in M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}$ and $H_{i}:=H o l_{p_{i}}\left(M_{i}\right)$ be the holonomy group of $M_{i}$ at $p_{i}$. By the Berger-Simons theorem (cf. Simons, [Sim62]), either $H_{i}$ acts transitively on the unit sphere in $T_{p_{i}} M_{i}=: V_{i}$, or $M_{i}$ is a locally symmetric space of higher-rank. Without loss of generality, assume the first $m$ factors are of the first type and the rest are of the second type.

For the first type, choose a unit vector $e_{i} \in V_{i}$. Then $\Sigma_{i}:=\left\langle e_{i}\right\rangle$ intersects all $H_{i}$-orbits, and the stabilizer $W_{i}:=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{i}}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)$ contains an element which restricted to $\Sigma_{i}$ is the reflection $e_{i} \mapsto-e_{i}$. Indeed, by transitivity, for any other unit vector $v \in V_{i}$, there exists $h \in H_{i}$ such that $h\left(e_{i}\right)=v$. Thus the $H_{i}$-orbit of $e_{i}$ is the entire unit sphere in $V_{i}$, and hence $\Sigma_{i}$ intersects all $H_{i^{-}}$ orbits. Furthermore, since $-e_{i}$ is also a unit vector, there exists $g \in H_{i}$ such that $g\left(e_{i}\right)=-e_{i}$. As $g\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)=\Sigma_{i}, g \in W_{i}=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{i}}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)$, and $g$ restricted to $\Sigma_{i}$ is the reflection $e_{i} \mapsto-e_{i}$.

For the second type, choose an immersed, maximal flat submanifold $F_{i}$. Then $\Sigma_{i}:=T_{p_{i}} F_{i}$ intersects all $H_{i}$-orbits orthogonally, and the stabilizer $W_{i}:=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{i}}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)$ acts irreducibly on $\Sigma_{i}$ (cf. Eschenburg, [Esc09, Sections $9,10])$.

We define $V:=T_{p}\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}\right) \cong V_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus V_{n}$ and $H:=H o l_{p}\left(M_{1} \times\right.$ $\left.\ldots \times M_{n}\right) \cong H_{1} \times \ldots \times H_{n}$. Since $H_{1} \times \ldots \times H_{n}$ acts component-wise on $V_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus V_{n}, \Sigma:=\Sigma_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus \Sigma_{n}$ intersects all $H$-orbits.

For $v \in T\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}\right)$, define $|v|^{f}:=\frac{d\left(f\left(\gamma_{v}(t)\right), f\left(\gamma_{v}\left(t^{\prime}\right)\right)\right)}{|t-t^{\prime}|}$ for sufficiently small $t, t^{\prime}$, where $\gamma_{v}$ is the Riemannian geodesic with $\gamma_{v}^{\prime}(0)=v$. This is well-defined precisely because $f$ is affine, and $|v|^{f}$ is the reparametrization factor of the (locally metric) geodesic $\gamma_{v}$ under $f$. By Lytchak [Lyt12, Theorem 1.5], $|\cdot|^{f}$ is a continuous family of semi-norms invariant under parallel transport.

To prove our claim, it suffices to show that $|\cdot|^{f}$ is induced by a metric of the form $c_{1} g_{1}+\ldots+c_{n} g_{n}$ for some $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} \geq 0$.

Since $|\cdot|^{f}$ is invariant under parallel transport, it suffices to show that its restriction to $V$, denoted $|\cdot|^{f}\left.\right|_{V}$, is induced by $c_{1} g_{1}+\cdots+c_{n} g_{n} \mid_{V \times V}$, and we know that $|\cdot|^{f} \mid_{V}$ is invariant under the action of $H$. Consequently, as $\Sigma:=\Sigma_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Sigma_{n}$ intersects all $H$-orbits, it suffices to show that $|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma$ is induced by $c_{1} g_{1}+\cdots+c_{n} g_{n} \mid \Sigma \times \Sigma$.

Let $W:=W_{1} \times \ldots \times W_{n} \leq H$. As a side note, we remark that by Lytchak [Lyt12, 4.4], the restriction $q \mapsto q \mid \Sigma$ is actually a bijection between $H$-invariant norms on $V$ and $W$-invariant norms on $\Sigma$.

We define $F:=\operatorname{im}\left(\gamma_{e_{1}}\right) \times \cdots \times \operatorname{im}\left(\gamma_{e_{m}}\right) \times F_{m+1} \times \cdots \times F_{n}$, This is an immersed flat submanifold of $M_{1} \times \cdots \times M_{n}$ with $T_{p} F \cong \Sigma$. Thus there exists a neighbourhood $U(0) \subset\left(\Sigma, g_{1}+\ldots+g_{n} \mid \Sigma \times \Sigma\right)$ which embeds isometrically into $\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}, g_{1}+\ldots+g_{n}\right)$. The image of $U(0)$ under this embedding is denoted $N(p) \subset M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}$ and the image $f(N(p)) \subset Y$ is isometric to $N(p) \subset\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n},|\cdot|^{f}\right)$. Since $|\cdot|^{f}$ is invariant under parallel transport, $f(N(p)) \subset Y$ is isometric to $U(0) \subset\left(\Sigma,|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma\right)$. Thus, by Lemma 2.11, $|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma$ is induced by a semi-definite symmetric bilinear form $h: \Sigma \times \Sigma \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.

Since $|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma$ is invariant under the action of $W$, the bilinear form $h$ is of course also invariant under the same action.

By representation-theoretic arguments, $W$-invariant inner products on $\Sigma$ are linear combinations of $W_{i}$-invariant inner products on $\Sigma_{i}$. This extends to semi-definite symmetric bilinear forms like $h$. Nonetheless, in the following we will provide an alternative, more direct argument:

Restricting $h$ to $\Sigma_{i}$, we have $W_{i}$-invariant semi-definite symmetric bilinear forms $h_{i}$ on $\Sigma_{i}$.

For $i \leq m$, we see directly that $h_{i}=c_{i} g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}$ for some $c_{i} \geq 0$.
For $i>m$, we first notice that $\Sigma_{i}^{0}:=\left\{v \in \Sigma_{i}:|v|^{f}=0\right\} \subset \Sigma_{i}$ is a $W_{i}$-invariant subspace and therefore, by irreducibility, either $|v|^{f} \mid \Sigma_{i} \equiv 0$ or $|v|^{f} \mid \Sigma_{i}$ is a norm. In the former case, $h_{i}=0$. In the latter case, $h_{i}$ is a scalar product invariant under the irreducible action of $W_{i} \leq O\left(\Sigma_{i}, g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}\right)$ and thus by the lemma of Schur, there exists $c_{i}>0$ such that $h_{i}=c_{i} g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}$.

Thus for all $1 \leq i \leq n$, there exists $c_{i} \geq 0$ such that $h_{i}=c_{i} g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}$.
Now it just remains to show that $h=h_{1}+\ldots+h_{n}$. This is equivalent to showing that for $i \neq j, v \in \Sigma_{i}$ and $w \in \Sigma_{j}$, we have that $h(v, w)=0$.

If $i \leq m$, recall that $W_{i} \leq W$ contains an element which restricted to $\Sigma_{i}$ is the reflection $e_{i} \mapsto-e_{i}$. Thus, by the $W$-invariance, we have that $h(v, w)=h(-v, w)=-h(v, w)$ and therefore $h(v, w)=0$.

If on the other hand, $i, j>m$, we focus on the linear map $f: \Sigma \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by $f(u):=h(v, u)$. We observe that $\operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j} \leq \Sigma_{j}$ is a $W_{j^{-}}$ invariant subspace of $\Sigma_{j}$. Indeed to see this, simply note that for $w=$ $(\mathrm{id}, \ldots, w_{j}, \ldots, \mathrm{id}) \in W_{j} \leq W$ and $u \in \operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j}$, we have that $f(w \cdot u)=$ $h(v, w \cdot u)=h(w \cdot v, w \cdot u)=h(v, u)=0$. Since $\operatorname{im}(f) \neq\{0\}, \operatorname{dim}(\operatorname{ker}(f))=$ $n-1$ and since also $\operatorname{dim}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right) \geq 2$, we deduce that $\operatorname{dim}\left(\operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j}\right) \geq 1$. Since the action of $W_{j}$ on $\Sigma_{j}$ is irreducible, we therefore have that $\operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j}=\Sigma_{j}$, i.e. $h(v, w)=0$.

In other words, we have shown that under the given assumptions, for an affine map $f: M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n} \rightarrow Y$, there exist constants $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} \geq 0$ such that for any $\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}\right),\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}$,

$$
d_{Y}^{2}\left(f\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}\right), f\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)\right)=\sum_{i=0}^{n} c_{i}^{2} d_{M_{i}}^{2}\left(p_{i}, q_{i}\right)
$$

Note that here $d_{M_{i}}$ denotes the Riemannian distance on $M_{i}$.
In particular, this holds for affine maps $f: M^{n} \rightarrow Y$ and the objective of the next part is to extend this to $L^{2}(\Omega, M)$.

For $n=1$, we obtain the following special case of the above result. In this situation, the claim also trivially holds for $\operatorname{dim}(M)=1$.

Corollary 3.2. Let $(M, g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold with irreducible universal covering. For a geodesic metric space $Y$ with angles, every affine map $f: M \rightarrow Y$ is, up to a rescaling by some $c \geq 0$, an isometry $(M, c g) \rightarrow f(M)$.

question: What happens to the concentration of total original molecules in the voxel over time?
answer: The concentration decreases over time.

evidence.text:
# 4. RESULTS
### 4.1 Simulated multi-Gaussian IVIM

A diagram of the simulated kidney voxel with tissue, tubular, and vascular physiology (Fig. 1A) is shown with the corresponding Gaussian diffusions over time ${ }^{15,16}$ (Fig. 1B). The concentration of total original molecules in the voxel decreased over time (Fig. 1C, black) with each individual compartment diffusing at different rates, with three separate WTT times (Fig. 1C, red, blue, grey).

The corresponding DWI decay curve is a tri-exponential (Fig. 1D, black) sum of each individual compartment (Fig. 1D red, blue, grey). Spectral diffusion of the decay curve in 1D is shown in Fig. 1E; comparison between Fig. 1B and Fig. 1E shows the spectral peaks agree well with the three original isotropic Gaussians.

question: What does the Pseudo-Power Theorem state about an omega-inaccessible cardinal with cofinality omega?
answer: The Pseudo-Power Theorem states that if $\lambda$ is an omega-inaccessible cardinal and cf($\lambda)=\omega$, then pp$_{\omega}(\lambda) \leq \lambda^{\omega}$, and if $\lambda$ is not a fixed-point of the aleph-function, then pp$_{\omega}(\lambda)=\lambda^{\omega}$ and it is not weakly inaccessible.

evidence.text:
# 3 HC on an interval-partition of the cardinals 

In this section, we introduce a cardinal function $\urcorner$ that will assist in determining when HC holds or fails. The function $\urcorner$ tracks $\omega$-inaccessible cardinals.

Shelah's PCF Theory plays an important role in determining Halin's conjecture, in particular, we will resort to the $p p_{\omega}$ operator.

Definition 7 (Scale and $p p_{\omega}$ ). We say that a sequence of functions $\left\langle f_{\alpha} \mid \alpha<\kappa\right\rangle$ is a $\kappa$-scale for $\lambda$ if there is a set of regular cardinals $\mathfrak{a}=\left\{\kappa_{n} \mid n \in \omega\right\}$ such that the following hold:
(a) $\sup (a)=\lambda$,
(b) $n<m$ implies $\kappa_{n}<\kappa_{m}$,
(c) $f_{\alpha} \in \prod_{n \in \omega} \kappa_{n}$ for every $\alpha<\kappa$
and there is an ideal $J$ on $\omega$ such that the following hold:
(i) every bounded subset of $\omega$ belongs to $J$;
(ii) for all $\alpha, \beta<\kappa$ such that $\alpha<\beta$, we have that $f_{\alpha}<_{J} f_{\beta}$; and
(iii) for all $g \in \prod_{n \in \omega} \kappa_{n}$, there is $\alpha<\kappa$ such that $g<_{J} f_{\alpha}$.

The operator $p p_{\omega}(\lambda)$ is defined as

$$
p p_{\omega}(\lambda)=\sup \{\kappa \mid \text { there is a } \kappa \text {-scale for } \lambda\}
$$

We will need the following result, due to Shelah, on the pseudo-power operator:
Pseudo-Power Theorem. [10, Ch II §5, Ch IX §2] Suppose that $\lambda$ is a $\omega$-inaccessible cardinal and $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)=\omega$. Then $\mathrm{pp}_{\omega}(\lambda) \leq \lambda^{\omega}$. Moreover, if $\lambda$ is not a fixed-point of the $\aleph$-function, then $\mathrm{pp}_{\omega}(\lambda)=\lambda^{\omega}$ and $\mathrm{pp}_{\omega}(\lambda)$ is not a weakly inaccessible cardinal.

The following result tells how the existence of $\kappa$-scales for $\lambda$ implies that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.

Counter-Examples from Scales. [3, Theorem 8.1] [3, Proposition 7.4] If $\lambda$ and $\kappa$ are cardinals, $\operatorname{cf}(\lambda)=\omega$ and there is a $\kappa$-scale for $\lambda$, then there is a graph $G$ with an end $\varepsilon$ such that $\operatorname{deg}(\varepsilon)=\kappa$ and for all regular cardinals $\kappa^{\prime}$ such that $\lambda<\kappa^{\prime} \leq \kappa$ there is no ray graph of cardinality $\kappa^{\prime}$.

The statement in Counter-Examples from Scales. is stronger than what is presented in [3, Theorem 8.1], however, the proof provided in [3] also establishes this stronger result. The next lemma will be used to deal with $H C(\kappa)$ when $\kappa$ is singular.

Lemma 3.1. Suppose that $\kappa$ and $\mu$ are cardinals such that $\omega_{2} \leq \operatorname{cf}(\kappa)<\kappa, \mu<\kappa$ and $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)<\operatorname{cf}(\mu)$. If there is a increasing sequence of regular cardinals greater than $\mu,\left\langle\mu_{\alpha} \mid \alpha<\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)\right\rangle$, cofinal in $\kappa$ such that for every $\alpha<\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ there is a graph $G_{\alpha}$ with exactly one end $\varepsilon_{\alpha}, \operatorname{deg}\left(\varepsilon_{\alpha}\right)=\mu_{\alpha}$ with no ray graph of cardinality $\geq \mu$. Then $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.

Proof. We will build a graph $\mathcal{G}$ with an end $\varepsilon$ of degree $\kappa$ with no ray graph of size $\kappa$. Suppose that the graphs $G_{\alpha}$ from our hypothesis are mutually disjoint. Let $r=\left\{v_{n} \mid n \in \omega\right\}$ be a set disjoint from each $G_{\alpha}$ for $\alpha \in \operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$. We start defining our graph $G$ by adding $\left\{v_{n}, v_{n+1}\right\}$ to the set of edges of the graph for every $n \in \omega$. For each $\alpha<\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$, we fix a ray $t_{\alpha} \in G_{\alpha}$ and add the vertices $\left\{\left(v_{n},\left(t_{\alpha}\right)_{n}\right\}\right.$ to $G$ for every $\alpha<\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ and every $n \in \omega$, that concludes our definition of $G$. It readily follows that $G$ has only one end $\varepsilon$ and $\operatorname{deg}(\varepsilon)=\kappa$.

Suppose that $\mathcal{F}_{0} \subseteq \varepsilon$ is a collection of pairwise disjoint rays with $\left|\mathcal{F}_{0}\right|=\kappa$. Suppose towards a contradiction that there is $\mathcal{F} \subseteq \mathcal{F}_{0}$ with $|\mathcal{F}|=\kappa$ and a family of paths $\mathcal{P}$ such that $(\mathcal{F}, \mathcal{P})$ is a ray graph of $G$. We will find an $\alpha<\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ such that there is a ray graph in $\varepsilon_{\alpha} \cap \mathcal{F}$ of size $\mu$.

The hypothesis that $\operatorname{cf}(\mu)>\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ implies that there is $\alpha<\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ such that $|\mathcal{F} \cap$ $\varepsilon_{\alpha} \mid \geq \mu$. We will find a ray graph of $\varepsilon_{\alpha}$ of cardinality $\geq \mu$ reaching a contradiction.

Recall that $r=\left\{v_{n} \mid n \in \omega\right\}$ is somewhat the center of $G$. We consider two cases, on the first case we suppose that $t_{\alpha} \notin \mathcal{F}$. Given $z_{0}, z_{1}, w_{0}, w_{1}$ mutually disjoint elements of $\mathcal{F} \cap \varepsilon_{\alpha}$, such that there are $p, s \in \mathcal{P}$ that $p$ connects $z_{0}$ to $z_{1}$ and $s$ connects $w_{0}$ to $w_{1}, p \cap r \neq \emptyset$ and $s \cap r \neq \emptyset$. Then $p \cap r \cap s=\emptyset$, since $\mathcal{P}$ is a family of independent paths. Therefore the set of pair of rays $z_{0}, z_{1} \in \mathcal{F}$ such that there exists a path $p \in \mathcal{P}$ connecting $z_{0}$ to $z_{1}$ and $p \cap r \neq \emptyset$ is a countable set. Then we let $\mathcal{R}$ to be the set of $w \in \varepsilon_{\alpha} \cap \mathcal{F}$ such that for every $u \in \varepsilon_{\alpha} \cap \mathcal{F}$ for all $p \in \mathcal{P}$ that connects $u$ to $w$ we have that $p \cap r=\emptyset$. We let $\mathcal{C}=\left\{p \in \mathcal{P} \mid p \subseteq G_{\alpha}\right\}$. Then $(\mathcal{R}, \mathcal{C})$ is a ray graph in $\varepsilon_{\alpha}$ of cardinality $\geq \mu$ that we seek.

On the second case we assume that $t_{\alpha} \in \mathcal{F}$. We let $\mathcal{C}$ be the paths of the form $p \cap G_{\alpha}$ such that $p$ connects rays $v_{0}, v_{1} \in \varepsilon_{\alpha}$. From the construction of $G$, it follows that $p \cap G_{\alpha}$ also connectes $v_{0}$ to $v_{1}$. Since $\left|\varepsilon_{\alpha} \cap \mathcal{F}\right|=\kappa$, if $\mathcal{R}=\varepsilon_{\alpha} \cap \mathcal{F}$, then it follows that $(\mathcal{R}, \mathcal{C})$ is a ray graph in $G_{\alpha}$ of cardinality $\geq \mu$ that we seek.

In both cases we reach a contradiction to our hypothesis that $G_{\alpha}$ has no ray graph of cardinality $\geq \mu$.

Theorem 3.2. Let $\urcorner: \mathrm{ON} \rightarrow \mathrm{CARD}$, such that for $\beta \in O R D$

$$
\urcorner(\beta)= \begin{cases}2 & \text { if } \beta=0 \\ \mathfrak{c} & \text { if } \beta=1 \\ \left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)^{\omega} & \text { if } \beta=\gamma+1 \text { for some ordinal } \gamma \text { such that } \operatorname{cf}(\gamma) \neq \aleph_{0} \\ \urcorner(\gamma)^{\omega} & \text { if } \beta=\gamma+1 \text { for some limit ordinal } \gamma \text { such that } \operatorname{cf}(\gamma)=\aleph_{0} \\ \bigcup_{\alpha \in \beta} \urcorner(\alpha) & \text { if } \beta \text { is a limit ordinal }\end{cases}
$$

Suppose $\kappa>\mathfrak{c}$ is any cardinal and $\gamma$ is an ordinal such that $\urcorner(\gamma)$ is not a fixedpoint of the $\aleph$-function. The following hold:
(a) If $\kappa \in\left(\urcorner(\gamma), \urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right]$ and $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) \neq \omega$, then $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ holds,
(b) If $\kappa \in\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}, \urcorner(\gamma+1)\right]$ and $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) \neq \omega$, then $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails,
(c) If $\kappa \in\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}, \urcorner(\gamma+1)\right]$ and $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma)=\omega$, then $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails
(d) $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ holds if $\kappa=\urcorner(\gamma)$ is a singular cardinal such that $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma)=\omega$ or $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma)$ is a $\omega$-inaccessible cardinal.
(e) $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ holds for all regular cardinals $\kappa$ that are fixed-points of the function $\urcorner$.

Proof. Case (a): An easy induction argument proves that for every cardinal $\kappa \in$ $\left\lceil\urcorner(\gamma), \urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)$ we have that $\kappa^{\omega}=\kappa$. Thus, applying Lemma 2.2 for $\kappa \in\left(\urcorner(\gamma), \urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)$ we have $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$. Since $\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}$ is $\omega$-inaccessible and $\operatorname{cf}\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)=\omega$, it follows from Lemma 2.5 that $\mathrm{HC}\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)$ holds.

Case (b): We consider two sub-cases of (b):
Sub-case (b)(i): Suppose $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma) \neq \aleph_{0}$ and $\kappa \in\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}, \urcorner(\gamma+1)\right)$. By the Pseudo-Power Theorem applied to $\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}$ we have that

$$
\operatorname{pp}_{\omega}\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)=\left(\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}\right)^{\omega}=\urcorner(\gamma+1)
$$

Thus we can find $\tau \in(\neg(\gamma)^{+\omega}, \neg(\gamma+1))$ such that $\tau \geq \kappa$ and there is a $\tau$-scale for $\urcorner(\gamma)^{+\omega}$. We can apply Counter-Examples from Scales. to $\tau$ and obtain a graph $G$ which witnesses that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.

Sub-case (b)(ii): suppose that $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma) \neq \aleph_{0}$ and $\kappa=\neg(\gamma+1)$. If there is a $\neg(\gamma+1)$ scale for $\neg(\gamma)^{+\omega}$, it follows as in the previous case that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails, otherwise from Pseudo-Power Theorem it follows that $\urcorner(\gamma+1)$ is not a weakly inaccessible cardinal and hence it is a singular cardinal. Then we can apply Lemma 3.1 and obtain the failure of $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$.

Case (c): We consider two sub-cases of (c):
Case (c)(i): Suppose $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma)=\omega$ and $\kappa \in(\neg(\gamma), \neg(\gamma+1))$. From our hypothesis that $\urcorner(\gamma)$ is not a fixed-point of the $\aleph$ function we can apply Pseudo-Power Theorem to $\urcorner(\gamma)$ and by the definition of $\urcorner(\gamma+1)$, in the case $\operatorname{cf}(\gamma)=\omega$, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{pp}_{\omega}(\neg(\gamma))=\neg(\gamma)^{\omega}=\neg(\gamma+1)
$$

Applying Theorem Counter-Examples from Scales. it follows that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.
Case (c)(ii): Suppose that $\kappa=\neg(\gamma+1)$. If there is a $\neg(\gamma+1)$-scale for $\neg(\gamma)$, it follows, as in the previous case, that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails. Otherwise, $\neg(\gamma+1)$ is a singular cardinals and by Lemma 3.1 it follows that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.

Case (d): Note that $\kappa=\neg(\gamma)$ is $\omega$-inaccessible. Applying Lemma 2.5 we obtain $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$.

Case(e): Follows from Lemma 2.2.
We introduce the following notation: If $\mu$ is not a $\omega$-inaccessible cardinal, we denote by $\theta(\mu)$ the least cardinal $\theta<\mu$ such that $\theta^{\omega}>\mu$. Notice that if $\alpha<\theta(\mu)$, since $\left(\alpha^{\omega}\right)^{\omega}=\alpha^{\omega}<\mu$, it follows that $\alpha^{\omega}<\theta(\mu)$. Moreover, $\operatorname{cf}(\mu)=\omega$, as otherwise, we have $\mu^{\omega}=\mu$ from the fact that $\mu$ is a $\omega$-inaccessible cardinal.

Corollary 3.3. Suppose that $\kappa=\neg(\gamma)$ for some limit ordinal $\gamma$. If $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ is not $\omega$-inaccessible, $\theta(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa))$ is not a fixed point of the $\aleph$-function and $\theta(c f(\kappa))>\mathfrak{c}$, then $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.

Proof. An induction argument proves that every $\omega$-inaccessible cardinals is of the form $\neg(\gamma)$ for some ordinal $\gamma$. Let $\mu=\theta(c f(\kappa))$, then $\theta(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa)$ is a $\omega$-inaccessible cardinal and there is an ordinal $\gamma$ such that $\neg(\gamma)=\theta(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa))$. Then $\operatorname{cf}(\kappa) \in(\neg(\gamma), \neg(\gamma+1)]$ and $\operatorname{cf}(\neg(\gamma))=\omega$. From Theorem 3.2 item (1)(b) we have that $\mathrm{HC}(\operatorname{cf}(\kappa))$ fails. By [3, Theorem 9.1], it follows that $\mathrm{HC}(\kappa)$ fails.

question: Is the non-tokenized early fusion (NTEF) method cost-effective?
answer: Yes, the NTEF method tends to be more cost-effective as it involves multiple training phases where most components are frozen.

evidence.text:
### 6.2.1 Non-Tokenized Early Fusion

The most common approach to enable cross-modal perception in LLMs is to connect pre-trained encoders of other modalities as adaptors. This method involves adding a speech encoder before the LLM and finetuning the entire model for speech understanding capabilities. These models excel in tasks such as speech recognition, speech translation, and general speech-to-text tasks [Chu et al., 2024, Tang et al., 2023, Shu et al., 2023, Deshmukh et al., 2023, Hu et al., 2024, Das et al., 2024, Fang et al., 2024]. Notable examples of this approach are Llama-omni [Fang et al., 2024] and LLaSM [Shu et al., 2023], which extend LLM capabilities to audio modality by integrating a pre-trained speech encoder, a speech adaptor, and a streaming speech decoder. SALMONN [Tang et al., 2023] takes a step further in capturing both speech and non-speech audio information using dual auditory encoders. Qwen2 Audio [Chu et al., 2024] introduce the new architecture to combine an audio encoder with a large language model, training to maximize next text token probability conditioned on audio representations.

This NTEF tends to be more cost-effective, as it involves multiple training phases where most components are frozen, and it can be effective even when training with Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning techniques [Hu et al., 2021].

question: What does it mean for functions $f_{x}: \Phi \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ to be lower semicontinuous?
answer: It means that for all $x \in X$, the set $\left\{\phi \in \Phi : f_{x}(\phi) \leq s\right\}$ is closed for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$.

In this section, we present our representation results for maxitive functions with respect to general orders. Since we do not assume any form of completeness on the order, we consider monotone functions with countably upwards directed sublevel sets. In contrast to bounded countable maxitivity, these concepts do not require that the order is countably complete, allowing us to derive more general statements without relying on the assumption of countable completeness.

For the remainder of this section, $X$ is endowed with an operation $+: X \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow X$. A function $\psi: X \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty]$ satisfies the translation property if $\psi(x+c)=\psi(x)+c$ for all $x \in X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$. A function $\psi: X \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty]$ satisfies the deviation property if $\psi(x+c)=\psi(x)$ for all $x \in X$ and $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
Corollary 4.4. Suppose that every $\phi \in \Phi$ has the translation property. Let $\psi: X \rightarrow$ $(-\infty, \infty]$ be a function with $A_{s}:=\{x \in X: \psi(x) \leq s\}$ for all $s \in \mathbb{R}$. Then, the following statements are equivalent:
(i) $\psi$ has the translation property, is monotone, and has countably upwards directed sublevel sets.
(ii) There exists a countably stable function $\gamma: \Phi \rightarrow[-\infty, \infty]$ with

$$

$$

(iii) The mapping $\phi \mapsto \alpha_{\min }(0, \phi):=\sup _{x \in A_{0}} \phi(x)$ is countably stable and

$$

$$

Hence, since every $\phi \in \Phi$ has the translation property, we obtain for every $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\phi \in \Phi$,

$$
\alpha_{\min }(s, \phi)=\sup _{x \in A_{s}} \phi(x)=\sup _{x \in A_{0}} \phi(x+s)=\sup _{x \in A_{0}} \phi(x)+s=\alpha_{\min }(0, \phi)+s
$$

It follows from Theorem 4.1 that for every $x \in X$,

$$

question: How is the degree matrix formulated in terms of its elements?
answer: The degree matrix $\mathbf{D}$ is formulated as $\operatorname{diag}(d_1, \ldots, d_N)$ where $d_i = \sum_{j=1}^{N} \mathbf{A}_{ij}$.

# 2.1 Graph Theory Fundamentals 

A graph can be denoted as $\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V}, \mathcal{E})$, where $\mathcal{V}$ is the node set and $\mathcal{E}$ is the edge set of the graph. An edge $e_{i j} \in \mathcal{E}$ can be formulated as $e_{i j}=\left(v_{i}, v_{j}\right)$, which indicates that the edge $e_{i j}$ connects node $v_{i}$ and node $v_{j}$. Edges can have attributes such as directions and weights. The direction of an edge defines how information flows between nodes, and the weight of an edge represents the importance or strength of the connection.

The adjacency matrix $\mathbf{A}$ is used to capture the structure of graphs. If graph $\mathcal{G}$ has $N$ nodes, $\mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}$. For an undirected graph, its adjacency matrix is always symmetric because if $\left(v_{i}, v_{j}\right) \in \mathcal{E},\left(v_{j}, v_{i}\right) \in \mathcal{E}$ as well. Otherwise, the adjacency matrix of a directed graph is asymmetric. Elements in $\mathbf{A}$ reflect the edge weights. Suppose the weight attached to edge $e_{i j}$ is a positive real number $w_{i j}$. The formulation of the adjacency matrix is presented below:

$$
\mathbf{A}_{i j}= \begin{cases}w_{i j}, & \left(v_{i}, v_{j}\right) \in \mathcal{E} \\ 0, & \left(v_{i}, v_{j}\right) \notin \mathcal{E}\end{cases}
$$

The degree matrix $D$ is formulated as $\mathbf{D}=\operatorname{diag}\left(d_{1}, \ldots, d_{N}\right)$, where $d_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{N} \mathbf{A}_{i j}$.

question: What does the holonomy group $H_i$ act on in a Riemannian manifold?
answer: The holonomy group $H_i$ acts transitively on the unit sphere in the tangent space $T_{p_{i}} M_{i}$ or makes $M_{i}$ a locally symmetric space of higher-rank.

# 3. Affine maps on certain products 

We characterize affine maps on products of Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least two with irreducible universal coverings.

Theorem 3.1. Let $\left(M_{1}, g_{1}\right), \ldots,\left(M_{n}, g_{n}\right)$ be complete Riemannian manifolds of dimension at least two with irreducible universal covers. For a geodesic metric space $Y$ with angles, every affine map

$$
f: M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n} \rightarrow Y
$$

is, up to factor-wise rescaling with some $c_{i} \geq 0$, an isometry $\left(M_{1}, c_{1} g_{1}\right) \times$ $\ldots \times\left(M_{n}, c_{n} g_{n}\right) \rightarrow f\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}\right)$.

We stress that, by allowing $c_{i}=0$, we allow for the case in which $\left(M_{i}, c_{i} g_{i}\right)$ collapses to a point.

Proof. Let $p=\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}\right) \in M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}$ and $H_{i}:=H o l_{p_{i}}\left(M_{i}\right)$ be the holonomy group of $M_{i}$ at $p_{i}$. By the Berger-Simons theorem (cf. Simons, [Sim62]), either $H_{i}$ acts transitively on the unit sphere in $T_{p_{i}} M_{i}=: V_{i}$, or $M_{i}$ is a locally symmetric space of higher-rank. Without loss of generality, assume the first $m$ factors are of the first type and the rest are of the second type.

For the first type, choose a unit vector $e_{i} \in V_{i}$. Then $\Sigma_{i}:=\left\langle e_{i}\right\rangle$ intersects all $H_{i}$-orbits, and the stabilizer $W_{i}:=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{i}}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)$ contains an element which restricted to $\Sigma_{i}$ is the reflection $e_{i} \mapsto-e_{i}$. Indeed, by transitivity, for any other unit vector $v \in V_{i}$, there exists $h \in H_{i}$ such that $h\left(e_{i}\right)=v$. Thus the $H_{i}$-orbit of $e_{i}$ is the entire unit sphere in $V_{i}$, and hence $\Sigma_{i}$ intersects all $H_{i^{-}}$ orbits. Furthermore, since $-e_{i}$ is also a unit vector, there exists $g \in H_{i}$ such that $g\left(e_{i}\right)=-e_{i}$. As $g\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)=\Sigma_{i}, g \in W_{i}=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{i}}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)$, and $g$ restricted to $\Sigma_{i}$ is the reflection $e_{i} \mapsto-e_{i}$.

For the second type, choose an immersed, maximal flat submanifold $F_{i}$. Then $\Sigma_{i}:=T_{p_{i}} F_{i}$ intersects all $H_{i}$-orbits orthogonally, and the stabilizer $W_{i}:=\operatorname{Stab}_{H_{i}}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right)$ acts irreducibly on $\Sigma_{i}$ (cf. Eschenburg, [Esc09, Sections $9,10])$.

We define $V:=T_{p}\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}\right) \cong V_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus V_{n}$ and $H:=H o l_{p}\left(M_{1} \times\right.$ $\left.\ldots \times M_{n}\right) \cong H_{1} \times \ldots \times H_{n}$. Since $H_{1} \times \ldots \times H_{n}$ acts component-wise on $V_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus V_{n}, \Sigma:=\Sigma_{1} \oplus \ldots \oplus \Sigma_{n}$ intersects all $H$-orbits.

For $v \in T\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}\right)$, define $|v|^{f}:=\frac{d\left(f\left(\gamma_{v}(t)\right), f\left(\gamma_{v}\left(t^{\prime}\right)\right)\right)}{|t-t^{\prime}|}$ for sufficiently small $t, t^{\prime}$, where $\gamma_{v}$ is the Riemannian geodesic with $\gamma_{v}^{\prime}(0)=v$. This is well-defined precisely because $f$ is affine, and $|v|^{f}$ is the reparametrization factor of the (locally metric) geodesic $\gamma_{v}$ under $f$. By Lytchak [Lyt12, Theorem 1.5], $|\cdot|^{f}$ is a continuous family of semi-norms invariant under parallel transport.

To prove our claim, it suffices to show that $|\cdot|^{f}$ is induced by a metric of the form $c_{1} g_{1}+\ldots+c_{n} g_{n}$ for some $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} \geq 0$.

Since $|\cdot|^{f}$ is invariant under parallel transport, it suffices to show that its restriction to $V$, denoted $|\cdot|^{f}\left.\right|_{V}$, is induced by $c_{1} g_{1}+\cdots+c_{n} g_{n} \mid_{V \times V}$, and we know that $|\cdot|^{f} \mid_{V}$ is invariant under the action of $H$. Consequently, as $\Sigma:=\Sigma_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus \Sigma_{n}$ intersects all $H$-orbits, it suffices to show that $|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma$ is induced by $c_{1} g_{1}+\cdots+c_{n} g_{n} \mid \Sigma \times \Sigma$.

Let $W:=W_{1} \times \ldots \times W_{n} \leq H$. As a side note, we remark that by Lytchak [Lyt12, 4.4], the restriction $q \mapsto q \mid \Sigma$ is actually a bijection between $H$-invariant norms on $V$ and $W$-invariant norms on $\Sigma$.

We define $F:=\operatorname{im}\left(\gamma_{e_{1}}\right) \times \cdots \times \operatorname{im}\left(\gamma_{e_{m}}\right) \times F_{m+1} \times \cdots \times F_{n}$, This is an immersed flat submanifold of $M_{1} \times \cdots \times M_{n}$ with $T_{p} F \cong \Sigma$. Thus there exists a neighbourhood $U(0) \subset\left(\Sigma, g_{1}+\ldots+g_{n} \mid \Sigma \times \Sigma\right)$ which embeds isometrically into $\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}, g_{1}+\ldots+g_{n}\right)$. The image of $U(0)$ under this embedding is denoted $N(p) \subset M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}$ and the image $f(N(p)) \subset Y$ is isometric to $N(p) \subset\left(M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n},|\cdot|^{f}\right)$. Since $|\cdot|^{f}$ is invariant under parallel transport, $f(N(p)) \subset Y$ is isometric to $U(0) \subset\left(\Sigma,|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma\right)$. Thus, by Lemma 2.11, $|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma$ is induced by a semi-definite symmetric bilinear form $h: \Sigma \times \Sigma \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.

Since $|\cdot|^{f} \mid \Sigma$ is invariant under the action of $W$, the bilinear form $h$ is of course also invariant under the same action.

By representation-theoretic arguments, $W$-invariant inner products on $\Sigma$ are linear combinations of $W_{i}$-invariant inner products on $\Sigma_{i}$. This extends to semi-definite symmetric bilinear forms like $h$. Nonetheless, in the following we will provide an alternative, more direct argument:

Restricting $h$ to $\Sigma_{i}$, we have $W_{i}$-invariant semi-definite symmetric bilinear forms $h_{i}$ on $\Sigma_{i}$.

For $i \leq m$, we see directly that $h_{i}=c_{i} g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}$ for some $c_{i} \geq 0$.
For $i>m$, we first notice that $\Sigma_{i}^{0}:=\left\{v \in \Sigma_{i}:|v|^{f}=0\right\} \subset \Sigma_{i}$ is a $W_{i}$-invariant subspace and therefore, by irreducibility, either $|v|^{f} \mid \Sigma_{i} \equiv 0$ or $|v|^{f} \mid \Sigma_{i}$ is a norm. In the former case, $h_{i}=0$. In the latter case, $h_{i}$ is a scalar product invariant under the irreducible action of $W_{i} \leq O\left(\Sigma_{i}, g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}\right)$ and thus by the lemma of Schur, there exists $c_{i}>0$ such that $h_{i}=c_{i} g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}$.

Thus for all $1 \leq i \leq n$, there exists $c_{i} \geq 0$ such that $h_{i}=c_{i} g_{i} \mid \Sigma_{i} \times \Sigma_{i}$.
Now it just remains to show that $h=h_{1}+\ldots+h_{n}$. This is equivalent to showing that for $i \neq j, v \in \Sigma_{i}$ and $w \in \Sigma_{j}$, we have that $h(v, w)=0$.

If $i \leq m$, recall that $W_{i} \leq W$ contains an element which restricted to $\Sigma_{i}$ is the reflection $e_{i} \mapsto-e_{i}$. Thus, by the $W$-invariance, we have that $h(v, w)=h(-v, w)=-h(v, w)$ and therefore $h(v, w)=0$.

If on the other hand, $i, j>m$, we focus on the linear map $f: \Sigma \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ given by $f(u):=h(v, u)$. We observe that $\operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j} \leq \Sigma_{j}$ is a $W_{j^{-}}$ invariant subspace of $\Sigma_{j}$. Indeed to see this, simply note that for $w=$ $(\mathrm{id}, \ldots, w_{j}, \ldots, \mathrm{id}) \in W_{j} \leq W$ and $u \in \operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j}$, we have that $f(w \cdot u)=$ $h(v, w \cdot u)=h(w \cdot v, w \cdot u)=h(v, u)=0$. Since $\operatorname{im}(f) \neq\{0\}, \operatorname{dim}(\operatorname{ker}(f))=$ $n-1$ and since also $\operatorname{dim}\left(\Sigma_{i}\right) \geq 2$, we deduce that $\operatorname{dim}\left(\operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j}\right) \geq 1$. Since the action of $W_{j}$ on $\Sigma_{j}$ is irreducible, we therefore have that $\operatorname{ker}(f) \cap \Sigma_{j}=\Sigma_{j}$, i.e. $h(v, w)=0$.

In other words, we have shown that under the given assumptions, for an affine map $f: M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n} \rightarrow Y$, there exist constants $c_{1}, \ldots, c_{n} \geq 0$ such that for any $\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}\right),\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right) \in M_{1} \times \ldots \times M_{n}$,

$$
d_{Y}^{2}\left(f\left(p_{1}, \ldots, p_{n}\right), f\left(q_{1}, \ldots, q_{n}\right)\right)=\sum_{i=0}^{n} c_{i}^{2} d_{M_{i}}^{2}\left(p_{i}, q_{i}\right)
$$

Note that here $d_{M_{i}}$ denotes the Riemannian distance on $M_{i}$.
In particular, this holds for affine maps $f: M^{n} \rightarrow Y$ and the objective of the next part is to extend this to $L^{2}(\Omega, M)$.

For $n=1$, we obtain the following special case of the above result. In this situation, the claim also trivially holds for $\operatorname{dim}(M)=1$.

Corollary 3.2. Let $(M, g)$ be a complete Riemannian manifold with irreducible universal covering. For a geodesic metric space $Y$ with angles, every affine map $f: M \rightarrow Y$ is, up to a rescaling by some $c \geq 0$, an isometry $(M, c g) \rightarrow f(M)$.

question: How is the integral of a function with surreal values over a set expressed in terms of numerosity?
answer: It is expressed as \(\int_{S} w d t = \pi N(S) \partial(w)\).

evidence.text:
# 3. Integration of a surreal value over a subset of reals 

Generalizing relation (3) to any analytic function $f$ of $\omega$, we have:
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\begin{cases}f(\tilde{\delta}(0)) & x=0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0\end{cases}\right) d x=f^{\prime}(a)+\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{a}^{\infty} f^{\prime \prime}(x) d x^{\prime}$
for arbitrary real $a$ where the expression converges. This is equal to $f^{\prime}(\tilde{\delta}(0))$, if $f^{\prime}(\tilde{\delta}(0)) \in \mathbb{J}$ according to the definition (1).

Noticing that our H-field is equipped with operation of derivation $\partial()$, we can re-write it like this:
$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left(\begin{cases}w & x=0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0\end{cases}\right) d x=\pi \partial(w)^{\prime}$

where $w \in \mathbb{J}$. But if we are integrating over a set where the expression under the integral can take surreal values at several points, it is natural to multiply this result by the numerosity of the support:
$\int_{S} w d t=\pi N(S) \partial(w)$
One can easily notice that surreal integration defined this way does not generally satisfy the linearity against an infinite factor $\alpha$ :
$\int_{S}(\alpha f) \neq \alpha \int_{S} f$
For instance, if $u(x)$ is a unit impulse function $\mathrm{u}(\mathrm{x})=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}1 & x=0 \\ 0 & x \neq 0\end{array}\right.$, then
$\int_{-1}^{1} \omega u(x) d x=\pi \neq \omega \int_{-1}^{1} u(x) d x=0$
In our opinion, the struggle to keep this rule intact is the reason for many failed attempts to define the surreal integration. Still, there are ongoing efforts by other authors to keep this rule [7].

As a consequence,
$\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{S} \omega d t=\int_{S} \bar{\delta}(0) d t=N(S)$.

question: Is it known if every $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-small contactomorphism has a path connecting it to identity?
answer: No, it is not known if for every $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-small contactomorphism there exists a $\mathcal{C}^{0}$ small path connecting it to the identity.

evidence.text:
# 4. EXAMPLES AND APPLICATIONS 

4.1. The contact Hofer norm and the $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-topology. Another consequence of Proposition 3.1 is that the contact Hofer norm can be bounded along $\mathcal{C}^{0}$ small isotopies.

Corollary 4.1. Let $(M, \operatorname{ker} \alpha)$ be a closed contact manifold. Then there exists a $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-neighbourhood $V$ of id in $\mathcal{G}$ such that $|\cdot|_{\alpha}$ is bounded on the path-connected component $V^{\prime}$ of $V$ containing id. Moreover, the Hofer norm is bounded on the image $\widetilde{V}^{\prime} \rightarrow \widetilde{\mathcal{G}}$.

Note that this statement is in striking contrast to the case of the group $\operatorname{Ham}(M, \omega)$ Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of symplectic manifolds. It is known, due originally to an argument of Ostrover, that there are autonomous Hamiltonian flows with arbitrarily small support with linearly growing Hofer norm in the universal cover $\widetilde{\operatorname{Ham}}(M, \omega)$ of $\operatorname{Ham}(M, \omega)$ for every closed symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$. This often produces linear growth in the group $\operatorname{Ham}(M, \omega)$ itself, for instance whenever $(M, \omega)$ is symplectically aspherical. We refer to [47, Section 6.3.1] for details.

Proof. Let $(K, \theta)$ be an open book decomposition and $L_{ \pm}$be the skeletons of two different pages. We can choose $V$ small enough such that for any $\varphi \in V$ in the path-connected component of the identity, there exists a path $\varphi_{t}$ in $V$ with $\varphi_{0}=\mathrm{id}$ and $\varphi_{1}=\varphi$ such that $\varphi_{t}\left(L_{-}\right) \cap L_{+}=\emptyset$ for all $t \in[0,1]$. By Lemma 3.2 we can decompose $\varphi_{t}=f_{t}^{-} f_{t}^{+}$, where $f_{t}^{ \pm}$are compactly supported in $M \backslash L_{ \pm}$. Then Proposition 3.1 implies that the contact Hofer norm of any such $\varphi$ is bounded from above independent of $\varphi$ and in fact the same is true for the homotopy class of the path $\left\{\varphi_{t}\right\}$ with fixed endpoints.

Note that it is not known if for every $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-small contactomorphism there exists a $\mathcal{C}^{0}$ small path connecting it to the identity. Therefore we pose the following questions.

Question 4.2. Is $\mathcal{G}$ with the $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-topology locally path-connected?

Note that in the symplectic case, it is known that the group $\operatorname{Ham}_{c}(M, \omega)$ of Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms with compact supports is locally path connected in the $\mathcal{C}^{0}$ topology for $(M, \omega)$ the standard symplectic open ball and compact symplectic surfaces, see [50].

Question 4.3. Is it true that the contact Hofer norm is bounded for $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-small contactomorphisms (not necessarily connected to id with a $\mathcal{C}^{0}$-small path)?
4.2. Translated points. Let $\alpha$ be a contact form on a closed manifold $M$ and $\varphi \in \mathcal{G}$. Following Sandon [49], we call a point $x \in M$ a translated point of $\varphi$, if $\left(\varphi^{*} \alpha\right)_{x}=\alpha_{x}$ and $\varphi(x)=\varphi_{t}^{\alpha}(x)$ for some $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

A first relation between translated points and the contact Hofer norm was found in [51, Theorem B], where it was proved that in the case of Liouville filable contact manifolds, any contactomorphism whose distance to the Reeb flow is sufficiently small, admits a translated point. In [13] it is shown that on the standard contact sphere this result is sharp, i.e. that there exist contactomorphisms without translated points and contact Hofer norm arbitrarily close to the bound in [51].

Note that the tools for constructing contactomorphisms without translated points introduced by Cant [12] are very similar to the tools used in the proof of Theorem 1.1. In particular, the flow constructed in Lemma 2.7 has similar focal properties as the contactomorphisms used in [12] and [13].

In the spirit of Theorem 1.1 one can show:

Theorem 4.4. Let $(M, \xi)$ be a closed contact manifold that admits an open book decomposition $(K, \theta)$ whose pages are 1-stabilizations of a Liouville manifold with respect to some ideal Giroux form $\beta$. Let $\alpha$ be a contact form whose Reeb flow coincides with the $S^{1}$-fibration $\theta$ in a neighbourhood around the skeletons of the pages. Then there exists a contactomorphism without translated points for $\alpha$.

Proof. We follow the idea of the proof in [12]. Let $L_{ \pm}$be the skeletons of two different pages of the open book decomposition $(K, \theta)$. First note that the flow $\varphi_{t}$ of the vector field $X$ from Lemma 2.7 has a similar focal property as in [12, Definition 5] with respect to $\left(L_{-}, L_{+}\right)$. Instead of contracting to a single point, we have for all $z \in M \backslash L_{-}$that

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \varphi_{t}(z) \in L_{+}
$$

Note that at $L_{ \pm}$the scaling factor of $\varphi_{t}$ with respect to $\beta$ and hence with respect to $\alpha$ is given by $e^{ \pm t}$. Analogously to [12, Lemma 2] one can show that the scaling factor 1-set $\Sigma_{t}:=\{z \in M \mid \varphi_{t}^{*} \alpha=\alpha\}$ satisfies that

$$
\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \operatorname{dist}\left(\Sigma_{t}, L_{-}\right)+\operatorname{dist}\left(\varphi_{t}\left(\Sigma_{t}\right), L_{+}\right)=0
$$

As in [12, Lemma 4] one can easily check that given a contactomorphism $\sigma$, the flow $\sigma \varphi_{t} \sigma^{-1}$ has the focal property for the sets $\sigma\left(L_{ \pm}\right)$. Let $U$ be a neighbourhood of the skeletons such that the Reeb vector field of $\alpha$ is given by $\partial_{\theta}$ on $U$. Since $L_{-}$ is the skeleton of a 1-stabilization, there exists a contactomorphism $\sigma$ supported away from $L_{+}$that displaces $L_{-}$from $U$. Then, analogously to [12], for $T$ large the contactomorphism $\sigma \varphi_{T} \sigma^{-1}$ does not have translated points for $\alpha$.

The existence of translated points for every contactomorphism and every contact form, has been proven in several cases including hypertight contact manifolds [1, 43], certain lens spaces [35, 4] and certain prequantization spaces [53, 5]. However, it is likely that all of these examples are orderable, see e.g. [1, 9]. Given the considerations above it seems that the non-existence of translated points is related to non-orderability of the underlying contact manifold. Therefore we post the following question.

Question 4.5. Is it true that a cooriented closed contact manifold $(M, \xi)$ is nonorderable if and only if there exists a contact form $\alpha$ with $\operatorname{ker} \alpha=\xi$ and a contactomorphism $\varphi$ having no translated points for $\alpha$ ?

As a first step it would be for instance interesting to consider the case $T^{n} \times S^{n+1}$ which is non-orderable by Corollary 1.12 but on which, to our knowledge, the general existence of translated points is not known. Similarly, it would be interesting to know if abstract open books with flexible pages admit contactomorphisms without translated points.
4.3. Orderability and the Weinstein conjecture. In view of [1, Theorem 1.1], on a non-orderable closed contact manifold, any contact form has a contractible closed Reeb orbit. In particular the Weinstein conjecture holds for such manifolds. Even though it seems to be very hard to obtain examples from Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.10 for which the Weinstein conjecture is not known to hold, we obtain the following criterion for the existence of contractible closed Reeb orbits in terms of open book decompositions.

Corollary 4.6. Let $(M, \xi)$ be a closed contact manifold that satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 1.1 or Theorem 1.10. Then every contact form for $\xi$ has a contractible closed Reeb orbit.

Corollary 4.6 might be for instance applied to the case of prequantization spaces, giving a criterion in terms of open book decompositions for the fibre to be torsion.
4.4. Prequantization spaces and subcritical polarizations. Given a closed integral symplectic manifold $(Y, \omega)$ (meaning that $[\omega]$ lies in the image of the natural $\operatorname{map} H^{2}(Y, \mathbb{Z}) \rightarrow H^{2}(Y, \mathbb{R}))$, there exists a unique complex line bundle over $Y$ with Euler class $[\omega]$. The associated principal $S^{1}$-bundle $P \rightarrow Y$, called prequatization bundle or Boothby-Wang bundle, carries a contact form $\alpha$ whose Reeb flow is given by the $S^{1}$-action, see e.g. [30, Section 7.2].

Given an integral symplectic manifold $(Y, \omega)$ with Donaldson hypersurface $\Sigma$ that is Poincaré dual to $[\omega]$, there exists an open book decomposition of $(P, \operatorname{ker} \alpha)$ whose page is given by $Y \backslash \Sigma$, see [20]. In the context of Kähler manifolds, the choice of such a hypersurface is also called a polarization [6, Section 2]. Together with Theorem 1.1 this proves Corollary 1.7. In fact, Theorem 1.16 implies the following generalization of this corollary.

Corollary 4.7. Let $P$ be an orderable prequantization of a symplectic manifold. Then it does not admit an open book whose pages have loose skeleta.

Biran and Cieliebak provide several examples of Kähler manifolds that admit a subcritical polarization of degree 1, i.e., Kähler manifolds with a Donaldson hypersurface Poincaré dual to the symplectic form and a complement that is a subcritical Weinstein manifold. Examples include for instance the standard $\mathbb{C} P^{n}$

(with $\omega_{0}=\frac{1}{\pi} \omega_{F S}$ ) or products of $\mathbb{C} P^{n}$ with its closed algebraic submanifolds of complex dimension $m<n$.

A direct consequence of Corollary 4.7 is that symplectic manifolds whose prequantization space is orderable do not admit subcritical polarizations of degree 1. An easy class of example is given by $\left(\mathbb{C} P^{n}, k \omega_{0}\right)$ for any natural number $k \geq 2$, whose prequantization spaces are orderable Lens spaces [35, 4]. In particular it follows that $\left(\mathbb{C} P^{n}, \omega_{0}\right)$ does not admit any subcritical polarizations of degree $k$ for $k \geq 2$.

Similarly, Theorem 4.4 implies that every symplectic manifold whose prequantization satisfies Sandon's conjecture, namely every $\psi \in \operatorname{Cont}_{0}(P, \xi)$ has translated points, does not admit a subcritical polarization. For instance, by [53], this is the case for $(M, \omega)$ being any monotone toric manifold with $[\omega]$ integral and primitive, other than $\left(\mathbb{C} P^{n}, \omega_{0}\right)$, does not admit a subcritical polarization. This reproves and greatly generalizes a folklore fact attributed to Biran that $\mathbb{C} P^{n} \times \mathbb{C} P^{n}$ does not admit subcritical polarizations. One gets a similar conclusion for degree $k \geq 2$ polarizations of a large class of monotone (not necessarily toric) symplectic manifolds by $[2,5]$. For other obstructions on the polarization hypersurfaces of subcritical polarizations see [7].

In a similar spirit, we immediately see from Theorem 4.4 that contact manifolds satisfying Sandon's conjecture, including the examples above as well as hypertight contact manifolds [1, 43] and certain lens spaces [35, 4], do not admit open books with subcritical pages.
4.5. Non-displacement of pre-Lagrangians. Recall that a submanifold $K$ in a contact manifold $(M, \xi)$ is called pre-Lagrangian if it has a Lagrangian lift to the symplectisation $S M$, i.e., if there exists a Lagrangian $L$ in $S M$ such that the projection of $S M$ onto $M$ maps $L$ diffeomorphically onto $K$. A first connection between non-displacement results for Legendrians and pre-Lagrangians and orderability was already found by Eliashberg and Polterovich [28]. In particular [28, Theorem 2.3.A] proves that a contact manifold is orderable if there exists a pre-Lagrangian or Legendrian $A$ whose stabilization can not be displaced from the stabilization of a given pre-Lagrangian $K$ in $M \times T^{*} S^{1}$ (the pair $(K, A)$ has the stable intersection property). A further connections between the displacement of pre-Lagrangian tori and orderability are discussed for instance in [9, 41] in the setting of toric contact manifolds.

A direct consequence of Theorem 1.1 is that orderable contact manifolds only have Weinstein open book decompositions with critical pages. As pointed out in the proof of corollary 1.12, in the case of an open book with critical Weinstein page it happens in many cases, that the image of a skeleton under a Reeb flow is a preLagrangian submanifold. For instance using the standard open book of $\mathbb{R} P^{2 n+1}$ with page given by $T^{*} \mathbb{R} P^{n}$, we recover the non displacement of the Legendrian $\mathbb{R} P^{n}$ from its image under the Reeb flow described in [9, Corollary 1.24].

In this sense, Theorem 1.10 can be seen as a weak converse direction to the implication in [28, Theorem 2.3.A].

Question 4.8. Is a closed contact manifold orderable if and only if it contains a pair $(K, A)$ with the stable intersection property?
4.6. An explicit construction for positive loops. It is a natural question to ask whether our methods can be used to provide an explicit construction for contractible positive loops. For example, let us focus on Theorem 1.1(i) and Theorem 1.10.

The flow from Lemma 2.7 can be used in certain cases to shorten the contact Hofer length of a path supported in the complement of a skeleton of a page of some open book. Together with Lemma 2.3 this observation can be used to obtain contractible positive loops from a Reeb flow with certain properties.
Let $\left(K_{1}, \theta_{1}\right)$ and $\left(K_{2}, \theta_{2}\right)$ be two (possibly different) open book decompositions supporting $(M, \xi)$. Assume there exist a page $W_{1}$ of $\left(K_{1}, \theta_{1}\right)$ with skeleton $L_{1}$, a page $W_{2}$ of $\left(K_{2}, \theta_{2}\right)$ with skeleton $L_{2}$ and a Reeb flow $\varphi_{t}^{\alpha}$ such that $\varphi_{t}^{\alpha}\left(L_{1}\right) \cap L_{2}=\emptyset$. Set $U_{i}:=M \backslash L_{i}$. By Lemma 3.2 we have

$$
\varphi_{t}^{\alpha}=f_{t}^{1} f_{t}^{2}
$$

where $f_{t}^{i}$ is compactly supported in $K_{i}$. Lemma 2.7 provides flows $\psi_{i}^{i}$ contracting $U_{i}$ onto the skeleton of some page of $\left(K_{i}, \theta_{i}\right)$. As in the proof of Proposition 3.1, the flows $\varphi_{t}^{i}$ can be used to define flows $g_{t}^{i}$ compactly supported in $U_{i}$ that coincide on the support of $f_{t}^{i}$ with $\psi_{i}^{i}$. For $s \in[0,1]$ and fixed $T>0, C>0$ define the paths

$$
\varphi_{s}^{i}:=g_{s T}^{i}\left(g_{T}^{i}\right)^{-1} f_{s C}^{i} g_{T}^{i}\left(g_{s T}^{i}\right)^{-1}
$$

Then $\varphi_{s}^{i}$ defines a path from the identity to $f_{C}^{i}$. As pointed out in the proof of [51, Theorem A], the triangle inequality and the naturality of the contact Hofer metric already hold on the level of the contact Hofer length $l_{\alpha}$. In particular one has

$$
l_{\alpha}\left(\varphi_{s}^{i}\right) \leq 2 l_{\alpha}\left(g_{s T}^{i}\right)+l_{\left(g_{s T}^{i}\right)^{*} \alpha}\left(f_{s C}^{i}\right)
$$

As in the proof of Proposition 3.1, there exists a constant $D_{i}$ such that for any $C$ one can find a sufficiently large $T$ with $l_{\alpha}\left(\varphi_{s}^{i}\right) \leq D_{i}$. Choose $C>D_{1}+D_{2}$. Then the path $a_{s}:=\varphi_{s C}^{\alpha}\left(\varphi_{s}^{2}\right)^{-1}\left(\varphi_{s}^{1}\right)^{-1}$ is a non-constant loop based at the identity with

$$
\int_{0}^{1} \min _{M} \alpha\left(\frac{d}{d s} a_{s}\right) d s>0
$$

As in the proof of Lemma [36, Lemma 3.1] a positive contractible loop is given by $a_{s} \varphi_{\tau(s)}^{\alpha}$, where $\tau:[0,1] \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is a suitable reparametrisation.
Note that the maps $g_{t}^{i}$ have similar properties as the map $b$ used in [26, Remark 8.2] to construct an explicit positive contractible loop on $S^{3}$ (see also [12]). This raises the following questions:

Question 4.9. Do there exist Reeb flows and open book decompositions on $S^{3}$ (and more generally the contact boundary of a 2-stabilization) such that the positive contractible loop constructed by the method above coincides with the loop from [26]?

Question 4.10. Are the positive contractible loops constructed from different Reeb flows and open book decompositions always homotopic via a homotopy consisting of positive contractible loops? See [26, Section 6.3] for related questions.
4.7. Asymptotically near-Reeb contractible loops. An amusing fact due to J. Zhang and the second author is that the asymptotic contact Hofer norm of the Reeb flow is reflected in a certain measure of positive contractible loops. We state this relation here without proof, as we do not use it in the rest of the paper.

For a strictly positive contractible loop $\left\{\theta_{t}\right\}$ of contactomorphisms with contact Hamiltonian $h \in C^{\infty}([0,1] \times M, \mathbb{R}_{>0})$ set

$$
C(\theta)=\frac{\int_{0}^{1} \max _{M} h_{s} d s}{\int_{0}^{1} \min _{M} h_{s} d s}
$$

Note that $C(\theta) \geq 1$. Set

$$
C(\alpha)=\inf _{\theta} C(\theta)
$$

with the infimum running over all positive loops $\theta$. Let

$$
\mu(\alpha)=\lim _{t \rightarrow \infty} \frac{\left|\widetilde{\varphi}_{R_{\alpha}}\right|_{\alpha}}{t}
$$

be the asymptotic contact Hofer growth of the Reeb flow in $\widetilde{\operatorname{Cont}}(M, \xi)$.
Proposition 4.11. The following identity holds:

$$
\mu(\alpha)=1-\frac{2}{C(\alpha)+1}
$$

In particular, for the manifolds $(M, \alpha)$ from the proof of Theorems 1.1,1.10 and from Corollaries 1.3,1.12,1.13,1.7 where we have proven that $\mu(\alpha)=0$, we obtain that $C(\alpha)=1$, or in other words there exist positive contractible loops with $C(\theta)$ is arbitrarily close to 1 . We can consider them to be "close" to the Reeb flow in a certain quantitative sense.

Note that for orderable manifolds $\mu(\alpha)=1$ for all $\alpha$, whence $C(\alpha)=+\infty$. It would be interesting to study possible values of $C(\alpha)$ for non-orderable manifolds other than those mentioned above and see if intermediate values $C(\alpha) \in(0, \infty)$ could be achieved.

question: What is one reason why decisions to import are considered more complex than decisions to export?
answer: Decisions to import are considered more complex because incorporating foreign inputs into production processes affects marginal costs depending intricately on the firm's current input mix.

evidence.text:
# 2 Relation to the Literature 

Since the seminal paper of Rauch (1999), trade information frictions and the role of networks in overcoming them have been studied theoretically and empirically (Chaney, 2016). Forming a new trade relation typically requires substantial effort in gathering information that is not freely available but is acquired through search and learning efforts. Indeed, to start to trade, firms first need to be aware of the existence of a trading opportunity. Once the potential trading partner has been identified, there are additional obstacles to establishing a successful trade relationship, including learning how to do business in the presence of non-tariff barriers (safety regulations, formal trade procedures, etc.) and issues related to incomplete information (Allen, 2014). For example, a firm's decision to start purchasing an input from a new provider is always, to some extent, characterized by uncertainty about the ability of the potential seller to fulfil its needs in terms of price, quality, and delivery (Rauch and Watson, 2003) and about the cost of integrating the outsourced input into the production process.

Knowledge spillovers are an important topic in the international trade literature. The knowledge spillovers associated with importing have been theoretically and empirically explored, although receiving significantly less attention than those associated with exporting. For instance, Allen (2014) shows that, in the context of regional agricultural trade flows in the Philippines, producers/sellers' search costs for acquiring information about market conditions in other locations can explain about half of the observed price dispersion across regions. Related to our study, a few papers provide theory models in which firms use their connections as a source of information to form new trade relations. For instance, in Rauch and Watson (2004), agents with networks of foreign contacts have the option to either leverage these networks for their own production or offer them for use by others while Chaney (2018) provides a stylized model in which symmetric firms can buy information about new suppliers from the current suppliers for a fixed and exogenously given price.

Although importing has been shown to be crucial for determining firm productivity and export outcomes, ${ }^{4}$ there are only a few papers that empirically study knowledge spillovers in importing. López and Yadav (2010) finds that, for Chilean plants, the probability of importing is increasing in the number of importers in the same region. Bisztray et al. (2018) use a very fine-grained definition of neighbourhood (i.e., being in the same building) considering all types of imported products in the town of Budapest, while

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{4}$ Imported inputs have been recognized as one of the main sources of technological diffusion and, consequently, of productivity growth (Coe and Helpman, 1995; Keller, 2002). Bernard et al. (2009) and Castellani et al. (2010) demonstrate that the heterogeneity among importers is significant, highlighting notable differences between importers and non-importers. The use of foreign intermediate inputs increases productivity due to the higher quality of the foreign technology embodied in imported inputs and to the complementarity between foreign and domestic inputs (Amiti and Konings, 2007; Kasahara and Rodrigue, 2008; Halpern et al., 2015). The literature also suggests that the use of foreign intermediates promotes quality upgrading (Kugler and Verhoogen, 2009, 2011), the introduction of new final products (Goldberg et al., 2010; Colantone and Crinò, 2014) and R\&D investments (Bøler et al., 2015). The literature on firm-to-firm trade has emphasized the importance of having more and better suppliers for the performance of downstream firms both in domestic and international production networks (Chaney, 2018; Bernard et al., 2019; Bernard and Moxnes, 2018).

Békés and Harasztosi (2020) concentrate only on machine imports but analyze the whole territory of Hungary. Both studies provide evidence of import spillovers and highlight that their significance grows with proximity to peers. Additionally, Corcos and Haller (2023) shows that removing Multi-Fibre Agreement quotas leads firms to import more in commuting zones with a higher concentration of importing peers. All this literature focuses on spatial spillovers and does not consider information transmission through the production network as a potential determinant of importing. Furthermore, by not studying information propagation via buyer-supplier connections, these papers cannot leverage the intransitivities in the network structure to disentangle peer effects, which we crucially exploit in our identification strategy.

Our paper also relates to the recent literature on firm-to-firm trade. Focusing on domestic production networks, Bernard et al. (2019) proposes a model in which downstream firms search for suppliers with fixed search costs, while in Carvalho and Voigtländer (2014), firms search for new inputs through vertical connections. Eaton et al. (2022) and Eaton et al. (2024) model transnational business relationships by resorting to search frictions and random matching. In these frameworks, search costs depend on search intensity and the number of accumulated successful matches. In Hanwei et al. (2024), buyer-supplier matching is characterized by fixed costs paid by the buyer proportional to the number of providers, among which the firm can choose within a given origin country-industry. We contribute to this literature by empirically investigating a specific and important channel through which firms search and find foreign suppliers - domestic production network.

The paper that is closest to ours is Dhyne et al. (2023). The authors use Belgian data on firm-level production networks to study peer effects in exporting. While both their paper and ours consider information transmission through production networks, our approach differs from theirs in several important ways, a few of which we highlight here. Our focus is on importing - a significantly less studied topic in international trade. As noted by Antras et al. (2017), decisions to import are inherently more complex than decisions to export. In contrast with selling in foreign markets, incorporating foreign inputs

into production processes affects marginal costs, with this impact depending intricately on the firm's current input mix. This complexity may partially explain why importing has received less attention in the literature. Furthermore, the incentives for domestic suppliers and customers to share information with other firms depend on whether the information pertains to imports or exports, and so happens with the relevance of that information in each case. ${ }^{5}$ While Dhyne et al. (2023) focuses on learning from customers only, we find significant information transmission from both suppliers and customers. Methodologically, Dhyne et al. (2023) employs a similar identification strategy to ours: a combination of multidimensional fixed effects and instruments leveraging the network structure. However, their analysis does not account for geographical and industry-level spillovers. We show that neglecting these factors can lead to overestimating downstream and upstream effects. Finally, we provide explicit conditions under which the previous importing behaviour of distant network connections can serve as a valid instrument to address issues of correlated effects, an aspect absent in Dhyne et al. (2023). Our approach and findings, therefore, complement those in Dhyne et al. (2023).

In a nutshell, our contribution to the literature can be summarized as follows: we study yet unexplored firm-level sources of heterogeneity in importing arising from production network spillovers. Thanks to the richness of the data at our disposal, we go beyond the spatial and the aggregate input-output dimensions of spillovers. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to provide empirical evidence that information relevant to importing propagates through supplier-buyer connections in a domestic production network. We show that both upstream and downstream propagation are significant, and

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{5}$ As discussed before, domestic suppliers may hesitate to disclose potential foreign suppliers to avoid being replaced, while domestic customers might share such information to try to improve the quality or reduce the price of the inputs sourced domestically. Instead, in the case of exports, domestic suppliers may be interested in increasing the sales of their buyers to stimulate their derived demand for the intermediate inputs they sell to them. At the same time, customers may not wish to transmit the knowledge to their suppliers as exporting may increase suppliers' bargaining power in their relationship. Finally, information coming from suppliers (customers) could be more relevant for importing (exporting) due to their upstream (downstream) position in the network.

we also document important heterogeneities in such propagation effects.

question: Does a model ignoring dark energy acceleration imply a universe older than its minimum age derived from stars?
answer: No, it implies a universe that is only about $11.25\,\text{Gyr}$ old, which is less than its minimum age of $12.5\,\text{Gyr}$.

evidence.text:
## $\Lambda=0$ has Low Probability with Modern Observations

The simplest evidence against $\Lambda=0$ stemmed from the age discrepancy, which emerged in 1995 and holds even with modern 2024 measurements. Modern Universe measurements show that $\mathrm{H}_{0}=70 \pm 3 \mathrm{~km}$

$\mathrm{s}^{-1} \mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$ and $\Omega_{\mathrm{M}}=0.30 \pm 0.01$, implying an expansion age of the Universe (assuming $\Lambda=0$ ) of 11.25 Gyr. In contrast, the age of oldest globular clusters is $12.3+-0.6 \mathrm{Gyr}$, and they formed at least 0.2 Gyr after the Big Bang. Thus the oldest stars show the Universe is at least 12.5 Gyr old. A model of cosmic expansion that ignores acceleration from dark energy implies the universe is only 11.25 billion years old, which is not possible given its minimum age of 12.5 billion years derived from the oldest stars. The model is not favored.

The reasoning and the evidence against $\Lambda=0$ remain as valid with modern measurements as they were in 1996. In fact, the age discrepancy that arises from assuming $\Lambda=0$ has only become more pronounced with modern measurements.

question: Why is reputation important for regimes facing potential uprisings?
answer: Reputation is important because it allows regimes to influence expectations and actions of other players under conditions of strategic uncertainty. A strong reputation can help secure advantageous positions and deter challenges by creating predictable responses from others.

evidence.text:
#### Abstract

How valuable is reputation to a regime seeking to deter uprisings? I show the answer depends almost entirely on players' strategic uncertainty over other players actions. Without higher-order uncertainty, reputational effects are overshadowed by stage-game strategic complementarities: any payoff attainable in the complete-information repeated game remains attainable in the corresponding reputation game. However, when agents face globalized uncertainty over their payoffs, the regime's value for reputation rises sharply. In particular, the regime can leverage globalized strategic uncertainty to successful develop a reputation and secure their Stackelberg payoff in all pure equilibria of the reputation game, even as that same globalized strategic uncertainty forces them to their minimax payoff in the associated complete-information repeated game. Moreover, the globalized reputation game selects a unique pooling Markov equilibria among the continuum of Markov equilibria present in the complete-information game, refining predictions about equilibrium play. To establish these results, I develop new tools for analyzing non-normalized discounted repeated games with endogenous exit, where commitment actions vary with the regime's patience.


Keywords: Repeated Global Games, Reputation, Regime Change, Endogenous Exit. JEL Codes: C73, D74, I14.
