question: What is the statistical model used for mean estimation with known variance?
answer: The statistical model is given by $\mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{2}}=\left\{N\left(\theta, \sigma^{2}\right): \theta \in \mathbb{R}\right\}$.

evidence.text:
### 2.3 General variance

In this subsection, we describe how our efficient method for mean estimation can be adjusted to the case of a general, but known, variance. Consider original sensitive data $X_{1}, \ldots, X_{n}$ that are independently and identically distributed as $P_{\theta, \sigma^{2}}=N\left(\theta, \sigma^{2}\right)$ with a known variance $\sigma^{2}>0$. Hence, in this subsection, the statistical model is given by $\mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{2}}=\left\{N\left(\theta, \sigma^{2}\right): \theta \in \mathbb{R}\right\}$. The only conceptual challenge is to determine a lower bound on the asymptotic variance of any locally private method. Let

$$
I_{\theta}\left(Q \mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{2}}\right):=\mathbb{E}_{Z \sim Q P_{\theta, \sigma^{2}}}\left[\left(\frac{\partial \log Q P_{\theta, \sigma^{2}}(Z)}{\partial \theta}\right)^{2}\right]
$$

denote the information about $\theta$ contained in the $Q$-sanitized data when $\sigma^{2}$ is fixed. In particular, with our previous notation we have $\mathcal{P}_{1}=\mathcal{P}$. The following result extends Theorem 1 to the case of general $\sigma^{2}>0$.
Theorem 3. For $\theta \in \mathbb{R}, \sigma^{2}>0, \epsilon>0$ and $Q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon}$ we have

$$
I_{\theta}\left(Q \mathcal{P}_{\sigma^{2}}\right)=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}} I_{\frac{\epsilon}{2}}\left(Q_{\sigma} \mathcal{P}\right)
$$

for some mechanism $Q_{\sigma} \in \mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon}$ that depends only on $\sigma$. In particular, by Theorem 1, if $\epsilon \leq 1.04$, it holds that

$$
I_{\theta}\left(Q \mathcal{P}_{\sigma}\right) \leq \frac{1}{\sigma^{2}} I_{\frac{\epsilon}{2}}\left(Q_{\frac{\sigma}{2}, \epsilon}^{q g} \mathcal{P}\right)=\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}} \frac{2}{\pi} \frac{\left(e^{\epsilon}-1\right)^{2}}{\pi\left(e^{\epsilon}+1\right)^{2}}
$$

for all $Q \in \mathcal{Q}_{\epsilon}$.

In accordance with standard statistical intuition, Theorem 3 now shows that for general known $\sigma^{2}>0$ we should rescale the original data $X_{i} / \sigma \sim N\left(\frac{\theta}{\sigma}, 1\right)$, estimate the ratio $\frac{\theta}{\sigma}$ using the two-stage procedure in (8) and (9) based on the sign-mechanism and then scale back by $\sigma$ to achieve the optimal variance given by the inverse of the upper bound in (24). It is then clear that this final rescaling by the true $\sigma$ amounts exactly to the additional factor $\sigma^{2}$ in the asymptotic variance (cf. (24)).
If the variance $\sigma^{2}$ is actually unknown and has to be estimated from appropriately sanitized data, things become much more involved. Estimating the vector $\left(\theta, \sigma^{2}\right)$ efficiently appears to be an ill-posed problem under local differential privacy in the sense that there is no maximizing element $Q$ in the partial Loewner ordering of semidefinite matrices which maximizes the $2 \times 2$ Fisher-Information matrix $I_{\theta, \sigma^{2}}\left(Q \mathcal{P}^{(2)}\right), \mathcal{P}^{(2)}:=\left\{N\left(\theta, \sigma^{2}\right): \theta \in \mathbb{R}, \sigma^{2}>0\right\}$. Intuitively, this can be understood by noticing that in order to estimate both $\theta$ and $\sigma^{2}$ we would have to extract two different features of each sensitive $X_{i}$ in a locally private way and we have to make a decision on how to distribute the privacy budget $\epsilon$ over these two tasks, while for estimation of a single parameter, we can use the full privacy budget on that one. Even if $\sigma^{2}$ is only considered to be a nuisance parameter and the goal is still an efficient estimation of $\theta$, it is currently not clear what the appropriate lower bound for the asymptotic variance and an efficient procedure would look like. We defer these important and fundamental issues to future research.

We close this discussion by mentioning that for general unknown $\sigma^{2}>0$ our first stage estimator (8) is not even consistent for $\theta$. However, consistent locally private, yet inefficient, estimators for both $\theta$ and $\sigma^{2}$ can be constructed using the method of moments and clipping as explained, for instance, in Theorem 4.3 of Steinberger (2024).

question: What role does information about other agents play in mechanism design?
answer: In mechanism design, the information that agents have about other agents' preferences can significantly impact the outcomes of a game. The study explores how additional information about other agents can influence the implementability of social choice functions (SCFs), particularly in achieving desirable equilibrium outcomes.

evidence.text:
## 1 Introduction

The goal of a social planner in any mechanism design problem is to design a game under which a desirable outcome emerges in equilibrium. In implementation theory, agents have private information consisting of their own preferences over a set of outcomes as well as information about the preferences of other agents. Naturally, the set of equilibrium outcomes that can emerge from a mechanism is sensitive to the details of the information available to agents. A considerable body of mechanism design literature focuses on the effects of changing information structures on achieving desirable outcomes. Most of this work focuses on how much agents know about variables that directly affect their own payoffs - for example, the information a bidder knows about her own valuation for an object (Bergemann et al. (2022)) - rather than information about other agents' preferences.

In this paper, we examine how the planner can have an interest in agents possessing additional information about the preferences of other agents, revisiting the Bayesian implementation problem as studied by Jackson (1991), as well as Postlewaite and Schmeidler (1986) and Palfrey and Srivastava (1989). In this setting, agents fully understand their own preferences over a set of outcomes but do not know the preferences of other agents. Agents' beliefs about the preferences of other agents are drawn from a common prior, which will be

[^0]
[^0]:    *This article subsumes my undergraduate thesis at Harvard University. I am indebted to my thesis advisor Eric Maskin for constant and invaluable guidance and Stephen Morris for generous discussions, as well as Michal Kowalik, Shengwu Li, Matthew Rabin, Madison Shirazi, and Charlie Yang for helpful comments.

assumed to have full support. This paper additionally supposes that agents can receive a full-support signal regarding the preferences of other agents. The model, which is explained in section 2, considers how the implementability of a social choice function (SCF) changes as the information structure varies. The question is whether and when there exist SCFs that are not implementable when agents have no information about the types of other agents but are implementable when one or more agents receive additional information about other agents.

This question can be asked with respect to either partial or full implementation. Partial implementation requires only that the planner's desired outcome is achieved by some equilibrium of the game, while full implementation demands that every equilibrium of the game yields a desirable outcome. It is well-known that the partial implementability of an SCF depends only on whether it satisfies incentive compatibility, which requires that it is a best response for an agent to behave truthfully if all other agents are behaving truthfully. In section 3, we show that any SCF which satisfies incentive compatibility when agents receive informative signals about the types of other agents also satisfies incentive compatibility when agents do not have this additional information. This implies that a planner concerned only with partial implementation will never prefer an agent to have additional information about other agents. The reason is when an agent has access to an informative signal about the preferences of other agents, the planner must ensure that the agent is incentivized to report truthfully in each signal realization. However, a weighted average of these constraints across signal realizations yields the incentive constraint needed for the agent if she did not have access to additional information, making this latter constraint easier to satisfy.

The remainder of the paper shows how additional information about the types of other agents can help an agent signal to the planner that an undesirable equilibrium is being played, which is relevant if the planner is concerned with full implementation. In section 4 we present the main example of the paper: an SCF that is not fully implementable when agents do not have access to informative signals about the preferences of other agents but is fully implementable when agents have access to a sufficiently accurate signal about other agents. The condition that rules out undesired equilibria in Bayesian implementation settings is Bayesian monotonicity, which guarantees that agents have sufficient incentives to signal to the planner that an undesirable equilibrium strategy is being played. Much of this paper examines how Bayesian monotonicity varies with the information agents have about other agents. Section 5 presents a sufficient condition under which an SCF that is not fully implementable when agents have no information about the types of other agents becomes fully implementable under a more informative information structure.

An obvious concern with endowing an agent with additional information about the pref-

erences of other agents is that it can affect their own incentive to report truthfully to the mechanism. Indeed, the conclusion of section 3 is that incentive compatibility becomes harder to satisfy as agents receive additional information about other agents. To simplify the analysis, this paper focuses on the effects of modifying the beliefs of agents with dominant strategies. In both the main example and the general results, informative signals about other agents are only accessed by agents for which truth-telling is already a dominant strategy. This prevents the elimination of the planner's desired equilibrium outcome after the agents receive informative signals about the types of other agents and focuses the analysis on how additional information can allow an agent to signal undesirable deviations to the planner.

The signal we construct - in order to incentivize an agent $i$ to report to the planner that a specific untruthful equilibrium is being played - relies on a partition of the set of types of agents other than $i$ into two groups and informs agent $i$, with a sufficiently high degree of accuracy, whether the realized types of other agents belong to one group or the other. The intuition of this partition construction is the following: Each group should contain a type profile of other agents such that if the agent $i$ knew this type profile realized, she would prefer all other agents report truthfully rather than misreport according to the untruthful equilibrium, regardless of her own type. If agent $i$ is confident enough that the realized type profile is in one of these groups, she can propose an alternate SCF that swaps the outcomes implemented under the truthful strategy versus the untruthful strategy. By construction, this alternate SCF can only give agent $i$ a weakly lower payoff relative to the original if all other agents report truthfully, so agent $i$ would only propose it if an untruthful strategy profile is being played. Agent $i$ will have an incentive to propose this alternate SCF whenever the signal is sufficiently accurate.

Though a planner may want, for the goal of full implementation, agents to have access to informative signals about the types of other agents compared to no information, a key point of the analysis is that the planner does not always prefer a more informative signal structure. In particular, the signals constructed do not accurately inform any agent of the exact type profiles of other agents. One can imagine many reason why such a signal structure would be ineffective. For example, if there is a type profile of other agents such that all types of an agent $i$ would prefer play an untruthful equilibrium strategy as opposed to a truthful one, there will be no way to incentivize agent $i$ to report the untruthful equilibrium to the planner if she is sufficiently confident that this undesirable type profile has been realized. The conclusion that a designer may prefer information structures that are more informative, but not too much more informative, is consistent with the rapidly growing literature on information design spurred by Rayo and Segal (2010) and Kamenica and Gentzkow (2011). Thorough reviews of recent advancements in information design can be found in Bergemann and Morris (2019)

and Kamenica (2019).

Related Literature This paper most directly contributes to the literature on full Bayesian implementation, which began with Postlewaite and Schmeidler (1986), Palfrey and Srivastava (1989), and Jackson (1991). This paper also adds to the extensive literature on the effect of changing information structures in mechanism design settings pioneered by Bergemann and Välimäki (2002). It relates especially to the literature on information disclosure in mechanism design. In auction settings, Ganuza (2004) studies the optimal way for a seller to disclose a costly public signal about a good's characteristic in a second-price auction, which is a component of bidders' private valuations, while Bergemann and Pesendorfer (2007) investigate the joint design problem in which the seller controls the information bidders have about their own valuations and the auction rules. Other papers that have investigated the effects of information disclosure in auction settings include Esô and Szentes (2007), and Bergemann et al. (2022). Similar questions have also been investigated in screening settings by Li and Shi (2017) and Roesler and Szentes (2017). As previously stated, much of the current literature focuses on how much agents know about their own preferences. This thesis focuses on a mechanism designer's interest in agents knowing about other agents. Additionally, unlike the auction papers that portray the auctioneer as having the ability to provide information to agents, this thesis remains agnostic on where the information about other agents comes from. The emphasis is on how changing information structures can affect the planner's implementation goals. Finally, while our paper asks whether a planner can be interested in agents' information about other agents, one can also ask about an agent's incentives to acquire such information, as done in Gleyze and Pernoud (2023), who show that most economically meaningfully mechanisms cannot prevent an agent who has the option of acquiring information about her own type as well as types of other agents from choosing to acquire information about other agents.

question: What does WROBV stand for in high-frequency trading?
answer: WROBV stands for Windowed Relative On-Balance Volume.

evidence.text:
### 3.3.10 Windowed Relative OBV (WROBV)

The windowed relative OBV (WROBV) is a modified version of the OBV. It is the weighted sum of the values, for a rolling window of size $N$, of the cumulative OBV. This smooths out the indicator:

$$
\mathrm{WROBV}_{t}=\frac{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \mathrm{OBV}_{t-i}}{\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} V_{t-i}}
$$

This rolling normalization prevents the OBV from becoming excessively large, and focuses on recent price-volume dynamics.

question: What are the primary observables in the Koopman observable vector?
answer: The primary observables are the system states, control inputs $u$, and certain nonlinear observable functions $\eta(x, u)$.

evidence.text:
### 2.1 Observable vector

The Koopman observable functions are chosen by the user. Typically, they consist of functions of physical or application relevance, potentially including system states. Assuming the data is in discretized form, the Koopman observable vector used in this study is $\Psi_{n}=\left[1 \Psi_{\text {primary }, n}^{T} \Psi_{\text {aux }, n}^{T}\right]$. The primary observables $\Psi_{\text {primary }, n}$ denoting quantities of interest are chosen here to be the system states, control inputs $u$, and certain nonlinear observable functions $\eta(x, u)$,
$\Psi_{\text {primary }}^{T}=\left[\begin{array}{llllllll}x_{1} & \ldots & x_{N} & u_{1} & \ldots & u_{N_{u}} & \eta_{1} & \ldots & \eta_{N_{\eta}}\end{array}\right]$
Similar to EDMD, the auxiliary observables are used to accurately approximate the nonlinear behavior in the primary observables. Thus they are a rich set of basis functions for capturing nonlinear behavior. They must be included in identification of the Koopman operator, but may not be of inherent interest to a user. The auxiliary Koopman observables used here are based on the correlation functions given by
$\rho(i, j)=\prod_{k=1}^{4} \max \left[0,1-\theta_{k}\left|\Psi_{\text {primary }, i}^{(k)}-\Psi_{\text {primary }, j}^{(k)}\right|\right]$,
where the $(i, j)$ indices denote the discretized time step in the data and the index $k$ denotes the component of the $\Psi_{\text {primary }}$ vector. These correlation functions were chosen because they were found to provide accurate approximations while avoiding ill-conditioned correlation matrices. The choice of correlation function is user defined and a variety of options exist in the machine learning literature. The vector of auxiliary Koopman observables for time step $n$ is
$\Psi_{\text {aux }, n}=\left[\rho(n, 1) \rho(n, 2) \ldots \rho\left(n, N_{\Delta t}\right)\right]^{T}$. The parameters $\theta_{k}$ were found by training on data for time steps $>N_{\Delta t}$ to ensure that the identified Koopman models accurately predict for long periods of time. Finally, the constant 1 is used for the first component in $\Psi$ to account for constant trends (e.g. mean values). From Eqs. 5 and 6, $N_{\Psi}=1+N+N_{u}+N_{g}+$ $N_{\Delta t}$.

question: What is the Nash equilibrium in the context of Hilbert space-valued LQ mean field games?
answer: The Nash equilibrium is formed by the set of control laws $\left\{u_{i}^{\circ}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $u_{i}^{\circ}(t)=-K^{-1}(T-t)\left[L(T-t) x_{i}(t)+\Gamma_{2}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(t)+\sigma)^{*} \Pi(T-t)\right)+B^{*} q(T-t)\right]\right.$.

evidence.text:
# 4.2.4. Nash Equilibrium 

The following theorem concludes this section.
Theorem 4.7 (Nash Equilibrium). Consider the Hilbert space-valued limiting system, described by (4.3)-(4.4) for $i \in \mathbb{N}$, and the relevant Riesz mappings $\Delta_{k}, k=1,2,3, \Gamma_{k}, k=1,2$, given in Definition 4.1. Suppose A 4.1-A 4.3, and condition (4.42) hold. Then, the set of control laws $\left\{u_{i}^{\circ}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $u_{i}^{\circ}$ is given by

$$
\begin{gathered}
u_{i}^{\circ}(t)=-K^{-1}(T-t)\left[L(T-t) x_{i}(t)+\Gamma_{2}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(t)+\sigma)^{*} \Pi(T-t)\right)+B^{*} q(T-t)\right]\right. \\
K(t)=I+\Delta_{3}(\Pi(t)), \quad L(t)=B^{*} \Pi(t)+\Delta_{1}(\Pi(t))
\end{gathered}
$$

forms a unique Nash equilibrium for the limiting system where the mean field $\bar{x}(t) \in H$, the operator $\Pi(t) \in \mathcal{L}(H)$ and the offset term $q(t) \in H$, are characterized by the unique fixed point of the following set of consistency equations

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bar{x}(t)= & S(t) \bar{\xi}-\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left(B K^{-1}(T-r)\left(L(T-r) \bar{x}(r)+B^{*} q(T-r)\right.\right. \\
& \left.\left.+\Gamma_{2}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(r)+\sigma\right)^{*} \Pi(T-r)\right)\right)-F_{1} \bar{x}(r)\right) d r \\
\frac{d}{d t}\langle & \Pi(t) x, x\rangle=2\langle\Pi(t) x, A x\rangle-\left\langle L^{*} K^{-1} L(t) x, x\right\rangle+\left\langle\Delta_{2}(\Pi(t)) x, x\right\rangle+\langle M x, x\rangle \\
& \dot{q}(t)=\left(A^{*}-L^{*}(t) K^{-1}(t) B^{*}\right) q(t)+\Gamma_{1}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(T-t)+\sigma\right)^{*} \Pi(t)\right) \\
& -L^{*}(t) K^{-1}(t) \Gamma_{2}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(T-t)+\sigma\right)^{*} \Pi(t)\right)+\left(\Pi(t) F_{1}-M \widetilde{F}_{1}\right) \bar{x}(T-t)
\end{aligned}
$$

with $\Pi(0)=G, x \in \mathcal{D}(A)$, and $q(0)=-G \widetilde{F}_{2} \bar{x}(T)$.
Proof. According to the demonstrations in Section 4.2.3, if the contraction condition (4.42) holds, then there exist $\Pi \in C_{s}(\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{L}(H)), q \in C(\mathcal{T} ; H)$ and $\bar{x} \in C(\mathcal{T} ; H)$, which are the unique solution to the set of consistency equations give by (4.53)-(4.55). In addition, the set of feedback control laws $\left\{u_{i}^{\circ}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$, where $u_{i}^{\circ}$ is given by (4.51)-(4.52), forms a unique Nash equilibrium for the limiting system described by (4.3)-(4.4), i.e.

$$
J_{i}^{\infty}\left(u_{i}^{\circ}, u_{-i}^{\circ}\right)=\inf _{u_{i} \in \mathcal{U}_{i}} J_{i}^{\infty}\left(u_{i}, u_{-i}^{\circ}\right), \quad \forall i \in \mathbb{N}
$$

This is because, in the limit when the number of agents $N$ goes to infinity, the agents get decoupled from each other and hence the high-dimensional optimization problem faced by agent $i, i \in \mathbb{N}$, turns into a single-agent optimal control problem for which there is a unique solution. Hence, agent $i$ cannot improve its cost by deviating from the optimal strategy (4.51)-(4.52) and the set of these strategies yields a Nash equilibrium for the limiting system. In other words, the Nash equilibrium property, as defined in (4.56), holds trivially for the set of strategies $\left\{u_{i}^{\circ}\right\}_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ because the limiting cost functional of agent $i$, given by (4.4), is independent of the strategies of other agents.

Subsequently, the equilibrium state of agent $i$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{i}^{\circ}(t)= & S(t) \xi_{i}-\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left(B K^{-1}(T-r) L(T-r) x_{i}^{\circ}(r)+B \tau(r)-F_{1} \bar{x}(r)\right) d r \\
& +\int_{0}^{t} S(t-r)\left[\left(D-E K^{-1}(T-r) L(T-r)\right) x_{i}^{\circ}(r)-E \tau(r)+F_{2} \bar{x}(r)+\sigma\right] d W_{i}(r)
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\tau(t)=K^{-1}(T-t)\left[B^{*} q(T-t)+\Gamma_{2}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(t)+\sigma\right)^{*} \Pi(T-t)\right)\right]$. Moreover, we have $\mathbb{E}\left[x_{i}^{\circ}(t)\right]=$ $\bar{x}(t), \forall i \in \mathcal{N}, \forall t \in \mathcal{T}$, where $\bar{x}(t)$ is given by (4.53). We note that (4.53) represents the mild solution to the mean field equation

$$
\begin{aligned}
& d \bar{x}(t)=\left[A \bar{x}(t)-B K^{-1}(T-t)\left(L(T-t) \bar{x}(t)+B^{*} q(T-t)+\Gamma_{2}\left(\left(F_{2} \bar{x}(t)+\sigma\right)^{*} \Pi(T-t)\right)\right)\right. \\
& +F_{1} \bar{x}(t) \mid d t
\end{aligned}
$$

question: Does the Chapman-Enskog method depend on the precise form of the collision integral?
answer: No, the Chapman-Enskog method does not depend on the precise form of the collision integral.

evidence.text:
# 2.4 Collision integral 

In this section we look more closely at the collision integral $\mathcal{I}\left[\rho_{\mathrm{p}}\right]$ and discuss the most important properties of it. The collision integrals considered by us originate from integrabilitybreaking. In Ref. [35,63] it was shown how such terms arise due to perturbative treatment at the level of Fermi's Golden Rule (FGR). However, the ChE method does not depend on the precise form of the collision integral. Instead, it relies on two general and physically motivated properties that we now discuss. We refer to [51] for an example of a collision integral in the system of two coupled Lieb-Liniger models. It can be explicitly checked that collision integrals derived in $[35,63]$ have the properties listed below.

First of all, a characteristic feature of the collision integral $\mathcal{I}\left[\rho_{\mathrm{p}}\right]$ is a set of collision invariants, namely quantities conserved by it. The natural choice for the collision invariants are the particle number, momentum and energy and such choice yields the NS equations. For collision integral $\mathcal{I}$ respecting these three conservation laws we have

$$
\hat{\pi}_{a} \mathcal{I}=\int \mathrm{d} \theta \hat{\pi}_{a}(\theta) \mathcal{I}\left[\rho_{\mathrm{p}}\right](\theta)=0, \quad a=0,1,2
$$

Another choice, for example, is to respect only the particle number, the resulting hydrodynamic equations are the non-linear diffusion equations. We will investigate such situation in a future work.

The second important feature of the collision integral are the stationary states $\rho_{\mathrm{p}}^{\text {st }}$ fulfilling

$$
\mathcal{I}\left[\rho_{\mathrm{p}}^{\text {st }}\right]=0
$$

We will generally assume that the stationary states are TBA boosted thermal states described in the section above. This can be shown for classical Boltzmann collision kernel [2]. Moreover, in Ref. [35] it was demonstrated for collision integrals constructed from FGR that indeed the stationary states are TBA boosted thermal states with pseudoenergies of the form

$$
\epsilon_{0}(\theta)=-\beta \mu+v \hat{\pi}_{1}(\theta)+\beta \hat{\pi}_{2}(\theta)
$$

However, collision integrals might also posses non-thermal stationary states as discussed, for example, in [65]. Such situations are also beyond the scope of the present work.

In our calculations we will be mostly interested in the operator

$$
\Gamma=-\frac{\delta \mathcal{I}}{\delta \rho_{\mathrm{p}}} \mathcal{C}
$$

The conservation of energy, momentum and particle number by the collision integral implies that $\Gamma$ has three zero eigenvectors

$$
\int \mathrm{d} \lambda \mathscr{E}_{a}(\lambda) \Gamma(\lambda, \mu)=0, \quad a=0,1,2
$$

In our work, we also assume that $\Gamma$ beside these three zero eigenvalues, the rest of the spectrum is positive and gapped, with a gap $\gamma>0$ providing a characteristic time-scale for thermalization in the system. These assumptions were confirmed in a concrete example of coupled LiebLiniger models investigated in [51].

question: What is a trade-off between robustness and efficiency in wireless communications?
answer: Robust strategies that prioritize robustness to uncertainties often sacrifice resource efficiency because extra resources, which may remain idle, are occupied.

evidence.text:
## IV. Prices of Uncertainty Awareness

The law of "no free lunch" is philosophically and technically applicable to the systems engineering of almost all real-world designs, productions, and applications. Uncertainty awareness in wireless communications and sensing is no exception. Addressing uncertainties such as noise, interference, hardware imperfections, dynamic environments, data scarcity, and computational errors often requires balancing conflicting performance metrics. To be specific, optimizing for reliability, resilience, adaptability, and robustness often comes at the expense of other critical factors like computational complexity, resource efficiency, or nominal optimality. For example, some typical trade-offs can be highlighted as follows:

- Robustness vs Efficiency: Robust strategies that prioritize robustness to uncertainties, such as redundancy, diversity, and margin through employing conservative resource allocations, spectra spread, guard times, errorcorrection mechanisms, etc., often sacrifice resource efficiency because extra resources, which may remain idle, are occupied.
- Robustness vs Complexity: By introducing overengineering techniques (e.g., redundancy and diversity) and complicated optimization formulations (e.g., Table I), the structural and computational complexities of the system, model, or method are largely increased; see [13], [14].
- Robustness vs Optimality: Robustness against uncertainties loses nominal optimality under ideal or near-ideal conditions. To be specific, when significant uncertainties do not actually occur in practice since they are random,
the optimality cannot be reached by a robust solution because it pursues optimality under the worst case, not under the nominal situation.
- Modularization vs Integration: To isolate faults and facilitate maintenance, we prefer the modularization scheme. Yet, for the purposes of resource sharing and overall optimality, e.g., in ISAC and ML-based ITP systems, we may resort to integration.
- Centralization vs Decentralization: Centralized systems enable efficient global optimality of resource use and node interaction, but are prone to central-node failure and network attacks. Decentralized systems enhance robustness and scalability by distributing data storage and computation, but may face node-coordination challenges and suboptimal global performance.

question: What is the value of the bulk viscosity in the Navier-Stokes equations for a weakly perturbed ideal gas?
answer: The bulk viscosity is zero.

evidence.text:
# 3.2 Navier-Stokes scale 

We go now to the first order in $\delta$. We find an equation

$$
\partial_{t} \rho^{(0)}(x, v ; t)+\left.v \partial_{x} \rho^{(0)}(x, v ; t)=\left[\Gamma_{\beta} \rho^{(1)}\right](x, v ; t)
$$

where $\Gamma_{\beta}=-\left.-\left(\delta I_{\beta} / \delta \rho\right)\right|_{\rho^{(0)}} \rho^{(0)}$. More explicitly we have

$$
\sum_{a} \frac{\partial \rho^{(0)}}{\partial \varrho_{a}} G_{a}^{(0)}\left(\left\{\varrho_{b}\right\}\right)+v \sum_{a} \frac{\partial \rho^{(0)}}{\partial \varrho_{a}} \partial_{x} \varrho_{a}=\left[\Gamma_{\beta} \rho^{(1)}\right](x, v ; t)
$$

where derivatives $\frac{\partial \rho^{(0)}}{\partial \varrho_{a}}$ can be explicitly computed. Moreover, the operator $G_{a}^{(n)}\left(\left\{\varrho_{b}\right\}\right)$ defines the dynamics of hydrodynamic field $\varrho_{a}$ at $n$-th order in $\delta$ (dependence on $\delta$ enters via hydrodynamic pressure and heat current)

$$
\partial_{t} \varrho_{a}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \delta^{n} G_{a}^{(n)}\left(\left\{\varrho_{b}\right\}\right)
$$

The expressions for $G_{a}^{(0)}\left(\left\{\varrho_{b}\right\}\right)$ can be simply read off from (80). After short calculation we get

$$
\rho^{(0)}(x, v)\left(\frac{u(x)-v}{T(x)^{2}}\left(\frac{3}{2} T(x)-\frac{(v-u(x))^{2}}{2}\right) \partial_{x} T\right)=\left[\Gamma_{\beta} \rho^{(1)}\right](x, v)
$$

We evaluate this equation at $v=\xi+u$. In the relative $\xi$ variable, the equation can be expressed with local unboosted thermal state $\hat{\rho}^{(0)}(\xi)=\rho^{(0)}(\xi+u)$ (corresponding to the same hydrodynamic fields $\varrho(x), T(x)$ but with $u(x)=0$ ) and $\hat{\rho}^{(1)}(\xi)=\rho^{(1)}(\xi+u)$. We then find

$$
\hat{\rho}^{(0)}(\xi) \frac{\xi}{T^{2}}\left(\frac{\xi^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2} T\right) \partial_{x} T=\left[\hat{\Gamma}_{\beta} \hat{\rho}^{(1)}\right](\xi)
$$

Transformation between Eqs. (84) and (85) is in fact a Galilean boost and illustrates Galilean invariance of the theory and as a result of the transport coefficients.

Assuming that $\hat{\rho}^{(1)}(\xi)=\hat{\phi}(\xi) \partial_{x} T$, we find that function $\hat{\phi}(\xi)$ fulfills an integral equation

$$
\left[\hat{\Gamma}_{\beta} \hat{\phi}\right](\xi)=\chi(\xi), \quad \chi(\xi)=\hat{\rho}^{(0)}(\xi) \frac{\xi}{T^{2}}\left(\frac{\xi^{2}}{2}-\frac{3}{2} T\right)
$$

with additional conditions (75)

$$
\left(\mathscr{H}_{a} \mid \hat{\phi}\right)=0, \quad a=0,1,2
$$

We note that the function $\hat{\phi}(\xi)$ is antisymmetric (this follows from antisymmetry of $\chi(\xi)$ and properties of $\hat{\Gamma}_{\beta}$ ) and compute corrections to hydrodynamic pressure and heat current finding

$$
\mathcal{P}^{(1)}=0, \quad \mathcal{J}^{(1)}=-\frac{1}{2} \int \mathrm{~d} \xi \hat{\rho}^{(0)}(\xi) \xi^{3} \hat{\phi}(\xi) \partial_{x} T
$$

recovering Newton's and Fourier's laws (2) with

$$
\eta=0, \quad \kappa=\frac{1}{2} \int \mathrm{~d} \xi \hat{\rho}^{(0)}(\xi) \xi^{3} \hat{\phi}(\xi)
$$

We have thus found NS equations with vanishing bulk viscosity. This is a known result for a weakly perturbed ideal gas $[2,3]$. In order to evaluate thermal conductivity $\kappa$ one has to find $\hat{\phi}(\xi)$ which involves solving the integral equation (86).

The expansion in $\delta$ can be carried out to higher orders which leads to so-called Burnett hydrodynamic equations [2]. We close our discussion at the first order and point out that the found expressions for transport coefficients (89) can be understood as special cases of the general formulas (143) (or (197)) derived by us in this work. One can recover them by plugging non-interacting limits of hydrodynamic matrices, diffusion operator and thermodynamic quantities computed for ideal gas.

question: What is the purpose of conjugacy residuals in comparing dynamical systems?
answer: Conjugacy residuals serve as vector components in an objective function space to quantify dissimilarity between dynamical systems based on deviations from topological conjugacy.

evidence.text:
### 4.1 Deviation from conjugacy

Motivated conceptually by the homeomorphic defect approach [31], dissimilarity between dynamical systems can be accounted for by quantifying how much the systems deviate from topological conjugacy. The perspective in [31] was based on having a "commuter" $h$ that satisfies Eq. 7 and then quantifying dissimilarity in terms of how $h$ differs from being a homeomoprhism. A somewhat inverse perpsective is taken here in that it is assumed that $h$ is a homeomorphism and dissimilarity is based on the error with respect to Eq. 7. These errors (and their $\Phi$-space instantiations), which are referred to as conjugacy residuals here, serve as vector components in an objective function space. Deviations from conjugacy
pseudometrics are then defined based on magnitudes of these vectors.

The conjugacy residuals follow from rewriting Eq. 7 as
$y=h(x)+\tilde{r}_{1}(f, g, h)$,
$h \circ f(x)=g \circ h(x)+\tilde{r}_{2}(f, g, h)$.
where residual vectors $\tilde{r}_{1}, \tilde{r}_{2} \in \mathbb{C}^{N_{\Psi}}$ are zero if the systems are topologically conjugate and non-zero otherwise. Therefore we seek to find $h$ that minimizes $\tilde{r}_{1}$ and $\tilde{r}_{2}$. Two immediate observations are worth noting: first, in general the $h$ that minimizes $\tilde{r}_{1}$ can only be guaranteed to minimize $\tilde{r}_{2}$ when the two systems are conjugate (i.e. $\tilde{r}_{1}=\tilde{r}_{2}=0$ for some $h$ ) and second the best combinations of $\tilde{r}_{1}$ and $\tilde{r}_{2}$ can only be quantified in a Pareto optimal sense since minimizing $\tilde{r}_{1}$ will not in general minimize $\tilde{r}_{2}$ away from conjugacy. The transformation $h$ is restricted to be in the group of invertible matrices, i.e. $h=C \in G L\left(N_{\Psi}\right)$, which guarantees that only homeomorphisms are considered. Therefore in the data-driven context of Eqs. 11 and 12, the problem of finding the best residuals can be treated by minimizing the two scalar valued conjugacy residuals $r_{1}, r_{2}$ :
$\min _{C \in G L\left(N_{\Psi}\right)}\left(r_{1}, r_{2}\right)$,
$r_{1}=\left\|\Phi_{g}-C \Phi_{f}\right\|_{F}, r_{2}=\left\|\Lambda_{f}-C^{-1} \Lambda_{g} C\right\|_{F}$.
Appropriately normalized conjugacy residuals can also be used if desired. For instance, one could use
$r_{1}=\left\|\Phi_{g}-C \Phi_{f}\right\|_{F} /\left\|\Phi_{r e f}\right\|_{F}$
and
$r_{2}=\left\|\Lambda_{f}-C^{-1} \Lambda_{g} C\right\|_{F} /\left\|\Lambda_{r e f}\right\|_{F}$
where $\Phi_{r e f}$ and $\Lambda_{r e f}$ correspond to a chosen reference system.

The conjugacy residuals can be viewed as vector components in objective function space, where the origin corresponds to topologically conjugacy. Based on these residuals, deviation from conjugacy is defined as follows:
Definition 2 Deviation from conjugacy, $d\left(r_{1}, r_{2}\right)$, is defined as $d=\sqrt{r_{1}^{2}+r_{2}^{2}}$ where $\left(r_{1}, r_{2}\right)$ correspond to Pareto points of Eq. 18.

question: Does the Robustness@k metric effectively reflect true instruction-following performance?
answer: No, it does not effectively reflect true instruction-following performance.

evidence.text:
# B Evaluation Metrics Analysis 

To measure instruction-following performance for retrieval models is a challenge. Two metrics were specifically proposed in previous studies for this purpose: Robustness@k (Oh et al., 2024) and $p$-MRR (Weller et al., 2024a). We argue that neither of them effectively reflects true instructionfollowing performance.

Robustness@k is designed to assess a model's performance on the same query under different instructions. Specifically, it groups instances of the same query, calculates the minimum nDCG@k score within each group, and averages the group scores to generate the overall Robustness@k score. Let $Q=\left\{q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{n}\right\}$ be a set of queries. For each query $q_{i}$, there are $m_{i}$ distinct instruction variants $\left\{I_{i 1}, I_{i 2}, \ldots, I_{i m_{i}}\right\}$, calculate the minimum nDCG@k score across all its instruction:

$$
\min -\mathrm{nDCG}\left(q_{i}\right)=\min _{j \in\left(1,2, \ldots, m_{i}\right)} s_{i j}
$$

where $s_{i j}$ represents the nDCG@k score for query $q_{i}$ under instruction $I_{i j}$. Compute the overall Robustness@k score as the average of these minimum scores across all queries:

$$
\text { Robustness@k }=\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \min -\mathrm{nDCG}\left(q_{i}\right)
$$

However, the Robustness@k metric oversimplifies the evaluation of a model's ability to follow instructions. (1) Even if a model demonstrates strong performance across the majority of queries, a single anomalously low score can reduce the overall robustness score. (2) Furthermore, focusing solely on the lowest score disregards variations in the model's responses to different instructions, thus failing to capture the overall performance trend. ${ }^{4}$
As for $p$-MRR, it is based on the MRR metric and quantifies the model's ability to follow instructions by comparing the rankings of relevant documents in the original mode and the instruction mode. The following formula is applied to calculate the score for each relevant document within a query:

$$
p-\mathrm{MRR}= \begin{cases}\frac{M R R_{o g}}{M R R_{\text {new }}}-1, & \text { if } R_{o g}>R_{\text {new }} \\ 1-\frac{M R R_{\text {new }}}{M R R_{\text {oq }}}, & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$

[^0]
[^0]:    ${ }^{4}$ For instance, the nDCG@k scores for group A are $\{0.8,0.5,0.3,0.2\}$, while those for group B are $\{0.9,0.9$, $0.9,0.2\}$. Although group B exhibits a significantly better overall performance, Robustness@k assigns the same score to both groups.

where $M R R$ is mean reciprocal rank, $R_{o g}$ is the rank of the document in the original retrieval mode, and $R_{\text {new }}$ is the new rank in the instruction mode. However, (3) $p$-MRR fails to distinguish the importance of ranking, neglecting to highlight the critical role that top K results play in retrieval. (4) Moreover, the linear discount mechanism of $p$-MRR is insufficiently sensitive to changes in higher rankings, making it ineffective in capturing subtle movements at the top. (5) Lastly, $p$-MRR demonstrates limitations when addressing special cases and extreme performances. ${ }^{5}$

question: What are the benefits of using a perturbed cosine router in language modeling tasks compared to a vanilla cosine router?
answer: The perturbed cosine router consistently outperforms the vanilla cosine router across various datasets, showing improved performance in both character-level and word-level tasks. Specifically, it achieves lower Bit Per Character (BPC) scores on Enwik8 and Text8 datasets and slightly better Perplexity (PPL) scores on the Wikitext-103 dataset.

evidence.text:
### 5.2 LANGUAGE MODELING

In this section, we focus on the language modeling task (Bahl et al., 1983), a fundamental challenge in natural language processing that involves predicting the next word or character in a sequence to evaluate a model's ability to generate and understand text. To assess how different routers influence the model's ability to capture linguistic structures and enhance performance across varying levels of textual granularity, we compare the performance of perturbed and vanilla cosine router Mixture of Experts (MoEs) on both character-level (Graves, 2013) and word-level (Bengio et al., 2000) tasks.
Datasets. We evaluate the model's pre-training capabilities on character-level language modeling using Enwik8 and Text8 datasets (Mahoney, 2011), and assess its word-level language modeling performance on Wikitext-103 (Merity et al., 2016).

Table 2: Performance of vanilla and perturbed cosine routers on language modeling tasks.

![table_1](table_1)

Metrics. To quantify the performance of our perturbed cosine router relative to the vanilla cosine one, we utilize the Bit Per Character (BPC) metric (Graves, 2013) for character-level language modeling and Perplexity (PPL) (Jelinek et al., 1977) for word-level language modeling tasks.
Architecture and training procedure. In order to alleviate the representation collapse issue associated with estimating routing scores in the original space, we follow Chi et al. (2022) to first project input representations on lower-dimensional space and parameterize experts with corresponding lowerdimensional embeddings. Subsequently, we calculate the routing scores of inputs and embeddings in this reduced-dimensional space using our proposed perturbed cosine router. Our experiments adopt the Switch Transformer (Fedus et al., 2021), which is fundamentally a sparse variant of the T5 encoder-decoder (Raffel et al., 2020), with MoE layers replacing the MLPs. Detailed information regarding the datasets, metrics, training setup, and hyperparameters for this task is provided in Appendix E.2.
Results. The empirical advantage of our proposed cosine router over the vanilla version when applied to language modeling tasks is demonstrated in Table 2. The results indicate that the perturbed cosine router enhances the performance of the original cosine router in all datasets across both small and medium configurations. It notably improves results for the Enwik8 and Text8 datasets at various scales and slightly outperforms the original cosine router for the Wikitext-103 dataset.

question: What is the formula for calculating log returns in financial time series?
answer: The formula for calculating log returns is \(\text{log_return}_{t} = \log\left(\frac{P_{t}}{P_{t-1}}\right)\), where \(P_{t}\) is the price at time \(t\).

evidence.text:
### 3.1.1 Log Returns and Volatility

To normalize the stock price data and reduce the effects of scale, we compute the log returns for the opening, high, low, and close prices. Log returns are preferred in financial time series due to their ability to capture percentage changes and handle volatility over time [Box et al., 2015]. The log return for a price series $P_{t}$ is

$$
\text { log_return }_{t}=\log \left(\frac{P_{t}}{P_{t-1}}\right)
$$

where $P_{t}$ is the price at time $t$. This process is also defined for the opening, high, low, and closing prices, with the resulting log returns stored as additional columns in the dataset. Additionally, we compute rolling $Z$-scores for the trading volume to capture anomalies in the volume. The rolling $Z$-score of the volume is [Box et al., 2015]

$$
\operatorname{volz}_{t}=\frac{\text { volume }_{t}-\text { mean }(\text { volume })}{\operatorname{std}(\text { volume })}
$$

where the mean and standard deviation are computed over a rolling window of 60 minutes.
The 10-year US Treasury yield, provided on a daily basis, is used to compute a per-minute risk-free rate, which is necessary for calculating excess returns. For any minute $t$ within a trading day $d$, the transformation from the daily yield to a per-minute rate is given by

$$
r_{\text {per-minute }}(t)=\left(1+r_{\text {daily }}(d)\right)^{\frac{1}{1440}}-1
$$

where 1440 is the number of minutes in a day and $r_{\text {daily }}(d)$ is the daily risk-free rate derived from the most recently available Treasury yield prior to day $d$. This ensures that each minute's risk-free rate reflects the prevailing daily rate for its trading day.

question: What issue might arise with DMS in terms of time-series data characteristics?
answer: DMS may not incorporate seasonality/periodicity in the time-series.

evidence.text:
## E.2.1 Forecasting granularity in Time-Series Forcasting: IMS vs. DMS

In LTSF works, the decoding granularity is dichotomized in the following two categories:
I) Iterated/Incremental Multi-step (IMS) : This is auto-regressive language-modeling or generative style prediction decoding where each step in prediction horizon $H$ is iteratively predicted: $\hat{x}_{t+1}$, and is used for the prediction for the subsequent time-step. The common limitations of such forecasting granularity is 'error accumulation' over time as the decoder builds on the error from previous steps while iteratively making subsequent predictions. Additionally, the run-time complexity is to the order of the length of the horizon $H$.
II) Direct Multi-step (DMS) : As the name implies, in this decoding or forecasting approach, the entire forecasting horizon $H$ is predicted at one go: $\hat{x}_{t+1: t+H}$. While computationally more attractive (much faster than IMS), this approach may not incorporate seasonality/periodicity in the time-series. Modern TSF specialist models,

especially the transformer-based TSF architectures, tend to follow this scheme to avoid the quadratic cost (to the length of input) associated with attention.

question: Does economic singularity theory involve extreme exponential growth?
answer: Yes.

evidence.text:
# 5 Concluding Remarks 

According to Eden et al (2012), singularity hypotheses refer to two distinct scenarios. One is the intelligence explosion (Good, 1966), whereby machine intelligence surpasses human intelligence through computational advancement, which entails recursive self-improvement. The other scenario is the biointelligence explosion, which entails the amplification of human capabilities to overcome all existing human limitations (Kurzweil, 2005). In both ways, however, the concept of singularity (i.e., explosion) does not go beyond exponential growth, if not extreme. The economic singularity theory of Nordhaus (2021) also exploits the idea of extreme exponential growth of intelligence capital deepening by a large elasticity of substitution. In contrast, the singularity presented in this study is based on matrix singularity where the matrix is transformed by virtue of the substitution elasticity that is nonneutral.

Of course, positive singularity cannot take place unless some finite amount of non-labor commodity can completely substitute the primary factor of production. Our model allowed convergence towards positive singularity because our (standard) CES production function allowed production even at the extreme position of the isoquant near the axes. On the other hand, negative singularity is not an improbable event. With some productivity-diminishing innovations, such as those involving environmental conservation technologies, network transformation under inelastic network can encounter a state that some commodity cannot be produced in net. Finally, as regards the matter of industrial policy, whether to promote a portfolio of projects, or rather to take a selective policy, depends on the synergism inherent in the production network where the elasticity of substitution plays the important role.

question: What role do auxiliary variables play in evaluating causal effects?
answer: Auxiliary variables, such as intermediate variables, are crucial for evaluating causal effects and understanding the data-generating process. They help improve the estimation accuracy of causal effects by providing additional information that can be used in mediation analysis and other statistical methods.

evidence.text:
## Introduction
## Background

Auxiliary variables are those that are not considered to be of interest in themselves but help us to evaluate causal effects and/or understand the data-generating process in practical studies. For example, an intermediate variable is often considered an auxiliary variable because it is used to evaluate causal effects (Pearl 2001, 2009), to understand the data-generating process in the context of mediation analysis (Baron and Kenny 1986; Imai et al. 2011; Mackinnon 2008) and to improve the estimation accuracy of causal effects (Cox 1960; Hayashi and Kuroki 2014).

In the context of linear structural equation models, this paper focuses on estimating causal effects using intermediate variables. For cases in which the data-generating process for random variables can be described by nonparametric structural equation models and the corresponding directed acyclic graph, Pearl (2009) provided the front-door criterion as the identification condition for causal effects based on intermediate variables. In addition, in the framework of linear structural equation models, Kuroki (2000), Nanmo and Kuroki

[^0](2021), and Kuroki and Tezuka (2023) formulated the exact variance of causal effects based on the front-door criterion. Furthermore, Kuroki and Cai (2004), Hui and Zhongguo (2008), and Ramsahai (2012) compared some identification conditions in terms of the asymptotic estimation accuracy of causal effects. On the other hand, under the assumption that a treatment variable is associated with a response variable through a univariate intermediate variable, from the viewpoint of the asymptotic estimation accuracy, Cox (1960) showed that the estimation accuracy of the regression coefficient of the treatment variable on the response variable in the single linear regression model can be improved by using a joint linear regression model based on the response variable and the intermediate variable. In addition, Kuroki and Hayashi (2014) and Hayashi and Kuroki (2014) derived the same results as Cox (1960) in terms of the exact variance of causal effects. Gupta, Lipton, and Childers (2021) derived the same results as Kuroki and Hayashi (2014) and Hayashi and Kuroki (2014) for cases in which a multivariate intermediate variable is available.

In existing studies, it is noted that causal effects can be estimated by standard statistical estimation methods, e.g., the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) method and the ordinary least squares (OLS) method. Thus, many covariates affect both the treatment variable and the response variable and are highly correlated with each other in reality. This situation leads to a multicollinearity problem, which decreases the estimation accuracy of the causal effects and leads to the formulation of an unreliable plan that prevents us from conducting appropriate policy decision-making. In addition, when the sample size is smaller than the number of explanatory variables in the regression analysis, highdimensional data analysis also suffers from multicollinearity problems, which cause overfitting and interfere with obtaining admissible solutions for regression coefficients. Recently, due to the development of technological advances in collecting data with many variables to better understand a given phenomenon of interest, the multicollinearity problem has become serious in many domains. To overcome this difficulty, numerous kinds of variable selection techniques based on penalized regression analysis, e.g., the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), adaptive LASSO, and Elastic Net, have been proposed by many statistical and AI researchers and practitioners (Bühlmann and


[^0]:    Copyright (c) 2025, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved.

van de Geer 2011; Efron et al. 2004; Tibshirani 1996; Van et al. 2014; Zou 2006; Zou and Hastie 2005). However, the present countermeasures against the multicollinearity problem are formulated independently of the problem of identifying causal effects. Thus, although stable results of regression analysis may be derived by these countermeasures from the viewpoint of prediction, they may yield a seriously biased estimate of the causal effect. Nanmo and Kuroki (2022) proposed partially adaptive $\mathrm{L}_{p}$-penalized multiple regression analysis ( $\mathrm{PAL}_{p} \mathrm{MA}$ ) based on the back-door criterion to overcome these drawbacks. However, because of the formulation of $\mathrm{PAL}_{p} \mathrm{MA}$, this method is not applicable to situations where a sufficient set of confounders is not available. In addition, $\mathrm{PAL}_{p} \mathrm{MA}$ selects a set of covariates to derive a consistent or less biased estimator of causal effects but does not consider the estimation accuracy of the causal effects.

question: What is the main idea behind the Chapman-Enskog expansion for the Boltzmann equation?
answer: The main idea behind the Chapman-Enskog expansion is based on two important observations about the Boltzmann equation: that stationary states of collision integral are space-varying boosted thermal states, and that collision integral conserves density of particles, momentum, and energy.

evidence.text:
# 3 Chapman-Enskog theory for the Boltzmann equation 

ChE expansion [2-4] was the first theory, which successfully connected microscopic dynamics of Boltzmann equation to the equations of hydrodynamics. It was developed by S. Chapman and D. Enskog more than one hundred years ago. Originally formulated for three-dimensional classical gas, it has uncovered not only the universal NS equations but also provided quantative predicitions for transport coefficients in terms of explicit integral equations. In this section we write a summary of this classic result. It provides context for the generalization of the method to quantum integrable theories developed in the next section.

We start with the Boltzmann equation written as

$$
\partial_{t} \rho+v \partial_{x} \rho=I_{B}[\rho]
$$

where $\rho(x, v)$ is one-particle distribution function on a phase space and $I_{B}[\rho]$ is the Boltzmann collision integral, a nonlinear functional of the $\rho$ distribution. For the sake of this discussion, we do not discuss the of the operator $I_{B}$ and consider one-dimensional system. The main idea behind ChE expansion is based on two important observations about the Boltzmann equation:

- The only stationary states of collision integral $I_{B}[\rho]$ are space-varying boosted thermal states. For classical gas these are given by boosted Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions

$$
\rho_{\mathrm{bth}}(x, v)=\frac{\varrho(x)}{\sqrt{2 \pi T(x)}} \exp \left(-\frac{(v-u(x))^{2}}{2 T(x)}\right)
$$

where $\varrho(x), u(x), T(x)$ are density, velocity and temperature of the gas at the point $x$, respectively. We have set $m=1$ and $k_{B}=1$. The process of relaxation from a generic state towards local boosted thermal states happens on a characteristic relaxation time-scale $\tau_{I_{B}}$, which depends on the interaction potential between particles encoded in collision integral $I_{B}[\rho]$ and on the state itself.
We emphasize here that in general the states (66) are stationary states of collision integral term only and some dynamics is generated by the streaming term $v \partial_{x} \rho$. Global equilibrium states of (65) correspond to boosted thermal states with hydrodynamic fields uniform in space $\varrho(x), u(x), T(x)=$ const, for which the streaming term vanishes as well.

- Collision integral conserves density of particles, momentum and energy. This is equivalent to the existence of three collision invariants $\mathscr{G}_{0}(v)=1, \mathscr{G}_{1}(v)=v, \mathscr{G}_{2}(v)=\frac{1}{2} v^{2}$, such that

$$
\int \mathrm{d} v \mathscr{G}_{a}(v) I_{B}[\rho](v)=0, \quad a=0,1,2
$$

Naturally, collision invariants can be directly related to hydrodynamic fields $\varrho(x), u(x)$, $e(x)$, which are given by

$$
\varrho(x)=\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{0}\right\rangle, \quad u(x)=\frac{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{1}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{0}\right\rangle}, \quad e(x)=\frac{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{2}\right\rangle}{\left\langle\mathscr{E}_{0}\right\rangle}-\frac{1}{2} u(x)^{2}
$$

where $\langle\cdot\rangle$ denotes average over velocities with respect to $\rho$. What is more, the temperature field is simply given by $e(x)=\frac{1}{2} T(x)$, assuming that the system is in local thermodynamic equilibrium. We collectively denote the hydrodynamic fields as $\left\{\varrho_{a}(x, t)\right\}$.

The observations listed above point towards the existence of two characteristic timescales in the system. Starting from an initial distribution, on a timescale given by $\tau_{I_{B}}$ the system will locally thermalize, such that it can be described by hydrodynamic fields $\varrho(x), u(x)$ and $T(x)$. On a longer, hydrodynamic timescale $\tau_{\mathrm{h}}$ the streaming term will be dominant and these fields will evolve according to the standard equations of hydrodynamics. In order to see their structure explicitly, we multiply the Boltzmann equation with collision invariants and integrate over $\mathrm{d} v$, similarly as in Sec. 2.5. We recover three equations which read

$$
\begin{aligned}
& \partial_{t} \varrho+\partial_{x}(\varrho u)=0, \quad \partial_{t}(\varrho u)+\partial_{x}\left(\varrho u^{2}+\mathcal{P}\right)=0 \\
& \partial_{t}(\varrho e)+\partial_{x}(u \varrho e+\mathcal{J})+\mathcal{P} \partial_{x} u=0
\end{aligned}
$$

with dynamical pressure and heat current

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{P} & =\int \mathrm{d} v(v-u) v \rho(v) \\
\mathcal{J} & =\frac{1}{2} \int \mathrm{~d} v(v-u)^{3} \rho(v)
\end{aligned}
$$

The hydrodynamic equations presented above are not closed as the dynamical pressure and heat current depend on the whole distribution $\rho$, not only on its first three moments (or equivalently, on hydrodynamic fields). The closure of equation will be the central point of the ChE expansion procedure, which we now discuss.

The two observations about Boltzmann equation listed before can be turned into perturbative expansion. To formally motivate it, we start with estimating the order of terms in (65). We assume that the state varies at a hydrodynamic length-scale $l_{\mathrm{h}}$ and the particles have some characteristic velocity $\bar{v}$. Then the hydrodynamic timescale associated to the streaming term is $\tau_{\mathrm{h}}=l_{\mathrm{h}} / \bar{v}$. In the dimensionless units $\bar{x}=x / l_{\mathrm{h}}, \bar{t}=t / \tau_{\mathrm{h}}, \bar{v}=v / \bar{v}$ and explicitly extracting the timescale from collision term $\bar{I}_{B}=\frac{1}{\tau_{I_{B}}} I_{B}$ we can write Boltzmann equation as

$$
\partial_{t} \rho+\bar{v} \partial_{x} \rho=\frac{1}{\delta} \bar{I}_{B}[\rho]
$$

where $\delta=\tau_{I_{B}} / \tau_{\mathrm{h}}$ defines the so-called Knudsen number [2]. We wish to address hydrodynamic limit of slow (in comparison to microscopic scales) space and time variation, hence Knudsen number is considered to be small $\delta \ll 1$. The form of Boltzmann equation (72) suggests perturbative solution in $\delta$ and indeed, in the ChE method we essentially assume that

$$
\rho(x, v ; t)=\rho^{(0)}(x, v ; t)\left(1-\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \delta^{n} \rho^{(n)}(x, v ; t)\right)
$$

However, the expansion cannot be considered to be fully systematic as it is supplemented by additional assumptions which we will discuss now. Before that and in what follows we drop tildes from the notation.

Firstly, the crucial aspect of the method is the assumption about the time evolution of distribution $\rho$. We assume that it depends on time through three time-dependent hydrodynamic fields collectively denoted $\left\{\varrho_{a}(x, t)\right\}$,

$$
\rho(x, v ; t) \rightarrow \rho(x, v \mid\left\{\varrho_{a}(x, t)\right\})
$$

Moreover, there is an assumption about expansion which can be formulated as the following conditions

$$
\left\langle\mathscr{G}_{a}\right\rangle=\int \mathrm{d} v \mathscr{G}_{a}(v) \rho^{(0)}(x, v), \quad 0=\int \mathrm{d} v \rho^{(0)}(x, v) \mathscr{G}_{a}(v) \rho^{(n)}(x, v)=\left(\mathscr{G}_{a} \mid \rho^{(n)}\right)
$$

for $n \geq 1$, which means that the averages of collision invariants (and in consequence, hydrodynamic fields) are given solely by the zeroth order contribution to the distribution $\rho^{(0)}$. In other words, we essentially assume that the hydrodynamic fields are not expanded in $\delta$ and corrections $\left\{\rho^{(n)}\right\}_{n \geq 1}$ are orthogonal to collision invariants (in the sense of the hydrodynamic inner product $(\cdot \cdot \cdot)$, see (26), note that for classical particles $\mathcal{C}=\rho$ ). However, we crucially assume that dynamical pressure and heat current (70) do admit expansion in $\delta$

$$
\mathcal{P}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \delta^{n} \mathcal{P}^{(n)}, \quad \mathcal{J}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \delta^{n} \mathcal{J}^{(n)}
$$

Expanding now the problem to different orders in $\delta$ yields hydrodynamic equations at different scales.

question: In what ways are auditory LLMs used for evaluating text-to-speech models?
answer: Auditory LLMs are used in evaluating text-to-speech models by predicting quantitative metrics like MOS and SIM, conducting A/B testing between samples, and providing natural-language-based evaluations on aspects such as noisiness and distortion.

evidence.text:
## I. InTRODUCTION

With the rapid development of generative models, the task of automatic speech quality assessment has become increasingly more important, for purposes from training data filtering to evaluating text-to-speech (TTS) models [1]-[5]. However, considering the variety of aspects humans take into account in listening tests, it is challenging for small models trained for the end-to-end prediction of mean opinion score (MOS) [2], [3] and speaker similarity score (SIM) [6] to achieve as comprehensive and interpretable speech quality assessment as humans. Recently, auditory large language models (LLMs) [7][12] have been developed and demonstrated remarkable performance across a variety of speech perception and understanding tasks [13][16], which are thus possible to achieve evidence-based and multiperspective speech quality assessment using natural language.

In this paper, we propose to enhance existing auditory LLMs with the ability to evaluate speech quality from two key perspectives: MOS and SIM. Under an LLM multitask setting empowered by task-specific prompts, the auditory LLMs are evaluated using four speech quality evaluation tasks. These tasks include the predictions of real-valued quantitative metrics like MOS and SIM and an A/B testing to choose the better one from two speech samples, which are commonly used in TTS performance evaluation. Furthermore, we explore natural-language-based speech quality evaluation tasks, such as speech descriptions from the perspectives of noisiness, distortion, discontinuity, and overall quality. These tasks leverage the key strengths of the LLM backbone and are unique abilities of auditory LLMs. Experimental results on the widely used NISQA, BVCC,

SOMOS and VoxSim show that finetuned auditory LLMs can serve as a versatile evaluation model for speech quality, outperforming a strong self-supervised learning (SSL) baseline and being competitive to state-of-the-art results achieved using separate small models.

question: Why is there a need for an On-Chain Credit Risk Score in DeFi?
answer: An On-Chain Credit Risk Score (OCCR Score) is needed in DeFi to provide an objective measure of a wallet's creditworthiness by integrating historical performance with current status and future predictions. This score helps quantify the probability of default when opening borrow positions within the ecosystem, enabling more informed lending decisions based on data-driven risk assessments.

evidence.text:
# 1 Introduction 

The ongoing digital revolution is driving a profound transformation in the financial sector. A key development in this evolution is decentralized finance ( DeFi ), which uses blockchain technology to facilitate open and permissionless financial services (Sahu and Kumar, 2024). DeFi signifies a paradigm shift in financial systems that reshapes the future of global finance. DeFi provides financial services without the intervention of any centralized intermediaries. They operate mainly as automated protocols on a blockchain (Doerr et al., 2021). Although much more new in concept, DeFi is a fast-growing market for quick and safe interaction between lenders and borrowers. It is one of the best ways to seamlessly perform verifiable cross-border transactions in a much faster way compared to Traditional Finance. Numerous avenues can be explored to make DeFi more robust and capital-efficient. However, for such explorations, we need to understand the creditworthiness of each user. It should be noted that 'user' means the specific wallet interacting with the DeFi ecosystem, and in this article, user and wallet are used interchangeably.

Unlike conventional credit scoring, which depends on centralized credit bureaus and financial history of an user, DeFi credit scoring leverages on-chain data and smart contract interactions to evaluate an user's borrowing and repayment behavior. Credit risk scoring is a systematic process used to assess the risk involved in a user's creditworthiness by analyzing their on-chain transaction history, repayment behavior, outstanding liabilities, and other relevant economic indicators. This analytical approach enables financial institutions to quantify the probability of default, facilitating data-driven risk assessment and informed lending decisions (Moghe and Johri, n.d.). An 'On-Chain Credit Risk Score (OCCR Score)' for a wallet might be an answer to quantifying the credit risk of the particular wallet in DeFi ecosystem. Through the OCCR Score of a wallet, we have estimated the probability that the particular wallet may face liquidation when any borrow position is opened. Throughout the paper, we have used borrow positions and loans interchangeably.

There are different ways to give credit scores to users in the current TradFi landscape, but this is not very prevalent in DeFi. However, there have been previous attempts to measure the creditworthiness of a wallet, including those by Cred (CRED Protocol, n.d.), Credit Data Alliance (CreDA) (CreDA, 2022), Credit scoring of Aave accounts (Wolf et al., 2022) and Levon (Block Analitica, n.d.). The main limitation of these existing credit scoring models is the absence of a comprehensive framework that integrates historical, current, and future predictive scenarios. Lemma 3.1. $H: \mathbb{R}^{d} \times \mathbb{R}^{d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, defined in (1.2) is concave-convex (i.e. $H(\cdot, p)$ is convex for all $p \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ and $H(x, \cdot)$ is convex for all $x \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ ) if and only $L$ is jointly convex.

From this lemma we see that the global existence of classical solutions to the Hamilton-Jacobi equation (1.1) in the class $C_{\mathrm{loc}}^{1,1}$, from the Hamiltonian point of view, is intimately linked to the concave-convex properties of $H$ and convexity of the final condition $G$.

Definition 3.2. For a square matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$, we define the symmetric matrix

$$
\operatorname{Re} A:=\frac{1}{2}\left(A+A^{\top}\right)
$$

For a symmetric matrix $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$, we denote by $\lambda_{\min }(A)$ and $\lambda_{\max }(A)$ its smallest and largest eigenvalues, respectively.

$$
\alpha:=\inf _{\substack{(x, p, w) \in \mathbb{R}^{3 d} \\\|w\|=1}} \frac{w^{\top} \operatorname{Re} \partial_{x p} H(x, p) w+\sqrt{\left(w^{\top} \operatorname{Re} \partial_{x p} H(x, y) w\right)^{2}-\left(w^{\top} \partial_{p p} H(x, p) w\right)\left(w^{\top} \partial_{x x} H(x, p) w\right)}}{\left.\|w\|=1\right.} \frac{w^{\top} \operatorname{Re} \partial_{x p} H(x, p) w+\sqrt{\left(w^{\top} \operatorname{Re} \partial_{x p} H(x, p) w\right)^{2}-\left(w^{\top} \partial_{p p} H(x, p) w\right)\left(w^{\top} \partial_{x x} H(x, p) w\right)}}}{w^{\top} \partial_{p p} H(x, p) w}

question: Why is it important to consider articulatory patterns in assessing dysarthria severity?
answer: Considering articulatory patterns is important because they have different difficulty levels that can influence the performance of models used to assess dysarthria severity. Understanding these patterns helps improve model accuracy.

evidence.text:
## V. CONCLUSION

This study demonstrates that the proposed multi-modality model, which integrates both speech and text, provides a significant advantage over speech-only model in detecting and assessing dysarthria. By leveraging the complementary strengths of both acoustic and linguistic knowledge, this multi-modality model achieves greater accuracy and consistency, particularly when dealing with the complex phonetic properties associated with dysarthric speech. Notably, in speaker-independent settings which are more preferred in clinical environment, this model shows higher accuracies of $93.20 \%$ and $51.97 \%$ in dysarthric detection and severity assessment, respectively. Additionally, this study provides insights into the influence of articulatory patterns having different difficulty levels, on the performance of the model. In the future work, the focus will be on employing different strategies to combine various speech and text representations towards developing more robust models for diagnosis of dysarthria.

question: What happens to the empirical measure of neurons' membrane potentials as \( N \rightarrow \infty \)?
answer: As \( N \rightarrow \infty \), the empirical measure of the neurons' membrane potentials converges to the solution of a spatially-extended mean-field partial differential equation (PDE).
